Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan, except for three verses from His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ to the end of them [Yunus: 94–96]. Thus al-Qurtubi related it in his tafsir from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It is related from Muqatil that it is Meccan except for two verses, namely His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus: 94], for it was revealed in Medina.

It is related from al-Kalbi that it is Meccan except for His saying: ﴿And among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40], for it was revealed in Medina.

It is related from al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAta' and Jabir that it is Meccan without any exception.

Al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Surat Yunus was revealed in Mecca.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Sirin, who said: Surat Yunus came after the seventh (surah).

Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah has given me the Ra'iyat (the surahs beginning with Alif Lam Ra) to the Ta'sin (the surahs beginning with Ta Sin) in place of the Injil."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related in al-Musannaf from al-Ahnaf, who said: I prayed behind ʿUmar at dawn, and he recited Yunus, Hud and others.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: (Alif Lam Ra). The discussion of these letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs has already been dealt with fully at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it, as what was said there suffices.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, Khalaf and others read it with imalah (inclination of the vowel).

A group read it without imalah. It has been said that the meaning of (Alif Lam Ra) is: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing" (Ana Allahu ara).

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq inclining to this view, because Sibawayh related something similar from the Arabs, and he recited:

"With goodness, goodnesses; and if evil, then..."

meaning: and if evil, then (it is) evil.

Al-Hasan and ʿIkrimah said that (Alif Lam Ra) is an oath. Sa'id related from Qatadah that (Alif Lam Ra) is the name of the surah. It has been said other than that, which involves artificiality, since the knowledge of what Allah has reserved for Himself is unknown. The reciters agree that (Alif Lam Ra) is not a verse, and that Ta Ha is a verse. In Abu ʿAmr al-Dani's Muqni', the ones who count Ta Ha as a verse are the Kufans alone. It has been said: perhaps the difference is that (Alif Lam Ra) does not match the endings of the verses that follow it. The indication in His saying: (Those) refers to what the surah contains of verses, and the distancing is for magnification; the demonstrative is the subject and its predicate is what follows it.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: He meant the Torah, the Injil and the rest of the earlier Books, for (Those) is a demonstrative for an absent feminine referent. It has been said: (Those) has the meaning of (These): i.e., these are the verses of the Wise Book, which is the Qur'an. That the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an is supported by the fact that no mention of the earlier Books has preceded, and that "the Wise" is among the attributes of the Qur'an and not of anything else. The Wise (al-Hakim) means the one made firm (al-muhkam) with regard to the lawful and unlawful, the limits and the rulings; this was said by Abu ʿUbaydah and others. It has also been said that al-Hakim means the one who judges (al-hakim), so it is a fa'il-form (fa'il) in the sense of fa'il, as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, that it might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It has been said that al-Hakim means the one judged, so it is a fa'il-form in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., Allah has judged in it with justice and benevolence; this was said by al-Hasan and others. It has been said that al-Hakim means the possessor of wisdom, because it includes it.

The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people﴾ is for the denial of wonder, together with what it conveys of reproach and rebuke. The subject of kana (was) is ﴿that We revealed﴾ and its predicate is (a wonder), i.e., was Our revelation a wonder to the people?

Ibn Mas'ud read "ʿajabun" (a wonder) as the subject of kana, with kana being complete (taammah), and ﴿that We revealed﴾ is a substitute for (ʿajabun).

It is read with a sukun on the jim of "rajul" (man) in His saying: ﴿to a man from among them﴾, i.e., from their kind. There is nothing in this revelation to a man of their kind that requires wonder, for no one but one of their kind would mix with the kind, guide them and inform them from Allah, the Glorified; and if he were not of their kind, he would be of the angels or of the jinn, and the intended purpose of sending would then be impossible, for they would not be at ease with him nor see him. Even if we suppose that he took a form for them and appeared, either he would appear in a form other than the human species, which is more frightening to their hearts and further from their intimacy, or in human form, and then they must deny that he was originally not human. This is if the wonder was on their part because he is of their kind. If the wonder was because he is an orphan or poor, that does not prevent one who is such from combining the qualities of goodness and nobility that others do not combine, and reaching such a degree of perfection in attributes that the rich or the non-orphan falls short of it. Before Allah chose him for prophethood, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had among the Quraysh qualities of perfection more famous than the sun and more manifest than the daylight, so much so that they used to call him al-Amin (the Trustworthy).

His saying: ﴿that warn the people﴾ is in a position of accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "that you warn the people." It has been said that it is explanatory (mufassirah), since revelation contains the meaning of saying. It has been said that it is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form.

His saying: ﴿a sure standing (qadam sidq)﴾ means a station of truth (manzil sidq). Al-Zajjaj said: a high rank.

From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"For you is a qadam that people do not deny, whose station with high lineage has overflowed the sea."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the qadam is the one who precedes in nobility. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Kisa'i said: every precedence, whether of good or evil, is among the Arabs a qadam; one says: so-and-so has a qadam in Islam, and for him with me is a qadam of truth, a qadam of good, a qadam of evil. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjaj:

"The sons of al-ʿAwwam slipped from the family of al-Hakam, and left the kingdom to a lord of precedence (dhu qadam)."

Tha'lab said: the qadam is everything of good that you have sent forward. Ibn al-Anbari said: qadam is a metaphor for an action in which there is no delay or slowness. Qatadah said: a righteous predecessor (salaf sidq). Al-Rabi' said: a true reward (thawab sidq). Al-Hasan said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: his (ﷺ) qadam is in the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud). Muqatil said: deeds they sent forward, and Ibn Jarir chose this. From this is the saying of al-Wadah:

"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take for yourself a qadam that will save you on the day of dispute and slipping."

Other than what has preceded has been said, which needs no lengthy citation.

His saying: ﴿The disbelievers said: "Indeed, this is clearly a magician."﴾

Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read "lasahir" (a magician), on the basis that they meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by the demonstrative.

The rest read "lasihr" (sorcery), on the basis that they meant the Qur'an. The meaning of sihr has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The clause ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ is resumptive, as if it were said: what did they do after the wonderment? Al-Qaffal said: there is an ellipsis, and the estimate is: when he warned them, the disbelievers said that.

Then Allah, the Glorified, brought a statement by which He nullifies the wonder that arose in the disbelievers from the revelation to a man from among them. He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾, i.e., He who has this great power, which minds are too narrow to conceive, how can His sending a messenger from their own kind to the people be a cause for wonder, while the disbelievers themselves acknowledge that? How then do they not acknowledge the validity of this message through this messenger? The tafsir of this verse has already been given in al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne﴾, so we will not repeat it here. Then He mentioned what indicates greater power and great majesty, saying: ﴿He arranges the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾. The conjunction is omitted, because the clause (He arranges) is like an explanation and detail of what precedes it. It has been said that it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "istawa" (established). It has been said that it is resumptive, an answer to an implied question. The root meaning of tadbir is looking at the backs (adbar) of affairs and their consequences, so that they occur in an acceptable manner.

Mujahid said: He decrees it and determines it alone. It has been said: He sends the affair. It has been said: He sends down the affair. It has been said: He commands it and executes it. The meanings are close. Its derivation is from al-dubur (the back), and al-amr means the matter, which is the states of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, the Throne, and the rest of creation.

Al-Zajjaj said: The disbelievers addressed by this verse used to say: the idols are our intercessors with Allah. So Allah refuted them by saying that no one may intercede with Him for anything except after His permission, because He knows best the place of wisdom and correctness.

The meaning of intercession has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. In this there is a statement of His sole authority over affairs in everything, glorified and exalted is He. The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ refers to the doer of these things, of creation and arrangement, i.e., the One who did these great things is Allah your Lord. The demonstrative is the subject, its predicate is the noble name, and "your Lord" is a substitute for it, or an explanation of it, or a second predicate. In this sentence there is additional emphasis on His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Then He commanded them to worship Him, after showing them that He alone deserves it rather than anything else, for His wondrous making and great power. How then do they worship inanimate things that do not hear, do not see, neither benefit nor harm? The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ is for denial, reproach and rebuke, for whoever has the least remembrance and the slightest consideration knows this and it is not hidden from him.

Then He showed them what would be the end of their affair after the worldly life, saying: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾. In this there is a threat and warning that is not hidden. The accusative of (promise of Allah) is as a verbal noun, because in His saying "To Him is your return, all of you" there is the meaning of a promise; or it is governed by a verb understood. The intended meaning of return is returning to Him, glorified, either by death, or by resurrection, or by both. Then He emphasized that promise by saying: ﴿truly﴾, which is an emphasis upon an emphasis, so there is in the speech such firmness as is the utmost in that.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "The promise of Allah is true" as a new sentence.

Then the Glorified explained what preceded by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾, i.e., this is His manner: He begins His creation from dust, then returns it to dust; or the meaning of repetition is the recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

Mujahid said: He brings it into being, then causes it to die, then revives it for resurrection. It has been said: He brings it into being from water, then repeats it from state to state.

Yazid ibn al-Qaʻqaʻ read "annahu yabda'u al-khalq" with a fatha on the hamzah, so the clause is in the accusative position governed by what "promise of Allah" governs: i.e., He promised you that He originates creation then repeats it. It is also permissible that the estimate be "because He originates creation." Al-Farra' permitted that "anna" be in the nominative position, so that it is the subject. Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Tha'lab said: the estimate is: "truly, His originating the creation (is so)."

Then He mentioned the ultimate purpose of the repetition, saying: ﴿that He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾, i.e., with the justice in which there is no injustice. ﴿And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. It is possible that the second relative clause is conjoined to the first relative clause, i.e., that He may recompense those who believed and recompense those who disbelieved; and the clause "for them is a drink of scalding water" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, it and what is conjoined to it: i.e., and a painful punishment, and the estimate is thus: He recompenses those who disbelieved in the state in which they have this drink and this punishment. But this is problematic, because this drink and this painful punishment are themselves part of the recompense. It may be said that the relative pronoun in "those who disbelieved" is a subject and what follows it is its predicate, so it is not conjoined to the first conjoined element. The "bi" in "because they used to disbelieve" is causal, i.e., because of their disbelief. "Hamim" is hot water, and anything heated among the Arabs is hamim.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Ra," that he said: they are openings of names from the names of Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, and Ibn al-Najjar in his *Tarikh*, narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said concerning His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book.﴾ "I am Allah, I see."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak something similar as well.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "It means this."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "The Books that came before the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a Messenger, the Arabs, or some of them, denied this, and they said: "Allah is too great for His Messenger to be a human being like Muhammad." So Allah revealed: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We have revealed to a man from among them...﴾ up to His words: ﴿they will believe﴾, and ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed...﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7], the verse. When Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the proof against them, they said: "If he is a human being, then someone other than Muhammad would have been more worthy of the Message." ﴿Why was this Qur'an not revealed to a great man from one of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 31], meaning: more noble than Muhammad. They meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. So Allah revealed in reply to them: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 32], the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) concerning His words: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they will have a firm footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾ that he said: "It is what preceded for them of happiness in the first Remembrance (al-Dhikr al-Awwal, the primordial Record)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also, who said: "A good reward for what they had sent forward of their deeds."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The qadam is the deed which they sent forward."

Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And We write down what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin 12], and "the traces" are their walking places.

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked between two pillars of their mosque, then said: "This is a written trace."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His words: ﴿a firm footing (qadam sidq)﴾ that he said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) intercedes for them."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

al-Hakim narrated and declared authentic (sahhahahu), from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Salaf sidq" (a true predecessor).

The narrations from the Successors (tabi'un) and others on this are numerous, and we have already mentioned most of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿He governs the affair﴾ that he said: "He decrees it alone." And concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾ he said: "He gives it life, then makes it die, then gives it life again."

The meaning of intercession has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. In this there is a statement of His sole authority over affairs in everything, glorified and exalted is He. The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ refers to the doer of these things, of creation and arrangement, i.e., the One who did these great things is Allah your Lord. The demonstrative is the subject, its predicate is the noble name, and "your Lord" is a substitute for it, or an explanation of it, or a second predicate. In this sentence there is additional emphasis on His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Then He commanded them to worship Him, after showing them that He alone deserves it rather than anything else, for His wondrous making and great power. How then do they worship inanimate things that do not hear, do not see, neither benefit nor harm? The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ is for denial, reproach and rebuke, for whoever has the least remembrance and the slightest consideration knows this and it is not hidden from him.

Then He showed them what would be the end of their affair after the worldly life, saying: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾. In this there is a threat and warning that is not hidden. The accusative of (promise of Allah) is as a verbal noun, because in His saying "To Him is your return, all of you" there is the meaning of a promise; or it is governed by a verb understood. The intended meaning of return is returning to Him, glorified, either by death, or by resurrection, or by both. Then He emphasized that promise by saying: ﴿truly﴾, which is an emphasis upon an emphasis, so there is in the speech such firmness as is the utmost in that.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "The promise of Allah is true" as a new sentence.

Then the Glorified explained what preceded by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾, i.e., this is His manner: He begins His creation from dust, then returns it to dust; or the meaning of repetition is the recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

Mujahid said: He brings it into being, then causes it to die, then revives it for resurrection. It has been said: He brings it into being from water, then repeats it from state to state.

Yazid ibn al-Qaʻqaʻ read "annahu yabda'u al-khalq" with a fatha on the hamzah, so the clause is in the accusative position governed by what "promise of Allah" governs: i.e., He promised you that He originates creation then repeats it. It is also permissible that the estimate be "because He originates creation." Al-Farra' permitted that "anna" be in the nominative position, so that it is the subject. Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Tha'lab said: the estimate is: "truly, His originating the creation (is so)."

Then He mentioned the ultimate purpose of the repetition, saying: ﴿that He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾, i.e., with the justice in which there is no injustice. ﴿And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. It is possible that the second relative clause is conjoined to the first relative clause, i.e., that He may recompense those who believed and recompense those who disbelieved; and the clause "for them is a drink of scalding water" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, it and what is conjoined to it: i.e., and a painful punishment, and the estimate is thus: He recompenses those who disbelieved in the state in which they have this drink and this punishment. But this is problematic, because this drink and this painful punishment are themselves part of the recompense. It may be said that the relative pronoun in "those who disbelieved" is a subject and what follows it is its predicate, so it is not conjoined to the first conjoined element. The "bi" in "because they used to disbelieve" is causal, i.e., because of their disbelief. "Hamim" is hot water, and anything heated among the Arabs is hamim.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Ra," that he said: they are openings of names from the names of Allah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, and Ibn al-Najjar in his *Tarikh*, narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said concerning His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book.﴾ "I am Allah, I see."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak something similar as well.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "It means this."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "The Books that came before the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a Messenger, the Arabs, or some of them, denied this, and they said: "Allah is too great for His Messenger to be a human being like Muhammad." So Allah revealed: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We have revealed to a man from among them...﴾ up to His words: ﴿they will believe﴾, and ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed...﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7], the verse. When Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the proof against them, they said: "If he is a human being, then someone other than Muhammad would have been more worthy of the Message." ﴿Why was this Qur'an not revealed to a great man from one of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 31], meaning: more noble than Muhammad. They meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. So Allah revealed in reply to them: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 32], the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also, who said: "A good reward for what they had sent forward of their deeds."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The qadam is the deed which they sent forward."

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked between two pillars of their mosque, then said: "This is a written trace."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His words: ﴿a firm footing (qadam sidq)﴾ that he said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) intercedes for them."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

al-Hakim narrated and declared authentic (sahhahahu), from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Salaf sidq" (a true predecessor).

The narrations from the Successors (tabi'un) and others on this are numerous, and we have already mentioned most of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿He governs the affair﴾ that he said: "He decrees it alone." * *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: (Alif Lam Ra). The discussion of these letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs has already been dealt with fully at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it, as what was said there suffices.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, Khalaf and others read it with imalah (inclination of the vowel).

A group read it without imalah. It has been said that the meaning of (Alif Lam Ra) is: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing" (Ana Allahu ara).

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq inclining to this view, because Sibawayh related something similar from the Arabs, and he recited:

"With goodness, goodnesses; and if evil, then..."

meaning: and if evil, then (it is) evil.

Al-Hasan and ʿIkrimah said that (Alif Lam Ra) is an oath. Sa'id related from Qatadah that (Alif Lam Ra) is the name of the surah. It has been said other than that, which involves artificiality, since the knowledge of what Allah has reserved for Himself is unknown. The reciters agree that (Alif Lam Ra) is not a verse, and that Ta Ha is a verse. In Abu ʿAmr al-Dani's Muqni', the ones who count Ta Ha as a verse are the Kufans alone. It has been said: perhaps the difference is that (Alif Lam Ra) does not match the endings of the verses that follow it. The indication in His saying: (Those) refers to what the surah contains of verses, and the distancing is for magnification; the demonstrative is the subject and its predicate is what follows it.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: He meant the Torah, the Injil and the rest of the earlier Books, for (Those) is a demonstrative for an absent feminine referent. It has been said: (Those) has the meaning of (These): i.e., these are the verses of the Wise Book, which is the Qur'an. That the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an is supported by the fact that no mention of the earlier Books has preceded, and that "the Wise" is among the attributes of the Qur'an and not of anything else. The Wise (al-Hakim) means the one made firm (al-muhkam) with regard to the lawful and unlawful, the limits and the rulings; this was said by Abu ʿUbaydah and others. It has also been said that al-Hakim means the one who judges (al-hakim), so it is a fa'il-form (fa'il) in the sense of fa'il, as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, that it might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It has been said that al-Hakim means the one judged, so it is a fa'il-form in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., Allah has judged in it with justice and benevolence; this was said by al-Hasan and others. It has been said that al-Hakim means the possessor of wisdom, because it includes it.

The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people﴾ is for the denial of wonder, together with what it conveys of reproach and rebuke. The subject of kana (was) is ﴿that We revealed﴾ and its predicate is (a wonder), i.e., was Our revelation a wonder to the people?

Ibn Mas'ud read "ʿajabun" (a wonder) as the subject of kana, with kana being complete (taammah), and ﴿that We revealed﴾ is a substitute for (ʿajabun).

It is read with a sukun on the jim of "rajul" (man) in His saying: ﴿to a man from among them﴾, i.e., from their kind. There is nothing in this revelation to a man of their kind that requires wonder, for no one but one of their kind would mix with the kind, guide them and inform them from Allah, the Glorified; and if he were not of their kind, he would be of the angels or of the jinn, and the intended purpose of sending would then be impossible, for they would not be at ease with him nor see him. Even if we suppose that he took a form for them and appeared, either he would appear in a form other than the human species, which is more frightening to their hearts and further from their intimacy, or in human form, and then they must deny that he was originally not human. This is if the wonder was on their part because he is of their kind. If the wonder was because he is an orphan or poor, that does not prevent one who is such from combining the qualities of goodness and nobility that others do not combine, and reaching such a degree of perfection in attributes that the rich or the non-orphan falls short of it. Before Allah chose him for prophethood, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had among the Quraysh qualities of perfection more famous than the sun and more manifest than the daylight, so much so that they used to call him al-Amin (the Trustworthy).

His saying: ﴿that warn the people﴾ is in a position of accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "that you warn the people." It has been said that it is explanatory (mufassirah), since revelation contains the meaning of saying. It has been said that it is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form.

His saying: ﴿a sure standing (qadam sidq)﴾ means a station of truth (manzil sidq). Al-Zajjaj said: a high rank.

From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"For you is a qadam that people do not deny, whose station with high lineage has overflowed the sea."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the qadam is the one who precedes in nobility. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Kisa'i said: every precedence, whether of good or evil, is among the Arabs a qadam; one says: so-and-so has a qadam in Islam, and for him with me is a qadam of truth, a qadam of good, a qadam of evil. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjaj:

"The sons of al-ʿAwwam slipped from the family of al-Hakam, and left the kingdom to a lord of precedence (dhu qadam)."

Tha'lab said: the qadam is everything of good that you have sent forward. Ibn al-Anbari said: qadam is a metaphor for an action in which there is no delay or slowness. Qatadah said: a righteous predecessor (salaf sidq). Al-Rabi' said: a true reward (thawab sidq). Al-Hasan said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: his (ﷺ) qadam is in the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud). Muqatil said: deeds they sent forward, and Ibn Jarir chose this. From this is the saying of al-Wadah:

"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take for yourself a qadam that will save you on the day of dispute and slipping."

Other than what has preceded has been said, which needs no lengthy citation.

Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read "lasahir" (a magician), on the basis that they meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by the demonstrative.

The rest read "lasihr" (sorcery), on the basis that they meant the Qur'an. The meaning of sihr has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The clause ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ is resumptive, as if it were said: what did they do after the wonderment? Al-Qaffal said: there is an ellipsis, and the estimate is: when he warned them, the disbelievers said that.

It has been said that it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "istawa" (established). It has been said that it is resumptive, an answer to an implied question. The root meaning of tadbir is looking at the backs (adbar) of affairs and their consequences, so that they occur in an acceptable manner.

"With goodness, goodnesses; and if evil, then..."

meaning: and if evil, then (it is) evil.

Al-Hasan and ʿIkrimah said that (Alif Lam Ra) is an oath. Sa'id related from Qatadah that (Alif Lam Ra) is the name of the surah. It has been said other than that, which involves artificiality, since the knowledge of what Allah has reserved for Himself is unknown. The reciters agree that (Alif Lam Ra) is not a verse, and that Ta Ha is a verse. In Abu ʿAmr al-Dani's Muqni', the ones who count Ta Ha as a verse are the Kufans alone. It has been said: perhaps the difference is that (Alif Lam Ra) does not match the endings of the verses that follow it. The indication in His saying: (Those) refers to what the surah contains of verses, and the distancing is for magnification; the demonstrative is the subject and its predicate is what follows it.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: He meant the Torah, the Injil and the rest of the earlier Books, for (Those) is a demonstrative for an absent feminine referent. It has been said: (Those) has the meaning of (These): i.e., these are the verses of the Wise Book, which is the Qur'an. That the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an is supported by the fact that no mention of the earlier Books has preceded, and that "the Wise" is among the attributes of the Qur'an and not of anything else. The Wise (al-Hakim) means the one made firm (al-muhkam) with regard to the lawful and unlawful, the limits and the rulings; this was said by Abu ʿUbaydah and others. It has also been said that al-Hakim means the one who judges (al-hakim), so it is a fa'il-form (fa'il) in the sense of fa'il, as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, that it might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It has been said that al-Hakim means the one judged, so it is a fa'il-form in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., Allah has judged in it with justice and benevolence; this was said by al-Hasan and others. It has been said that al-Hakim means the possessor of wisdom, because it includes it.

The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people﴾ is for the denial of wonder, together with what it conveys of reproach and rebuke. The subject of kana (was) is ﴿that We revealed﴾ and its predicate is (a wonder), i.e., was Our revelation a wonder to the people?

Ibn Mas'ud read "ʿajabun" (a wonder) as the subject of kana, with kana being complete (taammah), and ﴿that We revealed﴾ is a substitute for (ʿajabun).

It is read with a sukun on the jim of "rajul" (man) in His saying: ﴿to a man from among them﴾, i.e., from their kind. There is nothing in this revelation to a man of their kind that requires wonder, for no one but one of their kind would mix with the kind, guide them and inform them from Allah, the Glorified; and if he were not of their kind, he would be of the angels or of the jinn, and the intended purpose of sending would then be impossible, for they would not be at ease with him nor see him. Even if we suppose that he took a form for them and appeared, either he would appear in a form other than the human species, which is more frightening to their hearts and further from their intimacy, or in human form, and then they must deny that he was originally not human. This is if the wonder was on their part because he is of their kind. If the wonder was because he is an orphan or poor, that does not prevent one who is such from combining the qualities of goodness and nobility that others do not combine, and reaching such a degree of perfection in attributes that the rich or the non-orphan falls short of it. Before Allah chose him for prophethood, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had among the Quraysh qualities of perfection more famous than the sun and more manifest than the daylight, so much so that they used to call him al-Amin (the Trustworthy).

His saying: ﴿that warn the people﴾ is in a position of accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "that you warn the people." It has been said that it is explanatory (mufassirah), since revelation contains the meaning of saying. It has been said that it is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form.

His saying: ﴿a sure standing (qadam sidq)﴾ means a station of truth (manzil sidq). Al-Zajjaj said: a high rank.

From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"For you is a qadam that people do not deny, whose station with high lineage has overflowed the sea."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the qadam is the one who precedes in nobility. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Kisa'i said: every precedence, whether of good or evil, is among the Arabs a qadam; one says: so-and-so has a qadam in Islam, and for him with me is a qadam of truth, a qadam of good, a qadam of evil. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjaj:

"The sons of al-ʿAwwam slipped from the family of al-Hakam, and left the kingdom to a lord of precedence (dhu qadam)."

Tha'lab said: the qadam is everything of good that you have sent forward. Ibn al-Anbari said: qadam is a metaphor for an action in which there is no delay or slowness. Qatadah said: a righteous predecessor (salaf sidq). Al-Rabi' said: a true reward (thawab sidq). Al-Hasan said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi said: his (ﷺ) qadam is in the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud). Muqatil said: deeds they sent forward, and Ibn Jarir chose this. From this is the saying of al-Wadah:

"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take for yourself a qadam that will save you on the day of dispute and slipping."

Other than what has preceded has been said, which needs no lengthy citation.

His saying: ﴿The disbelievers said: "Indeed, this is clearly a magician."﴾

Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read "lasahir" (a magician), on the basis that they meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by the demonstrative.

The rest read "lasihr" (sorcery), on the basis that they meant the Qur'an. The meaning of sihr has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The clause ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ is resumptive, as if it were said: what did they do after the wonderment? Al-Qaffal said: there is an ellipsis, and the estimate is: when he warned them, the disbelievers said that.

Then Allah, the Glorified, brought a statement by which He nullifies the wonder that arose in the disbelievers from the revelation to a man from among them. He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾, i.e., He who has this great power, which minds are too narrow to conceive, how can His sending a messenger from their own kind to the people be a cause for wonder, while the disbelievers themselves acknowledge that? How then do they not acknowledge the validity of this message through this messenger? The tafsir of this verse has already been given in al-A'raf, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne﴾, so we will not repeat it here. Then He mentioned what indicates greater power and great majesty, saying: ﴿He arranges the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾. The conjunction is omitted, because the clause (He arranges) is like an explanation and detail of what precedes it. It has been said that it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "istawa" (established). It has been said that it is resumptive, an answer to an implied question. The root meaning of tadbir is looking at the backs (adbar) of affairs and their consequences, so that they occur in an acceptable manner.

Mujahid said: He decrees it and determines it alone. It has been said: He sends the affair. It has been said: He sends down the affair. It has been said: He commands it and executes it. The meanings are close. Its derivation is from al-dubur (the back), and al-amr means the matter, which is the states of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, the Throne, and the rest of creation.

Al-Zajjaj said: The disbelievers addressed by this verse used to say: the idols are our intercessors with Allah. So Allah refuted them by saying that no one may intercede with Him for anything except after His permission, because He knows best the place of wisdom and correctness.

The meaning of intercession has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. In this there is a statement of His sole authority over affairs in everything, glorified and exalted is He. The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ refers to the doer of these things, of creation and arrangement, i.e., the One who did these great things is Allah your Lord. The demonstrative is the subject, its predicate is the noble name, and "your Lord" is a substitute for it, or an explanation of it, or a second predicate. In this sentence there is additional emphasis on His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Then He commanded them to worship Him, after showing them that He alone deserves it rather than anything else, for His wondrous making and great power. How then do they worship inanimate things that do not hear, do not see, neither benefit nor harm? The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ is for denial, reproach and rebuke, for whoever has the least remembrance and the slightest consideration knows this and it is not hidden from him.

Then He showed them what would be the end of their affair after the worldly life, saying: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾. In this there is a threat and warning that is not hidden. The accusative of (promise of Allah) is as a verbal noun, because in His saying "To Him is your return, all of you" there is the meaning of a promise; or it is governed by a verb understood. The intended meaning of return is returning to Him, glorified, either by death, or by resurrection, or by both. Then He emphasized that promise by saying: ﴿truly﴾, which is an emphasis upon an emphasis, so there is in the speech such firmness as is the utmost in that.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "The promise of Allah is true" as a new sentence.

Then the Glorified explained what preceded by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾, i.e., this is His manner: He begins His creation from dust, then returns it to dust; or the meaning of repetition is the recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

Mujahid said: He brings it into being, then causes it to die, then revives it for resurrection. It has been said: He brings it into being from water, then repeats it from state to state.

Yazid ibn al-Qaʻqaʻ read "annahu yabda'u al-khalq" with a fatha on the hamzah, so the clause is in the accusative position governed by what "promise of Allah" governs: i.e., He promised you that He originates creation then repeats it. It is also permissible that the estimate be "because He originates creation." Al-Farra' permitted that "anna" be in the nominative position, so that it is the subject. Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Tha'lab said: the estimate is: "truly, His originating the creation (is so)."

Then He mentioned the ultimate purpose of the repetition, saying: ﴿that He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾, i.e., with the justice in which there is no injustice. ﴿And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. It is possible that the second relative clause is conjoined to the first relative clause, i.e., that He may recompense those who believed and recompense those who disbelieved; and the clause "for them is a drink of scalding water" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, it and what is conjoined to it: i.e., and a painful punishment, and the estimate is thus: He recompenses those who disbelieved in the state in which they have this drink and this punishment. But this is problematic, because this drink and this painful punishment are themselves part of the recompense. It may be said that the relative pronoun in "those who disbelieved" is a subject and what follows it is its predicate, so it is not conjoined to the first conjoined element. The "bi" in "because they used to disbelieve" is causal, i.e., because of their disbelief. "Hamim" is hot water, and anything heated among the Arabs is hamim.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Ra," that he said: they are openings of names from the names of Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, and Ibn al-Najjar in his *Tarikh*, narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said concerning His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book.﴾ "I am Allah, I see."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak something similar as well.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "It means this."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "The Books that came before the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) as a Messenger, the Arabs, or some of them, denied this, and they said: "Allah is too great for His Messenger to be a human being like Muhammad." So Allah revealed: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We have revealed to a man from among them...﴾ up to His words: ﴿they will believe﴾, and ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed...﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7], the verse. When Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the proof against them, they said: "If he is a human being, then someone other than Muhammad would have been more worthy of the Message." ﴿Why was this Qur'an not revealed to a great man from one of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 31], meaning: more noble than Muhammad. They meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah from Makkah, and Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. So Allah revealed in reply to them: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 32], the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) concerning His words: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they will have a firm footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾ that he said: "It is what preceded for them of happiness in the first Remembrance (al-Dhikr al-Awwal, the primordial Record)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also, who said: "A good reward for what they had sent forward of their deeds."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The qadam is the deed which they sent forward."

Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And We write down what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin 12], and "the traces" are their walking places.

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked between two pillars of their mosque, then said: "This is a written trace."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His words: ﴿a firm footing (qadam sidq)﴾ that he said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) intercedes for them."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

al-Hakim narrated and declared authentic (sahhahahu), from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Salaf sidq" (a true predecessor).

The narrations from the Successors (tabi'un) and others on this are numerous, and we have already mentioned most of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿He governs the affair﴾ that he said: "He decrees it alone." And concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾ he said: "He gives it life, then makes it die, then gives it life again."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 5–6:

He mentions here some of His blessings upon the responsible (mukallafun) people, namely that by which His existence, His oneness, His power, His knowledge and His wisdom may be inferred, through the perfection of His craftsmanship in these two luminaries that follow each other perpetually, after He had mentioned before this His origination of the heavens and the earth, His istiwa' (rising) over the Throne, and other things.

As for al-Diya' (the bright light), it is said that it is the plural of daw' (light), like al-siyat and al-hiyad.

Qunbul transmitted from Ibn Kathir the reading "di'a'" (ضِئاءً), making the ya' a hamza alongside the hamza. There is no basis for it, because its ya' was originally a fatha-vowelled waw, and its root is diwa', then it was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it.

Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads di'a' with a hamza, it is inverted (maqlub): the hamza that comes after the alif was moved so that it became before the alif, then the ya' was changed to a hamza. The preferable view is that (diya') is a verbal noun (masdar), not a plural, like qama yaqumu qiyaman and sama yasumu siyaman. And there must be an implied genitive construction (mudaf), i.e., He made the sun possessed of brightness (dhat diya') and the moon possessed of light (dha nur), unless it is taken as hyperbole, as though they were made the very essence of brightness and light.

It is said: al-diya' is stronger than al-nur. It is also said: al-diya' is that which is intrinsic (bi-l-dhat), and al-nur is that which is accidental (bi-l-'arad). From this the philosophers said: the light of the moon is derived from the light of the sun.

His saying: ﴿and He determined for it stations﴾ means: He determined its course in stations, or He determined it as possessing stations. The pronoun refers to the moon. The stations of the moon (manazil al-qamar) are the distance it covers in a day and a night by its own particular motion. Their total is twenty-eight, and they are well known. The moon descends each night into one of them, a station it does not overstep. So it appears small at the beginning of its stations, then grows slightly by slightly until it appears full; and when it is at the end of its stations it becomes thin and curved, then it is hidden for two nights if the month is complete, or for one night if it is deficient. The discussion of this is lengthy.

We have compiled on this a separate treatise, as a reply to a question raised to us by some of the scholars.

It is also said: the pronoun refers to each of the sun and the moon, as it was said regarding His saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they break away toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 11].

And in the verse of the poet:

"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, and opinions differ."

We have already established the verification of this in what preceded in this tafsir. The preferable view is that the pronoun refers to the moon alone, as in His saying: ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39]. Then He mentioned some of the benefits connected with this determination, saying: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. For in knowing the number of years there are countless religious and worldly benefits, and in knowing the reckoning of months, days and nights there is what is not hidden. Had it not been for this determination which Allah, glorified is He, ordained, people would not have known this, nor would they have recognized what many of their interests depend upon.

The year is made up of twelve months, and the month is made up of thirty days if it is complete, and the day is made up of known hours, which are twenty-four hours for night and day together. Each of them may have twelve hours at the times of equinox, and one of them exceeds the other in the days of increase and the days of decrease. The difference between the solar and the lunar year is well known. Then He, glorified is He, made clear that He did not create the sun and the moon and the variation of these conditions except with truth and rightness, not in vanity or aimlessness. So the reference in His saying "That" is to what was mentioned before it, and the exception is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of conditions. The meaning of "detailing the signs" is making them clear, and by "the signs" is meant the cosmic signs (takwiniyya), or the revealed signs (tanziliyya), or both together; and these cosmic signs mentioned here are included primarily in that.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Ya'qub read yufassilu with a ya' (third person).

Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "tufassalu" with a ta' on the passive form, and the rest read it with a nun.

Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose the first reading, and perhaps the reason for this choice is that before this verb is ﴿Allah did not create that except with truth﴾ and after it is ﴿and what Allah created in the heavens and the earth﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the benefits resulting from the alternation of night and day, and what He created in the heavens and the earth of those creatures, saying: ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, are signs for a people who fear Allah﴾, i.e., those who are mindful of Allah, glorified is He, and avoid His disobedience. He specified them with these signs because they are the ones who contemplate and reflect deeply upon the creatures of Allah, glorified is He, out of caution against falling into anything that opposes the will of Allah, glorified is He, and out of regard for the outcome of their affair and what will benefit them in their return.

Al-Qaffal said: Whoever reflects upon these conditions knows that the world was created for people to dwell in it, and that its Creator and their Creator did not leave them neglected, but made it for them a house of action; and if that is so, then there must be a command and a prohibition.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿He made the sun a brightness and the moon a light﴾, that he said: He did not make the sun like the form of the moon so that night might be distinguished from day, and this is His saying: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ [al-Isra': 12], and so on.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the verse, that he said: "Their faces are toward the heavens and their backs toward the earth."

Ibn Mardawayh related the like of it from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Khalifa al-'Abdi, who said: If Allah, blessed and exalted is He, were worshipped only out of seeing Him, no one would worship Him. But the believers reflected on the coming of this night when it comes and fills everything and covers everything, and on the coming of the authority of the day when it comes and effaces the authority of the night, and on the clouds subjected between heaven and earth, and on the stars, and on winter and summer. By Allah, the believers never ceased reflecting upon what their Lord, blessed and exalted is He, created, until their hearts were certain of their Lord.
