Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "al-Salam (Peace) is God, the Exalted, and His abode is Paradise."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And God calls to the Abode of Safety (al-salamah)." The meanings of al-salam and al-salamah are one, like al-rada' and al-radā'ah (suckling). From this is the poet's saying:

"She greets with safety, Umm Bakr,
And is there for you, after your people, any peace?"

It was also said: What is meant is the Abode of Peace which is the greeting (al-tahiyyah), because its people receive from God peace in the sense of greeting, as in His words: ﴿Their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. It was also said: al-Salam is the name of one of the seven gardens: the first is the Abode of Peace; the second is the Abode of Majesty; the third is the Garden of Eden; the fourth is the Garden of Refuge; the fifth is the Garden of Eternity; the sixth is the Garden of Paradise (al-Firdaws); and the seventh is the Garden of Bliss.

It was also said: what is meant is the Abode of Peace, the greeting that occurs among the believers, one to another, in Paradise. They agree that the Abode of Peace is Paradise, and they differ only over the reason for naming it the Abode of Peace.

﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Glory be to Him, He made the call to the Abode of Peace general, and guidance specific to whomever He wills to guide, to complete the proof and to show His independence from His creation.

Then, glory be to Him, He divided the people of the call into two groups, and explained the condition of each group, saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna) and more﴾. That is, those who did good by performing the deeds God made obligatory upon them, and by refraining from the sins He forbade them. What is meant by al-husna is the good reward.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The Arabs apply this word to the praiseworthy, desired quality, and for this reason its qualified noun is omitted." It was also said: what is meant by al-husna is Paradise. As for the "more" (ziyadah), it was said: what is meant by it is what exceeds the reward by way of bounty, as in His words: ﴿that He may pay them their wages and increase them of His bounty﴾. It was said: the ziyadah is gazing upon His noble Face. It was said: the ziyadah is the multiplying of a good deed up to ten times its like. It was said: the ziyadah is a chamber of pearl. It was said: the ziyadah is forgiveness from God and good pleasure. It was said: it is that He, glory be to Him, gives them in this world from His bounty what He does not reckon against them. And other things were said which have no benefit in mentioning, and the truth of the matter will come in the end of the discussion.

﴿And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces﴾. Yarhaqu (covers) means: reaches; from it is said "ghulam muraahiq" (a youth approaching manhood) when he reaches the men. It was said: it rises over; it was said: it covers. The meanings are close. Qatar means dust. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Crowned with the robe of kingship, followed by
A wave, over which you see the banners and the dust."

Al-Hasan read "qatr" with the tā' quiescent, and the meaning is one, as said by al-Nahhas. The singular of qatar is qatarah. Dhillah (humiliation) is what appears on the face of submission, abjection and disgrace. The meaning is that dust does not rise over their faces, and no disgrace appears upon them. It was said: qatar is sorrow; it was said: it is the blackness of faces; it was said: it is the smoke of fire.

﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾. The indication is to those characterised by the previous attributes: they are the companions of Paradise, abiding forever therein, enjoying every kind of its bliss.

﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like﴾. This is the second group of the people of the call, and it is conjoined to ﴿for those who did good﴾, as if it were said: "And for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like." Or it may be taken as: "And the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed like it," that is, one evil deed is repaid with one evil deed, without any increase over it. This is better than the first, because it is of the type of conjoining to the objects of two different governing words. What is meant by "evil deed" is either shirk or sins other than shirk, which are the sins that the disobedient are involved in. Ibn Kaysan said: the ba' is superfluous, and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed like it. It was also said: the ba' with what follows it is the predicate, and it is connected to an omitted element that stands in its place, and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed existing by its like, as when you say "innama ana bika" (I am only through you). It is permissible that it be connected to "recompense" (jaza'), and the estimate is: "recompense of an evil deed by its like existing," so the predicate of the subject is omitted. It is also permissible that jaza' be in the nominative, under the estimate of "for them is a recompense of an evil deed," which is like His words: ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], that is, "then upon him is a number." The ba' in this estimate is connected to an omitted element, as if he said: "For them is a recompense of an evil deed established by its like." Or it may be emphatic or superfluous.

His words: ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾: that is, disgrace and shame will overtake them. It was read "yarhaquhum" with the yā' (third person). ﴿They have no protector from God﴾: that is, no one protects them, whoever he may be, from the wrath of God and His punishment. Or: they have no one from God's side and from His presence who would protect them as believers have. The first is better. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new, independent sentence.

﴿It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the night, darkened﴾. Qit'an is the plural of qit'ah. On this reading, muzlaman (darkened) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the night: that is, their faces were covered with pieces of the night in the state of its darkness.

The majority of readers read it in the plural. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qit'an" with the tā' quiescent, so that "muzlaman" in this case is an adjective of "qit'an," and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial qualifier of "al-layl."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-qit' is a portion of the night.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾. The unrestricted use of "abiding forever" here is restricted by what is established by mass transmission (mutawatir) in the Sunnah regarding the release of disobedient monotheists.

His words: ﴿And the day We gather them all together﴾. Al-hashr is gathering. Jami'an (all together) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. "Yawma" (the day) is governed by an implied verb: that is, warn them of the day We gather them. The clause is a new, independent sentence explaining some of their ugly conditions.

The meaning is that God, glory be to Him, gathers the worshipper and the worshipped to question them. ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners [with God]﴾ at the time of gathering and the moment of assembly, as a rebuke to them before the witnesses, and a reproach to them for the presence of those who share in their worship and the presence of their objects of worship. ﴿Stay in your place﴾, that is: remain in your place, be firm in it, stand in your position. ﴿You and your partners﴾, with the waw being the waw of "with" (ma'a).

His words: ﴿Then We will separate them﴾: that is, We divided and severed what had been between them of connection in the world. It is said: "zayyaltuhu fa-tazayyal," meaning: I separated it and it separated; al-muzayalah is parting; one says "zayala-hu muzayalatan wa-ziyalan" when he parted from him; and al-tazayul is disparity.

Al-Farra' said: some read "فزايلنا" (fa-zayalna). The partners here are the angels; it was also said: the devils; it was said: the idols, and that God, glory be to Him, makes them speak at this time. It was also said: the Messiah and 'Uzayr. The apparent meaning is that it is every object of worship of the polytheists, whatever it may be.

His words: ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not worship us"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, with qad understood. The meaning is: their partners who were worshipped and made partners of God, glory be to Him, have said, "You did not worship us; rather, you worshipped your desires, your misguidance, and your devils who misled you." He attributed the partners to them, although they made them partners of God, glory be to Him, because they gave them a share of their wealth, so they are their partners in their wealth from this standpoint. It was also said: because they are their partners in this address. And this denial by the partners, though it contradicts what the polytheists did in worshipping them, means the denial that they worshipped them by their command to worship.

﴿Sufficient is God as witness between us and you﴾, if we commanded your worship or approved that from you. ﴿We were indeed unaware of your worship﴾. The particle in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy in (inna), and the lam is the distinguishing lam between it and the negative in (ma). The speakers of this statement are the ones who were worshipped.

[p. 620]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 24–30 (part 2 of 3):

They say to those among the polytheists who worshipped them: ﴿We were indeed unaware of your worship of us.﴾ The meaning of "unaware" here is: not approving of what the polytheists did in worshipping them. This is evidence that these objects of worship were not the devils, because they do not approve of the worship the polytheists directed at them. It is possible that they were devils, and this denial may be understood to mean that they did not compel them to worship them or force them into it.

﴿There, every soul will experience what it has sent ahead.﴾ That is, in that place and in that station, or at that time, using the name of time for place as a metaphor (isti'arah). Every soul will taste and be tested for the recompense of the deeds it sent ahead. So the meaning of "tabluu" (will experience) is "will taste" and "will be tested." It was also said: "will know," and it was said: "will follow." This is according to the reading of those who read "tabluu" with the feminine ta' (ta') and attribute the verb to "every soul." As for the reading of those who read "nabluu" with the nun, the meaning is that God tests every soul and examines it, and "what it has sent ahead" is then in apposition to "every soul."

The meaning is that He deals with it as one who tests it and inspects its conditions.

His words: ﴿and they will be returned to God, their true Master﴾ are coordinated with "We separated." The pronoun in "were returned" refers to those who associated partners with God, meaning: they will be returned to His recompense and the punishment He has prepared for them. "Their Master" means their Lord, and "the true" is an attribute of Him, meaning the one who is truly Lord, not what they had taken as false objects of worship. It was also read "al-haqqa" in the accusative as a form of praise, like their saying: "Praise belongs to God, the people of praise." ﴿And what they used to fabricate will have vanished from them.﴾ That is, what they used to fabricate has been lost and invalidated: the claim that the gods they had were truly deserving of worship, so that they would intercede for them with God and bring them near to Him.

The summary is that these polytheists will, in that position, return to the truth, acknowledge it, and affirm it, and they will admit the falsehood of what they used to worship and make a god. But that will be when it no longer benefits them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿so the vegetation of the earth mingled with it﴾, that he said: "It mingled, and every kind grew with the water: ﴿of what people eat﴾ such as wheat, barley, and the other grains of the earth, the herbs and fruits, and what livestock and beasts eat of grass and pasture."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿and it adorned itself﴾, that he said: "It sprouted and became beautiful." And regarding His words ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾, he said: "As if it had not lived, as if it had not been prosperous."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, and Marwan ibn al-Hakam that they used to recite, after His words ﴿and its people thought they had power over it﴾: "And God would not destroy it except for the sins of its people." (This is a variant reading, not part of the standard text.)

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman that he used to read: "And We did not destroy it except for the sins of its people," ﴿Thus do We detail the signs.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu Mijlaz, who said: "It was written in Surat Yunus, up to this verse ﴿until, when the earth took its adornment﴾ up to ﴿they reflect﴾: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would desire a third valley. Nothing fills the soul of the son of Adam except dust. And God accepts the repentance of whoever repents.'" Then it was erased.

Abu Nu'aym and al-Dimyati in his Mu'jam reported, through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾, that he said: "He calls to the deeds that lead to Paradise. As-Salam is God, and Paradise is His abode."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-'Aliya, regarding His words ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, that he said: "He guides them to the way out of doubts, trials, and misguidance."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no day on which its sun rises without two angels being assigned to its two sides, calling out a call that all of God's creatures hear except the two weighty ones (jinn and humans): 'O people, come to your Lord! What is little and sufficient is better than what is abundant and distracting.' And there is no day on which its sun sets without two angels being assigned to its two sides, calling out a call that all of God's creatures hear except the two weighty ones: 'O God, give the one who spends a replacement, and give the one who withholds destruction.'" Then the verses ﴿By the night when it covers, and the day when it reveals itself﴾ up to His words ﴿for hardship.﴾

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal: "I heard Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, and he recited: ﴿God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ Then he said: Jabir told me: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out to us one day and said: 'I saw in a dream as if Gabriel was at my head and Michael at my feet. One of them said to the other: Strike a parable for him. The other said: Listen, may your ear hear; understand, may your heart understand. Your parable and the parable of your community is that of a king who built a house, then built a room in it, then set up a feast in it, then sent a messenger calling people to his food. Some of them answered the messenger, and some of them refused. God is the King, the abode is Islam, the room is Paradise, and you, O Muhammad, are the messenger. Whoever answers you enters Islam, whoever enters Islam enters Paradise, and whoever enters Paradise eats from it.'"

Something of this meaning has been narrated through several chains.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾, that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that it is written in the Torah: 'O seeker of good, come forward! O seeker of evil, beware of it!'"

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan that whenever he recited ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾ he would say: "At Your service, our Lord, and at Your pleasure."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and others reported from Suhayb that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ and said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, God has a promise for you and wishes to fulfill it for you.' They will say: 'What is it? Did He not make our scales heavy, whiten our faces, admit us to Paradise, and save us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil will be lifted for them, and they will look at Him. By God, God has given them nothing more beloved to them than looking at Him, and nothing more comforting to their eyes."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Ru'ya, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Musa, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God will send, on the Day of Resurrection, a caller who calls with a voice that the first and last of them hear: 'God has promised you the best reward and more.'" So "the best reward" is Paradise, and "more" is looking at the Face of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'ya reported from Ka'b ibn Ujra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words: "﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more.﴾ He said: 'The more is looking at the Face of the Most Merciful.'"

These and al-Daraqutni and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His words: "﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more.﴾ He said: 'Those who did good are the people of monotheism (tawhid), the best reward is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Face of God.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn al-Najjar reported from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu Hurayra something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq regarding the verse that he said: "The best reward is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Face of God."

Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of al-Harith from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding the verse something like this.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Hudhayfa regarding the verse that he said: "The more is looking at the Face of God."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Musa something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported, through the chain of Ikrima from Ibn Abbas, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Lalaka'i reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ali, who said: "The more is a chamber of one pearl with four doors; its chambers and its doors are of one pearl."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words "and more," that he said: "It is like His words: ﴿And with Us is more.﴾ He says: He rewards them for their deeds and increases them from His bounty." And He said: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like.﴾

Narrations from the Successors (tabi'un) and those after them have been transmitted in explaining "the more," most of them saying that it is looking at the Face of God, glorified is He.

This interpretation has been established by the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore, no one has any further statement, nor any need to pay attention to the disputes that arise among the partisans of the legal schools (madhhab) who do not know from the purified Sunnah what would benefit them. If they knew it, they would refrain from much of their babbling. And God is the one sought for help.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces﴾, that he said: "It will not cover them. ﴿Dust﴾ is the blackness of the faces."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ata' regarding the verse that he said: "Dust is the blackness of the face."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding the verse that he said: "Disgrace."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Suhayb, "from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces,﴾ he said: 'After their looking at Him, Mighty and Majestic.'"

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿And those who earned misdeeds﴾, that he said: "Those who committed major sins. ﴿The recompense of an evil is its like﴾: the Fire. ﴿As if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkest night﴾: the 'pieces' are blackness. It was abrogated (naskh) by the verse in al-Baqara: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil﴾ (2:81), up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and humiliation will cover them﴾, that he said: "Humiliation and hardship will overwhelm them."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, regarding His words ﴿they will have no protector from God﴾, that he said: "No one who prevents."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And on the day We gather them﴾, that he said: "The gathering is death."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His words ﴿then We separate them﴾, that he said: "We separate them."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, who said: "The gods that they used to worship besides God will be set up, and He will say: 'Are these the ones you used to worship besides God?' They will say: 'Yes, these are the ones we used to worship.' Then the gods will say to them: 'By God, we did not hear, see, understand, or know that you were worshipping us.' They will say: 'Yes, by God, it was you we used to worship.' Then the gods will say to them: ﴿God suffices as witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verse 24–30 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection, what they used to worship besides Allah will be presented to them as an image, and they will follow them until they bring them into the Fire." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿There every soul will be tested for what it did before﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿There will be tested﴾, that he said: it means "will follow."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: "will be tested" means "will be examined."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding "will be tested," that he said: "will witness." ﴿Every soul will know what it sent forward﴾ means what it did. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾ means what they used to call upon besides Him of rivals.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: (p-623) ﴿And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master﴾, that he said: it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Allah is the Master of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no master﴾ [Muhammad: 11].

When God, glory be to Him, mentioned what had preceded about the enjoyments of this world, He introduced a new statement that encompasses an explanation of its condition and the speed with which it passes away, and that it returns after it has filled the eyes with its splendour, attracted souls with its delight, and driven its people to shed one another's blood and violate one another's sanctities, out of love for it and passion for its outward beauty, and eager rivalry for enjoying it, and rushing to obtain what souls desire from it, by means of a compound simile. So He said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of the life of this world is like water which We send down from the sky﴾, to the end of the verse.

The meaning is that its likeness, in the swiftness of its passing and in being characterised by a quality that is opposed to and contrary to what it had been, is the likeness of the plant-kinds that are on the earth, in the loss of their freshness, the departure of their delight, and the swiftness of their passing away, after they had been tender, green, and fresh, their swaying branches intertwined, their leaves that touch one another made beautiful, the lights of their brightness gleaming, and the flowers imitating the various kinds of their blossoms. The thing likened is not what is entered by the kaf (like) in His words ﴿like water which We send down from the sky﴾; rather, it is what is understood from the discourse. The ba' in ﴿so the plants of the earth mingled with it﴾ is causal (sababiyyah), i.e., the plants of the earth mingled because of it, by its intertwining with one another until they reached the limit of perfection. It is also possible that what is meant is that the plant, at the beginning of its emergence and the start of its appearance, was neither swaying nor growing vigorously; then when water descended upon it, it swayed and grew, until some kinds mingled with others ﴿of what men and cattle eat﴾, of grains, fruits, herbage, and straw, and the earth took its adornment.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah (the Dictionary): "Zukhruf is gold; then every gilded, falsely adorned thing is likened to it." End of quotation.

The meaning is that the earth took on a beautiful colour, some of which resembles the colour of gold, some the colour of silver, some the colour of rubies, and some the colour of emeralds.

The original form of ﴿ازّيّنت﴾ (azzayyanat) was تزيّنت (tazayyanat); the tා' was assimilated into the zay, and an alif of connection (alif al-wasl) was brought in, because the assimilated letter takes the place of two letters, the first of which is quiescent, and a quiescent letter cannot be begun with.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "وتزيّنت" (wa-tazayyanat) according to the original form.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Abu al-'Aliyah read "وأزيّنت" (wa-azyannat) on the pattern of أفعلت (af'alat), meaning: it made the adornment that was upon it beautiful; it likened it to the bride who wears fine garments of many colours.

'Awf ibn Abi Jamilah said: "Our teachers read 'وازيانّت' (wa-azyānnat) on the pattern of اسوادّت (iswadat)." In the transmission of al-Muqaddami it is "وازّايَنت" (wa-azzāyanat), and its original form is تزايَنت (tazāyanat) on the pattern of تفاعلت (tafā'alat).

Al-Sha'bi and Qatadah read "ازْيَنّت" (azyannat). The meanings of all these readings are what we have mentioned.

﴿And its people thought that they were able to control it﴾: that is, it overcame their assumptions, or they were certain that they were able to harvest it and benefit from it. The pronoun in ﴿عليها﴾ ('alayha, "over it") refers to the earth, and what is meant is the plant that is upon it.

﴿Then Our command came to it﴾: the answer to "idha" (when). That is, Our command came to it to destroy it, uproot it, and strike it with some blight.

﴿So We made it a harvest﴾: that is, We made its crop like the reaped, in being cut from its roots.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "al-Hasid (the harvest) is that which is uprooted."

﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾: that is, as if its crop had not existed in it yesterday, green and fresh. From ghaniya bi-al-makan (he dwelt in a place), with kasra in the first, yaghna with fatha in the second, when one stays in it. What is meant by "yesterday" is a near time. Al-maghani in the language means dwellings.

Qatadah said: "as if it had not enjoyed prosperity." Labid said:

"I dwelt in prosperity before the course of Dahis,
Had there been immortality for the stubborn soul."

Qatadah read "كأن لم يُغنِ" (ka-an lam yughni) with the yā' (third person masculine), referring the pronoun back to al-zukhruf (the adornment). The rest read "تُغنِ" (tughni) with the tā' (second person feminine), referring the pronoun back to the earth. ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that wondrous detailing, ﴿We detail the signs﴾, the Qur'anic signs, of which this verse is part, ﴿so that they may reflect﴾ upon what they contain. It is also permissible that what is meant is the signs of creation.

His words: ﴿And God calls to the Abode of Peace﴾. When He had repelled His servants from inclining towards this world through the previous parable He had set for them, He encouraged them towards the Hereafter by informing them of this call from Him, mighty and majestic, to the Abode of Peace. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "al-Salam (Peace) is God, the Exalted, and His abode is Paradise."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And God calls to the Abode of Safety (al-salamah)." The meanings of al-salam and al-salamah are one, like al-rada' and al-radā'ah (suckling). From this is the poet's saying:

"She greets with safety, Umm Bakr,
And is there for you, after your people, any peace?"

It was also said: What is meant is the Abode of Peace which is the greeting (al-tahiyyah), because its people receive from God peace in the sense of greeting, as in His words: ﴿Their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. It was also said: al-Salam is the name of one of the seven gardens: the first is the Abode of Peace; the second is the Abode of Majesty; the third is the Garden of Eden; the fourth is the Garden of Refuge; the fifth is the Garden of Eternity; the sixth is the Garden of Paradise (al-Firdaws); and the seventh is the Garden of Bliss.

It was also said: what is meant is the Abode of Peace, the greeting that occurs among the believers, one to another, in Paradise. They agree that the Abode of Peace is Paradise, and they differ only over the reason for naming it the Abode of Peace.

﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Glory be to Him, He made the call to the Abode of Peace general, and guidance specific to whomever He wills to guide, to complete the proof and to show His independence from His creation.

Then, glory be to Him, He divided the people of the call into two groups, and explained the condition of each group, saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna) and more﴾. That is, those who did good by performing the deeds God made obligatory upon them, and by refraining from the sins He forbade them. What is meant by al-husna is the good reward.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The Arabs apply this word to the praiseworthy, desired quality, and for this reason its qualified noun is omitted." It was also said: what is meant by al-husna is Paradise. As for the "more" (ziyadah), it was said: what is meant by it is what exceeds the reward by way of bounty, as in His words: ﴿that He may pay them their wages and increase them of His bounty﴾. It was said: the ziyadah is gazing upon His noble Face. It was said: the ziyadah is the multiplying of a good deed up to ten times its like. It was said: the ziyadah is a chamber of pearl. It was said: the ziyadah is forgiveness from God and good pleasure. It was said: it is that He, glory be to Him, gives them in this world from His bounty what He does not reckon against them. And other things were said which have no benefit in mentioning, and the truth of the matter will come in the end of the discussion.

﴿And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces﴾. Yarhaqu (covers) means: reaches; from it is said "ghulam muraahiq" (a youth approaching manhood) when he reaches the men. It was said: it rises over; it was said: it covers. The meanings are close. Qatar means dust. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Crowned with the robe of kingship, followed by
A wave, over which you see the banners and the dust."

Al-Hasan read "qatr" with the tā' quiescent, and the meaning is one, as said by al-Nahhas. The singular of qatar is qatarah. Dhillah (humiliation) is what appears on the face of submission, abjection and disgrace. The meaning is that dust does not rise over their faces, and no disgrace appears upon them. It was said: qatar is sorrow; it was said: it is the blackness of faces; it was said: it is the smoke of fire.

﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾. The indication is to those characterised by the previous attributes: they are the companions of Paradise, abiding forever therein, enjoying every kind of its bliss.

﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like﴾. This is the second group of the people of the call, and it is conjoined to ﴿for those who did good﴾, as if it were said: "And for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like." Or it may be taken as: "And the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed like it," that is, one evil deed is repaid with one evil deed, without any increase over it. This is better than the first, because it is of the type of conjoining to the objects of two different governing words. What is meant by "evil deed" is either shirk or sins other than shirk, which are the sins that the disobedient are involved in. Ibn Kaysan said: the ba' is superfluous, and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed like it. It was also said: the ba' with what follows it is the predicate, and it is connected to an omitted element that stands in its place, and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed existing by its like, as when you say "innama ana bika" (I am only through you). It is permissible that it be connected to "recompense" (jaza'), and the estimate is: "recompense of an evil deed by its like existing," so the predicate of the subject is omitted. It is also permissible that jaza' be in the nominative, under the estimate of "for them is a recompense of an evil deed," which is like His words: ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], that is, "then upon him is a number." The ba' in this estimate is connected to an omitted element, as if he said: "For them is a recompense of an evil deed established by its like." Or it may be emphatic or superfluous.

His words: ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾: that is, disgrace and shame will overtake them. It was read "yarhaquhum" with the yā' (third person). ﴿They have no protector from God﴾: that is, no one protects them, whoever he may be, from the wrath of God and His punishment. Or: they have no one from God's side and from His presence who would protect them as believers have. The first is better. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new, independent sentence.

﴿It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the night, darkened﴾. Qit'an is the plural of qit'ah. On this reading, muzlaman (darkened) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the night: that is, their faces were covered with pieces of the night in the state of its darkness.

The majority of readers read it in the plural. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qit'an" with the tā' quiescent, so that "muzlaman" in this case is an adjective of "qit'an," and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial qualifier of "al-layl."

Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-qit' is a portion of the night.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾. The unrestricted use of "abiding forever" here is restricted by what is established by mass transmission (mutawatir) in the Sunnah regarding the release of disobedient monotheists.

His words: ﴿And the day We gather them all together﴾. Al-hashr is gathering. Jami'an (all together) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. "Yawma" (the day) is governed by an implied verb: that is, warn them of the day We gather them. The clause is a new, independent sentence explaining some of their ugly conditions.

The meaning is that God, glory be to Him, gathers the worshipper and the worshipped to question them. ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners [with God]﴾ at the time of gathering and the moment of assembly, as a rebuke to them before the witnesses, and a reproach to them for the presence of those who share in their worship and the presence of their objects of worship. ﴿Stay in your place﴾, that is: remain in your place, be firm in it, stand in your position. ﴿You and your partners﴾, with the waw being the waw of "with" (ma'a).

His words: ﴿Then We will separate them﴾: that is, We divided and severed what had been between them of connection in the world. It is said: "zayyaltuhu fa-tazayyal," meaning: I separated it and it separated; al-muzayalah is parting; one says "zayala-hu muzayalatan wa-ziyalan" when he parted from him; and al-tazayul is disparity.

Al-Farra' said: some read "فزايلنا" (fa-zayalna). The partners here are the angels; it was also said: the devils; it was said: the idols, and that God, glory be to Him, makes them speak at this time. It was also said: the Messiah and 'Uzayr. The apparent meaning is that it is every object of worship of the polytheists, whatever it may be.

His words: ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not worship us"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, with qad understood. The meaning is: their partners who were worshipped and made partners of God, glory be to Him, have said, "You did not worship us; rather, you worshipped your desires, your misguidance, and your devils who misled you." He attributed the partners to them, although they made them partners of God, glory be to Him, because they gave them a share of their wealth, so they are their partners in their wealth from this standpoint. It was also said: because they are their partners in this address. And this denial by the partners, though it contradicts what the polytheists did in worshipping them, means the denial that they worshipped them by their command to worship.

﴿Sufficient is God as witness between us and you﴾, if we commanded your worship or approved that from you. ﴿We were indeed unaware of your worship﴾. The particle in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy in (inna), and the lam is the distinguishing lam between it and the negative in (ma). The speakers of this statement are the ones who were worshipped.

[p. 620]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 24–30 (part 2 of 3):

They say to those among the polytheists who worshipped them: ﴿We were indeed unaware of your worship of us.﴾ The meaning of "unaware" here is: not approving of what the polytheists did in worshipping them. This is evidence that these objects of worship were not the devils, because they do not approve of the worship the polytheists directed at them. It is possible that they were devils, and this denial may be understood to mean that they did not compel them to worship them or force them into it.

﴿There, every soul will experience what it has sent ahead.﴾ That is, in that place and in that station, or at that time, using the name of time for place as a metaphor (isti'arah). Every soul will taste and be tested for the recompense of the deeds it sent ahead. So the meaning of "tabluu" (will experience) is "will taste" and "will be tested." It was also said: "will know," and it was said: "will follow." This is according to the reading of those who read "tabluu" with the feminine ta' (ta') and attribute the verb to "every soul." As for the reading of those who read "nabluu" with the nun, the meaning is that God tests every soul and examines it, and "what it has sent ahead" is then in apposition to "every soul."

The meaning is that He deals with it as one who tests it and inspects its conditions.

His words: ﴿and they will be returned to God, their true Master﴾ are coordinated with "We separated." The pronoun in "were returned" refers to those who associated partners with God, meaning: they will be returned to His recompense and the punishment He has prepared for them. "Their Master" means their Lord, and "the true" is an attribute of Him, meaning the one who is truly Lord, not what they had taken as false objects of worship. It was also read "al-haqqa" in the accusative as a form of praise, like their saying: "Praise belongs to God, the people of praise." ﴿And what they used to fabricate will have vanished from them.﴾ That is, what they used to fabricate has been lost and invalidated: the claim that the gods they had were truly deserving of worship, so that they would intercede for them with God and bring them near to Him.

The summary is that these polytheists will, in that position, return to the truth, acknowledge it, and affirm it, and they will admit the falsehood of what they used to worship and make a god. But that will be when it no longer benefits them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿so the vegetation of the earth mingled with it﴾, that he said: "It mingled, and every kind grew with the water: ﴿of what people eat﴾ such as wheat, barley, and the other grains of the earth, the herbs and fruits, and what livestock and beasts eat of grass and pasture."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿and it adorned itself﴾, that he said: "It sprouted and became beautiful." And regarding His words ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾, he said: "As if it had not lived, as if it had not been prosperous."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, and Marwan ibn al-Hakam that they used to recite, after His words ﴿and its people thought they had power over it﴾: "And God would not destroy it except for the sins of its people." (This is a variant reading, not part of the standard text.)

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman that he used to read: "And We did not destroy it except for the sins of its people," ﴿Thus do We detail the signs.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu Mijlaz, who said: "It was written in Surat Yunus, up to this verse ﴿until, when the earth took its adornment﴾ up to ﴿they reflect﴾: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would desire a third valley. Nothing fills the soul of the son of Adam except dust. And God accepts the repentance of whoever repents.'" Then it was erased.

Abu Nu'aym and al-Dimyati in his Mu'jam reported, through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾, that he said: "He calls to the deeds that lead to Paradise. As-Salam is God, and Paradise is His abode."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-'Aliya, regarding His words ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, that he said: "He guides them to the way out of doubts, trials, and misguidance."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no day on which its sun rises without two angels being assigned to its two sides, calling out a call that all of God's creatures hear except the two weighty ones (jinn and humans): 'O people, come to your Lord! What is little and sufficient is better than what is abundant and distracting.' And there is no day on which its sun sets without two angels being assigned to its two sides, calling out a call that all of God's creatures hear except the two weighty ones: 'O God, give the one who spends a replacement, and give the one who withholds destruction.'" Then the verses ﴿By the night when it covers, and the day when it reveals itself﴾ up to His words ﴿for hardship.﴾

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal: "I heard Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, and he recited: ﴿God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ Then he said: Jabir told me: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out to us one day and said: 'I saw in a dream as if Gabriel was at my head and Michael at my feet. One of them said to the other: Strike a parable for him. The other said: Listen, may your ear hear; understand, may your heart understand. Your parable and the parable of your community is that of a king who built a house, then built a room in it, then set up a feast in it, then sent a messenger calling people to his food. Some of them answered the messenger, and some of them refused. God is the King, the abode is Islam, the room is Paradise, and you, O Muhammad, are the messenger. Whoever answers you enters Islam, whoever enters Islam enters Paradise, and whoever enters Paradise eats from it.'"

Something of this meaning has been narrated through several chains.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾, that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that it is written in the Torah: 'O seeker of good, come forward! O seeker of evil, beware of it!'"

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan that whenever he recited ﴿God calls to the abode of peace﴾ he would say: "At Your service, our Lord, and at Your pleasure."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and others reported from Suhayb that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ and said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, God has a promise for you and wishes to fulfill it for you.' They will say: 'What is it? Did He not make our scales heavy, whiten our faces, admit us to Paradise, and save us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil will be lifted for them, and they will look at Him. By God, God has given them nothing more beloved to them than looking at Him, and nothing more comforting to their eyes."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Ru'ya, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Musa, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God will send, on the Day of Resurrection, a caller who calls with a voice that the first and last of them hear: 'God has promised you the best reward and more.'" So "the best reward" is Paradise, and "more" is looking at the Face of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'ya reported from Ka'b ibn Ujra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words: "﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more.﴾ He said: 'The more is looking at the Face of the Most Merciful.'"

These and al-Daraqutni and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His words: "﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more.﴾ He said: 'Those who did good are the people of monotheism (tawhid), the best reward is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Face of God.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn al-Najjar reported from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu Hurayra something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq regarding the verse that he said: "The best reward is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Face of God."

Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of al-Harith from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding the verse something like this.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Hudhayfa regarding the verse that he said: "The more is looking at the Face of God."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Musa something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported, through the chain of Ikrima from Ibn Abbas, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Lalaka'i reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ali, who said: "The more is a chamber of one pearl with four doors; its chambers and its doors are of one pearl."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words "and more," that he said: "It is like His words: ﴿And with Us is more.﴾ He says: He rewards them for their deeds and increases them from His bounty." And He said: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like.﴾

Narrations from the Successors (tabi'un) and those after them have been transmitted in explaining "the more," most of them saying that it is looking at the Face of God, glorified is He.

This interpretation has been established by the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore, no one has any further statement, nor any need to pay attention to the disputes that arise among the partisans of the legal schools (madhhab) who do not know from the purified Sunnah what would benefit them. If they knew it, they would refrain from much of their babbling. And God is the one sought for help.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces﴾, that he said: "It will not cover them. ﴿Dust﴾ is the blackness of the faces."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ata' regarding the verse that he said: "Dust is the blackness of the face."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding the verse that he said: "Disgrace."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Suhayb, "from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces,﴾ he said: 'After their looking at Him, Mighty and Majestic.'"

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿And those who earned misdeeds﴾, that he said: "Those who committed major sins. ﴿The recompense of an evil is its like﴾: the Fire. ﴿As if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkest night﴾: the 'pieces' are blackness. It was abrogated (naskh) by the verse in al-Baqara: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil﴾ (2:81), up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and humiliation will cover them﴾, that he said: "Humiliation and hardship will overwhelm them."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, regarding His words ﴿they will have no protector from God﴾, that he said: "No one who prevents."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And on the day We gather them﴾, that he said: "The gathering is death."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His words ﴿then We separate them﴾, that he said: "We separate them."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, who said: "The gods that they used to worship besides God will be set up, and He will say: 'Are these the ones you used to worship besides God?' They will say: 'Yes, these are the ones we used to worship.' Then the gods will say to them: 'By God, we did not hear, see, understand, or know that you were worshipping us.' They will say: 'Yes, by God, it was you we used to worship.' Then the gods will say to them: ﴿God suffices as witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verse 24–30 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection, what they used to worship besides Allah will be presented to them as an image, and they will follow them until they bring them into the Fire." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿There every soul will be tested for what it did before﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿There will be tested﴾, that he said: it means "will follow."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: "will be tested" means "will be examined."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding "will be tested," that he said: "will witness." ﴿Every soul will know what it sent forward﴾ means what it did. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾ means what they used to call upon besides Him of rivals.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: (p-623) ﴿And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master﴾, that he said: it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Allah is the Master of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no master﴾ [Muhammad: 11].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verse 31–41 (part 1 of 2):

When He had made clear the disgraceful state of the polytheists, He followed it with the decisive proofs drawn from the conditions of provision, the senses, death, life, origination and return, and guidance and right direction. Glorified is He, He built the proofs on interrogation and on leaving the answer to those being questioned, so that the argument would be more eloquent in binding them and would have a stronger effect on souls. So He said: Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists, arguing for the truth of monotheism and the falsehood of what they hold of shirk: ﴿Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ From the heaven, by rain; and from the earth, by plants and minerals. If they acknowledge this, the aim is achieved; and if they do not acknowledge it, they must acknowledge that it is Allah who created both of them. ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight?﴾ Or who is it that is cut off? In this there is a movement from one question to another. Hearing and sight are singled out for mention because of the wondrous craftsmanship and the magnificent, overpowering power in them; that is: who is able to possess them and to fashion them in this wondrous quality and strange creation, so that they benefit from them this great benefit, and obtain from them benefits that do not fall under the enumeration of those who count? Then he moved to a third proof, and said: ﴿And who brings forth the living from the dead?﴾ The human from the drop, the bird from the egg, the plant from the seed; or the believer from the disbeliever. ﴿And who brings forth the dead from the living?﴾ That is, the drop from the human, or the disbeliever from the believer. The intent of this interrogation is: who gives life and causes death? Then he moved to a fourth proof, and said: ﴿And who governs the affair?﴾ That is, who decrees and determines it? This is the mention of the general after the particular, since it encompasses what preceded and other things. ﴿They will say, "Allah."﴾ That is: their answer to these interrogations will be that the doer of these matters is Allah, glorified is He, if they are fair and act according to what sound reason and upright intellect require. The noble name is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is omitted; that is, "Allah does that." Then, after they give this answer, Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet to say to them: ﴿Will you not then fear Him?﴾ The interrogative is for denunciation, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied element; that is: you know this, so will you not fear (Allah)? And do what this knowledge requires of the piety toward Allah who does these deeds.

﴿So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth.﴾ That is: so that One who does these deeds is your Lord, characterized as the Truth, not those whom you have made partners to Him. The interrogation in His words ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, if "mā" is interrogative, not if it is negative as the statement may allow. The meaning: what is there after the truth but error? For the affirmation of the Lordship of the Lord, glorified is He, is true by their own acknowledgment, so anything other than Him is false, because the Necessary Existent must be one in His essence and attributes. ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ That is: how do you permit yourselves to deviate from the manifest truth and fall into error, since there is no intermediary between the two? Whoever passes beyond one of them falls into the other. The interrogation is for denial, disapproval and wonder.

﴿Thus has the word of your Lord come true against those who defiantly disobeyed, that they will not believe.﴾ That is: just as it is established and confirmed that the truth after error is (only) truth, or just as it is established that they are turned away from the truth, thus the word of your Lord has come true, that is, His judgment and decree, ( against those who defiantly disobeyed, that is: who went out from the truth into falsehood and persisted in their disbelief out of obstinacy and arrogance. The clause "that they will not believe" is a substitute for "the word."

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, this word has come true against them, namely their not believing. It is also permissible for the clause to be causal for what precedes, with the lam implied: that is, because they do not believe.

Al-Farra' said: It is permissible (to read) "innahum" with a kasra, as a new sentence. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "kalimat Rabbi" (the words of my Lord) in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular.

His words: ﴿Say, "Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?"﴾ In this, He presented a fifth proof against the polytheists, which He commanded His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them. Although they do not acknowledge the Return, yet since it is a manifest and clear matter, and He had established the proofs for it in this surah in a form that cannot be repelled by one who is fair and does not obstinately deny, it was as if it were conceded by them, with no denial or refusal in it. Then Glorified is He commanded him to say to them: ﴿Say, "Allah originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you deluded?"﴾ That is: He is the One who does that, not other than Him. This statement which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said on the command of Allah, glorified is He, is a substitution for the polytheists in the answer, either by way of instructing them and informing them how to answer, and guiding them to what they should say, or because this meaning had reached such clarity that there is no need, with it, for the opponent's acknowledgment or knowledge of what he has; or because the polytheists would not utter the correct answer, fleeing from being bound by the proof or from being recorded against them as obstinate and arrogant if they swerved from the truth.

The meaning of "so how are you deluded?" is: how are you turned away from the truth and turned from it to something else?

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to present to them a sixth proof, so He said: ﴿Say, "Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?"﴾ (p-624) The interrogation here is like the preceding interrogations, and reasoning from guidance after reasoning from creation occurs often in the Qur'an, such as His words: ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78], His words: ﴿Who gave everything its form and then guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], and His words: ﴿Who created and proportioned, and who determined and then guided﴾ [al-A'la: 2, 3]. The verb "guide" comes transitively with the lam and with ila, and both have one meaning; this is related from al-Zajjaj.

The meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "Is there any of your partners who directs to the religion of Islam and calls people to the truth?" If they say no, then say to them: Allah guides to the truth, to the exclusion of others. The evidence for this is what has preceded of the proofs indicating that this belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He. Allah's guidance of His servants to the truth is by the signs He has set up for them in created things, by His sending of the messengers and His sending down of the books, and by His creating what the servants use to reach that: the intellects, understandings, hearing and sight. The interrogation in His words ﴿Is he who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not find guidance unless he is guided?﴾ is for affirmation and binding the proof.

The readers differed on "lā yahiddi". The people of Madina, except Nafi', read "yahiddi" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ha', and a shadda on the dal, thus joining two sukuns in their reading.

Al-Nahhas said: Joining two sukuns, no one can pronounce.

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: Whoever attempts such a reading must move the letter with a light vowel toward the kasra; Sibawayh calls this ikhtilas (a rapid, reduced vowel).

Abu 'Amr and Qalun in one narration read it between the fatha and the sukun.

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Warsh and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and a shadda on the dal.

Al-Nahhas said: This reading is clear in Arabic, and its origin is "yahtadi"; the ta' was assimilated into the dal and its vowel was transferred to the ha'.

Hafs, Ya'qub and al-A'mash read like the reading of Ibn Kathir, except that they gave the ha' a kasra; they said: because the kasra is the original vowel when two sukuns meet.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "yihiddi" with a kasra on the ya' and the ha', and a shadda on the dal, by way of assimilation of vowel (itba').

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Yahya ibn Thabit read "yahdi" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ha', and a light dal (from hada, yahdi).

Al-Nahhas said: This reading has two possible explanations in Arabic, though it is remote. The first: al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said that "yahdi" has the meaning of "yahtadi" (is guided). The second: Abu al-'Abbas said that the implied sense is: "am man la yahdi ghayrahu" (or he who does not guide others); then the speech is complete, and afterward he said: ﴿unless he is guided﴾, that is: but he needs to be guided. So it is an exceptive clause of the disjunctive kind, as you say: "So-and-so does not hear anything other than himself unless he hears," that is: but he needs to hear.

The meaning according to the preceding readings: Is he who guides people to the truth, and He is Allah, glorified is He, more worthy to be followed and taken as a model, or is he who does not guide himself by himself, unless another guides him, more worthy of being followed and taken as a model, let alone guiding others? The exception on this reading is an exception from the most general of states.

His words: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their condition, with two successive interrogations; that is: What is the matter with you, how do you judge by taking these as partners to Allah? Both interrogations are for rebuke and reproach, and "how" is in the accusative position governed by "you judge."

Then Glorified is He explained what these people are upon in the matter of their religion, and on what they built it, and by what they followed this false religion, which is shirk. So He said: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth.﴾ This is a new statement, not part of the preceding commands.

The meaning: These polytheists, in their association of others with Allah and their making rivals for Him, follow nothing but mere conjecture, guesswork and surmise, and this was not from insight. Rather, those among their predecessors who conjectured thought that these worshipped things would bring them near to Allah and intercede for them, and this conjecture had no basis at all, but was merely a corrupt imagination and false guesswork. Perhaps the indefiniteness of "conjecture" here is for belittling: that is, nothing but a weak conjecture that does not rest on what other conjectures rest on.

It was said: The intent of the verse is that most of them, in belief in Allah and acknowledging Him, follow nothing but conjecture; but the first is better.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed us that mere conjecture avails nothing against the truth, because the matter of religion is built only on knowledge, and by it the truth is distinguished from falsehood, while conjecture does not stand in the place of knowledge, and the truth is not attained by it, and it does not avail anything against the truth. The accusative of "shay'an" may be as a verbal noun or as its direct object, and "min al-haqq" (against the truth) is a circumstantial qualifier of it. The clause is a new sentence explaining the state of conjecture and its falsehood. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ of the evil deeds that proceed not from proof.

His words: ﴿And it is not for this Qur'an to be invented apart from Allah﴾. When Glorified is He finished with the proofs of monotheism and its arguments, He began to establish the matter of prophethood. That is: It is not right and not proper that this Qur'an, which includes clear proofs and manifest evidences, should be invented by the creatures apart from Allah; rather it is from Allah, mighty and majestic. How could it be proper for it to be invented, when the people who are the most eloquent of the Arabs in tongue and the most subtle in minds were unable to produce a single sura like it? But this Qur'an is ﴿a confirmation of what was before it﴾ of the books sent down to the prophets. This confirmation itself is an independent miracle, because its narratives agree with what is in the earlier books, although the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, had not learned of that, had not been taught it, had not asked about it, and had not connected with anyone who had knowledge of it. "Confirmation" is in the accusative as the predicate of the implied "kana" after "lakin" (but). It is also permissible for it to be accusative as an object of purpose for an omitted verb: that is, but Allah sent it down as a confirmation of what was before it.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is "and it is not befitting for this Qur'an to be invented," like His words: ﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161] and ﴿The believers should not all go out to fight﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122].

It was said: "an" (that) here has the meaning of "li" (for), that is: this Qur'an was not for it to be invented. It was also said: it has the meaning of "la" (not), that is: it is not invented.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the supposed (*taqdir*) reading of His words ﴿but a confirmation﴾ is "but there was a confirmation." According to them, the nominative is also permissible, meaning "but it is a confirmation." It was also said that the meaning is: "but the Qur'an is a confirmation of ﴿that which lies between its hands﴾ of the Books." That is, the earlier Books had already given good tidings of it before its revelation, so when it came it confirmed them. It was also said that the meaning is: "but the confirmation of the Prophet who lies between the hands of the Qur'an," and he is Muhammad (ﷺ), because they saw him before they heard the Qur'an from him.

His words ﴿and the detailed explanation of the Book﴾ are coordinated (*'atf*) with His words ﴿but a confirmation of that which lies between its hands﴾. So it may be read in the nominative or the accusative according to the two possibilities mentioned for *taṣdīq* (confirmation). *Tafṣīl* means clarification, that is, it makes clear what is in the earlier Books of God. "The Book" is generic, and it was also said that what is intended is the rulings clarified in the Qur'an, so "the Book" would refer to the Qur'an.

His words ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It falls within the scope of the corrective conjunction (*istidrak*) as a third predicate. This clause may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to "the Book." It may also be an independent resumptive clause with no grammatical position. ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a fourth predicate, meaning "originating from the Lord of the worlds." It may also be a circumstantial clause relating to "the Book" or to the pronoun of the Qur'an in His words ﴿there is no doubt in it,﴾ meaning "originating from the Lord of the worlds." It may also be connected to *taṣdīq* and *tafṣīl*, and the clause ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is a parenthetical insertion.

His words ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾: the interrogative is for rebuke against them, together with the establishment of the proof. The *am* here is the disjunctive *am*, which has the meaning of *bal* ("rather") plus the interrogative hamza, meaning: "Rather, do they say, 'He invented it and fabricated it'?"

Abu 'Ubayda said: *am* has the meaning of the conjunction *wa* ("and"), meaning: "and they say, 'He invented it.'" It was also said that the *mim* is superfluous, and the supposed reading is: "Do they say, 'He invented it'?" The interrogative is for reproach and censure.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to challenge them until their incapacity became evident and their weakness was made clear, so He said: ﴿Say: "Then bring a sūrah like it."﴾ That is, if the matter is as you claim, that Muhammad invented it, then you, by way of invention, bring a sūrah like it in eloquence and excellence of composition. You are like him in knowledge of the language of the Arabs, in the eloquence of tongues and the rhetoric of speech. And call upon your helpers and supporters ﴿whomever you can﴾ to call upon and seek help from among the tribes of the Arabs, and from your gods which you make partners with God.

His words ﴿other than God﴾ are connected to "call upon": that is, call upon whoever is other than God from His creation ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that this Qur'an is fabricated.

Glory be to God the Mighty! How strong, how clear, and how manifest this proof is to the minds! For when they attributed the invention to one of themselves in humanity and in Arabic, He said to them: "This which you attribute to me, though I am one of you, you are not required to do anything except bring, while you are the great multitude, a sūrah similar to one of its sūrahs. Seek help from whomever you wish of the people of this Arabic tongue, despite their great numbers and the diversity of their dwellings, or from others of the children of Adam, or from the jinn, or from the idols. If you do this after your fierce efforts, then you are truthful in what you have attributed to me and ascribed to me." But when they heard this fair speech and this far-reaching appeal, they did not produce a single word, nor did they utter a syllable. Instead, they shrank from answering and clung to the hem of cold obstinacy and bare arrogance devoid of proof, and this is something no falsifier is incapable of.

For this reason, after this far-reaching challenge, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge﴾. He thus turned away (*aḍraba*) from the first statement and moved to explain that they hastened to deny the Qur'an before they had reflected upon it and understood its meanings and what it contains. Thus does whoever is rigid in imitation and does not care about what was brought by one who calls to the truth, and who holds fast to the hems of fairness. Rather, he rejects it merely because it does not agree with his desire, nor does it come according to his claim, before he knows its meaning and understands its foundation, as you see plainly and know by intuition.

The conclusion is that whoever denies a clear proof and an evident demonstration before encompassing its knowledge has relied on nothing in this denial except the bare fact that he is ignorant of what he denies and does not know it. So by this denial he proclaims his own ignorance at the top of his voice, and records his inability to grasp proofs in the most eloquent record. Yet his denial brings nothing against the proof or against the one who brought it:

*What enemies can inflict upon a fool is not as much as what the fool inflicts upon himself.*

His words ﴿and its ultimate meaning (*ta'wīl*) has not yet come to them﴾ are coordinated with ﴿they did not encompass its knowledge﴾, meaning: "Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and what its *ta'wīl* had not yet come to them." Or this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they denied it while they had not understood the *ta'wīl* of what they denied, and their minds had not reached it.

The meaning is that their denial occurred before they encompassed its knowledge, and before they knew what it would lead to of the truth of what it contains: the narration of past reports of earlier messengers and earlier nations, and the narration of future events that it foretold before they occurred, or before they understood it properly and their minds grasped it. For if they had reflected upon it with complete reflection, they would have understood it as it should be understood and known what it contains of matters that indicate, with the greatest clarity, that it is the speech of God. According to this, the meaning of its *ta'wīl* is what it leads to for one who reflects upon it, of subtle meanings and delicate, elegant insights. The expression "expectation" (*tawaqqu'*) is most apparent in the first meaning.

﴿Thus did those before them deny﴾: that is, in the same manner did those nations before them deny when the messengers came to them with the proofs and evidences of God. They denied before encompassing its knowledge, and before its *ta'wīl* came to them. ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ among the former nations, of evil consequence through sinking into the earth, transformation, and similar punishments that befell them, as that Qur'an has related of them and as the Books of God revealed to them contain.

His words ﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾: that is, among those who denied the Qur'an, there are some who believe in it inwardly and know that it is true and right, but who denied it out of arrogance and obstinacy. It was also said that what is meant is: among them are those who will believe in it in the future, even though they deny it in the present. Here the relative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is "among them." ﴿And among them are those who do not believe in it﴾: who do not affirm it inwardly, but deny it out of ignorance, as its verification has already passed. Or they will not believe in it in the future, but will remain in their rejection and persistence. It was also said that the pronoun in both places refers to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It has been said that this division is specific to the people of Makkah, and it has been said that it is general to all the disbelievers. ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters﴾, so He will recompense them for their deeds. What is meant by "the corrupters" is those who persist and are obstinate, or both groups: those who believe in it inwardly while denying it outwardly, those who deny it out of ignorance, and those who will believe in it in the future, and those who will not believe in it.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them, if they persisted in denying him and continued in it: ﴿To me is my work, and to you is your work﴾: that is, for me is the recompense of my work, and for you is the recompense of your work. I have conveyed to you what I was commanded to convey, and nothing else is incumbent upon me. Then he emphasized this with His words, (p. 626) ﴿You are not responsible for what I do, and I am not responsible for what you do﴾: that is, you will not be held accountable for my deeds, and I will not be held accountable for your deeds.

It has been said that this is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse of the sword, as a group of the exegetes held.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Thus has the word of your Lord been fulfilled﴾, that he said: "The word of your Lord has preceded."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "It has come true."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿Is one who does not guide unless he is guided?﴾, that he said: "The idols."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd, regarding His words ﴿And if they deny you, then say: "To me is my work"﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "He commanded him with this, then abrogated it, and commanded him to fight them."

So He said: Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists, arguing for the truth of monotheism and the falsehood of what they hold of shirk: ﴿Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ From the heaven, by rain; and from the earth, by plants and minerals. If they acknowledge this, the aim is achieved; and if they do not acknowledge it, they must acknowledge that it is Allah who created both of them. ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight?﴾ Or who is it that is cut off?
