Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 42–49 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen [to you]﴾, etc.

In this, Allah the Glorified has shown that among those disbelievers are some whose state of aversion and enmity has reached this limit: they listen to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he recites the Qur'an and teaches the sacred laws, outwardly, but in reality they do not hear, because the effect of hearing does not take place, which is the acceptance of what they hear and acting upon it. For this reason He said: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ Meaning: these people, although they listen outwardly, are deaf, and deafness is a barrier to their hearing. So how can you hope to get them to hear with the barrier present, which is deafness? How much more so when added to that is that they do not reason. For whoever is deaf and does not reason understands nothing and does not hear what is said to him.

The plural pronoun in "yastami'una" (they listen) is used in accordance with the meaning of "man" (whoever), while the singular is used in ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ in accordance with its wording.

It has been said: the reason is the greater number of listeners compared with lookers, because hearing does not depend on what sight depends upon, such as facing, the absence of a screen, the separation of rays, and light matching the light of the eye.

The implied sense in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen﴾ and ﴿And among them are those who look﴾ is: "And among them are people who listen, and among them some who look." The two hamzas in ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ and ﴿Can you guide the blind?﴾ are for denial, and the fa' in both places is for coordination with an implied element, as if it were said: "Do they listen to you, and [then] you make them hear? Do they look at you, and [then] you guide them?" The statement in ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾ is like the statement in ﴿And among them are those who listen﴾, etc., because blindness is a barrier, so how can one hope from its possessor to look?

To the loss of sight has been added the loss of insight, because the blind man who has insight in his heart may have correct intuition by which he understands in some situations something that stands in place of sight. Likewise the deaf man who reasons may intuit in a way that yields him some benefit. This is unlike one in whom blindness of sight and of insight are combined, for perception is then impossible for him. Likewise one in whom deafness and loss of reason are combined: the door of guidance is then closed to him. The answer to "even if" (law) in both places is omitted, indicated by what precedes them. The purpose of this statement is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for when a physician sees a patient who does not accept treatment at all, he turns away from him and rests from being occupied with him.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but it is people who wrong themselves﴾: This is mentioned after what preceded about not being guided by hearing and sight, to explain that this was not because of any deficiency in what Allah created for them of hearing, reason, sight and insight, but because of what came to be in their natures of partisanship and obstinacy against the truth, disputing with falsehood, and persisting in disbelief. They are the ones who wronged themselves by that, and Allah did not wrong them in anything at all. Rather, He created them and made for them of perceptive faculties what by which they perceive with the most complete perception, and He composed in them of senses by which they reach what they want, and He amply provided their worldly interests for them, and left them free between themselves and their religious interests. "Upon itself Buraq's [wine] is spilled," i.e., each one bears the consequence of his own action.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa lakin an-nas" (but people) with the nun lightened and an-nas in the nominative. The rest read it with the nun doubled and an-nas in the accusative.

Al-Nahhas said: A group of grammarians, among them al-Farra', claimed that when the Arabs say "wa lakinna" with the waw, they double the nun, and when they drop the waw, they lighten it.

It has been said: the point in placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is the increase of specification and affirmation, and fronting the object before the verb serves to convey restriction, or merely for emphasis while observing the rhyme (fasila).

His saying: ﴿And the Day He gathers them﴾: The adverbial phrase is in the accusative governed by an implied verb: i.e., "and remember the Day He gathers them." ﴿As if they had not remained﴾, i.e., as if they had not remained, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, i.e., resembling one who did not remain ﴿but an hour of the day﴾, i.e., a little of it. The intended meaning of "remaining" is remaining in the world. It has been said: in the graves. They regarded the long period as short, either because they wasted their lives in the world, so they made its existence like non-existence, or they regarded it as short out of confusion and bewilderment, or because of the length of their standing at the place of gathering, or because of the severity of the punishment they were in, they forgot the pleasures of the world and it was as if it had never been. Similar to this is their saying: ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [Al-Kahf: 19]. The clause ﴿They will recognize one another﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or it is a new clause.

The meaning: each of them will recognize the other as if they had been separated only a little, and that is at their emergence from the graves; then the recognition among them will cease because of the matters before them that are stunning to minds and bewildering to understanding.

It has been said: this recognition is the recognition of rebuke and reproach, one saying to another: "You misled me and led me astray," not the recognition of compassion and tenderness, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And no close friend will ask about a close friend﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 10], and His saying: ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no ties of kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 101]. It is reconciled by saying that what is meant by recognition is the recognition of rebuke, and on this is understood His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, [and] returning statement to one another﴾ [Saba': 31]. The different verses have been reconciled regarding this and similar matters by saying that the stations on the Day of Resurrection differ, so in some stations there may be what there is not in others.

﴿They have certainly lost who denied the meeting with Allah and were not guided.﴾ This is a recording by Allah the Glorified against them of loss, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. What is meant by "the meeting with Allah" is the Day of Resurrection at the reckoning and recompense. He denied that they were of the category of those guided, due to their ignorance and their not seeking what would save and benefit them.

His saying: ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾: Its origin is "in nurika" (if We show you), with "ma" added to emphasize the meaning of the conditional, and the emphatic nun was added. The meaning: if We cause you to see some of what We have promised them of the manifestation of your religion during your life, by their killing and capture, the answer to the condition is omitted, and the estimate is "then you will see it" or "then that is it." The clause "or We cause you to die" is conjoined to what precedes it. The meaning: or We do not show you that during your life, but We cause you to die before that, then to Us is their return, and then We punish them in the Hereafter, so We show you their punishment in it. The answer to "or We cause you to die" is also omitted: the estimate being "or We cause you to die before the showing, then We show you that in the Hereafter." The summary meaning of this verse: if We do not take vengeance upon them quickly, We will take vengeance upon them later.

Allah the Glorified did show him their killing, their capture, their humiliation, the loss of their might, and the breaking of the fury of their pride, through what befell them at the Battle of Badr and the engagements after it. So to Allah belongs all praise.

The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. It is possible that what is meant by those who speak this saying is all the nations who did not submit to their messengers whom Allah sent to them.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is disjunctive, as the leading scholars of tafsir mentioned: i.e., but what Allah wills of that comes to pass, so how could I be able to possess for myself harm or benefit?

Then He, Glorified, mentioned another of the doubts of the disbelievers. That was that whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) threatened them with the descent of punishment, they would say: "When is this promise?" The question from them is for denial and considering it far-fetched, and for discrediting prophethood. "If you are truthful" is an address from them to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers. The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. It is possible that what is meant by those who speak this saying is all the nations who did not submit to their messengers whom Allah sent to them.

Then Allah, Glorified, commanded His Messenger to answer them with what cuts off the root of the doubt and ends the obstinacy, so He said: ﴿Say: I do not possess for myself any harm or benefit﴾, i.e., I am not able to bring about benefit for myself or to ward off harm from myself, so how could I be able to possess that for another? He placed "harm" first because the context is to show inability to bring about the promise they hastened and considered far-fetched. The exception in His saying: ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is disjunctive, as the leading scholars of tafsir mentioned: i.e., but what Allah wills of that comes to pass, so how could I be able to possess for myself harm or benefit?

and this is the greatest admonition and the most eloquent deterrent for one whose habit and constant practice is calling upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and seeking his aid when calamities descend that none can repel except Allah, glorified is He. Likewise, one who begins to ask the Messenger (ﷺ) for what none can bring about except Allah, glorified is He. For this is the station of the Lord of the Worlds, who created the prophets and the righteous and all created beings, provided for them, gave them life and causes them to die. How then does one ask from a prophet among the prophets, or an angel among the angels, or a righteous one among the righteous, what he is unable to do and incapable of, and leave the asking to the Lord of lords, who is capable of everything, the Creator, the Provider, the Giver and the Withholder? It is sufficient for you, in what is in this verse, as an admonition: this is the master of the sons of Adam and the seal of the messengers, whom Allah commands to say to His servants: "I do not possess for myself any harm or benefit," so how could he possess it for another, and how could it be possessed by another whose rank is below his rank and whose station does not reach his station, let alone possess it for another? But these people attribute to them power over harm and benefit, and call upon them at times independently and at times alongside the Lord of Majesty. Enough is it of the evil of hearing it. Indeed, Satan—may Allah disgrace him—has reached through this means what delights his eye and comforts his chest, namely the disbelief of many of this blessed nation (p-628) ﴿while they think that they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 104] ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we will return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 156].

Then He, glorified is He, made clear that for every group there is a fixed term that they do not exceed, so there is no point in hastening the punishment. So He said: ﴿For every nation there is a term﴾. When that time comes, He fulfils His promise and requites each according to what he deserves. The meaning: for every nation among those judged between them and their messenger, or among some of them and others, there is a specific term and a particular time at which what Allah, glorified is He, intends for them descends upon them when it arrives. ﴿When their term comes﴾, i.e., that specified time, and the pronoun refers back to "every nation". ﴿Then they cannot delay it⦅﴾ from that specified term by an hour, i.e., a small portion of time, ﴿nor can they advance it﴾. The phrase ﴿nor can they advance it﴾ is conjoined to the phrase ﴿they cannot delay it﴾. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. The discussion of this verse mentioned here has already been given in the commentary on the verse at the beginning of al-A'raf, so we will not repeat it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿they will recognize one another among themselves﴾, that he said: a man recognizes his companion beside him but cannot speak to him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿And whether We show you﴾ the verse, that he said: "the evil of the punishment during your life," ﴿or cause you to die [before that]﴾, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾. And regarding His saying ﴿And for every nation there is a messenger; when their messenger comes﴾, he said: "on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 42–49 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen [to you]﴾, etc.

In this, Allah the Glorified has shown that among those disbelievers are some whose state of aversion and enmity has reached this limit: they listen to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he recites the Qur'an and teaches the sacred laws, outwardly, but in reality they do not hear, because the effect of hearing does not take place, which is the acceptance of what they hear and acting upon it. For this reason He said: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ Meaning: these people, although they listen outwardly, are deaf, and deafness is a barrier to their hearing. So how can you hope to get them to hear with the barrier present, which is deafness? How much more so when added to that is that they do not reason. For whoever is deaf and does not reason understands nothing and does not hear what is said to him.

The plural pronoun in "yastami'una" (they listen) is used in accordance with the meaning of "man" (whoever), while the singular is used in ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ in accordance with its wording.

It has been said: the reason is the greater number of listeners compared with lookers, because hearing does not depend on what sight depends upon, such as facing, the absence of a screen, the separation of rays, and light matching the light of the eye.

The implied sense in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen﴾ and ﴿And among them are those who look﴾ is: "And among them are people who listen, and among them some who look." The two hamzas in ﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ and ﴿Can you guide the blind?﴾ are for denial, and the fa' in both places is for coordination with an implied element, as if it were said: "Do they listen to you, and [then] you make them hear? Do they look at you, and [then] you guide them?" The statement in ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾ is like the statement in ﴿And among them are those who listen﴾, etc., because blindness is a barrier, so how can one hope from its possessor to look?

To the loss of sight has been added the loss of insight, because the blind man who has insight in his heart may have correct intuition by which he understands in some situations something that stands in place of sight. Likewise the deaf man who reasons may intuit in a way that yields him some benefit. This is unlike one in whom blindness of sight and of insight are combined, for perception is then impossible for him. Likewise one in whom deafness and loss of reason are combined: the door of guidance is then closed to him. The answer to "even if" (law) in both places is omitted, indicated by what precedes them. The purpose of this statement is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for when a physician sees a patient who does not accept treatment at all, he turns away from him and rests from being occupied with him.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but it is people who wrong themselves﴾: This is mentioned after what preceded about not being guided by hearing and sight, to explain that this was not because of any deficiency in what Allah created for them of hearing, reason, sight and insight, but because of what came to be in their natures of partisanship and obstinacy against the truth, disputing with falsehood, and persisting in disbelief. They are the ones who wronged themselves by that, and Allah did not wrong them in anything at all. Rather, He created them and made for them of perceptive faculties what by which they perceive with the most complete perception, and He composed in them of senses by which they reach what they want, and He amply provided their worldly interests for them, and left them free between themselves and their religious interests. "Upon itself Buraq's [wine] is spilled," i.e., each one bears the consequence of his own action.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa lakin an-nas" (but people) with the nun lightened and an-nas in the nominative. The rest read it with the nun doubled and an-nas in the accusative.

Al-Nahhas said: A group of grammarians, among them al-Farra', claimed that when the Arabs say "wa lakinna" with the waw, they double the nun, and when they drop the waw, they lighten it.

It has been said: the point in placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is the increase of specification and affirmation, and fronting the object before the verb serves to convey restriction, or merely for emphasis while observing the rhyme (fasila).

His saying: ﴿And the Day He gathers them﴾: The adverbial phrase is in the accusative governed by an implied verb: i.e., "and remember the Day He gathers them." ﴿As if they had not remained﴾, i.e., as if they had not remained, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, i.e., resembling one who did not remain ﴿but an hour of the day﴾, i.e., a little of it. The intended meaning of "remaining" is remaining in the world. It has been said: in the graves. They regarded the long period as short, either because they wasted their lives in the world, so they made its existence like non-existence, or they regarded it as short out of confusion and bewilderment, or because of the length of their standing at the place of gathering, or because of the severity of the punishment they were in, they forgot the pleasures of the world and it was as if it had never been. Similar to this is their saying: ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [Al-Kahf: 19]. The clause ﴿They will recognize one another﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or it is a new clause.

The meaning: each of them will recognize the other as if they had been separated only a little, and that is at their emergence from the graves; then the recognition among them will cease because of the matters before them that are stunning to minds and bewildering to understanding.

It has been said: this recognition is the recognition of rebuke and reproach, one saying to another: "You misled me and led me astray," not the recognition of compassion and tenderness, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And no close friend will ask about a close friend﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 10], and His saying: ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no ties of kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 101]. It is reconciled by saying that what is meant by recognition is the recognition of rebuke, and on this is understood His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, [and] returning statement to one another﴾ [Saba': 31]. The different verses have been reconciled regarding this and similar matters by saying that the stations on the Day of Resurrection differ, so in some stations there may be what there is not in others.

﴿They have certainly lost who denied the meeting with Allah and were not guided.﴾ This is a recording by Allah the Glorified against them of loss, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. What is meant by "the meeting with Allah" is the Day of Resurrection at the reckoning and recompense. He denied that they were of the category of those guided, due to their ignorance and their not seeking what would save and benefit them.

His saying: ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾: Its origin is "in nurika" (if We show you), with "ma" added to emphasize the meaning of the conditional, and the emphatic nun was added. The meaning: if We cause you to see some of what We have promised them of the manifestation of your religion during your life, by their killing and capture, the answer to the condition is omitted, and the estimate is "then you will see it" or "then that is it." The clause "or We cause you to die" is conjoined to what precedes it. The meaning: or We do not show you that during your life, but We cause you to die before that, then to Us is their return, and then We punish them in the Hereafter, so We show you their punishment in it. The answer to "or We cause you to die" is also omitted: the estimate being "or We cause you to die before the showing, then We show you that in the Hereafter." It has been said: the answer to "or We cause you to die" is His saying "then to Us is their return," because it indicates what is meant by the Prophet (ﷺ) seeing their punishment in the Hereafter. It has been said: the shift to the future form in both places is to bring the scene to mind, and the original would be "We showed you or We caused you to die." But this is open to question, for the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing of some of the punishment Allah promised the polytheists had not yet occurred, as had death.

The summary meaning of this verse: if We do not take vengeance upon them quickly, We will take vengeance upon them later.

Allah the Glorified did show him their killing, their capture, their humiliation, the loss of their might, and the breaking of the fury of their pride, through what befell them at the Battle of Badr and the engagements after it. So to Allah belongs all praise.

His saying: ﴿Then Allah is Witness over what they do﴾: He used "thumma" (then), which indicates distance, even though Allah the Glorified is a witness over what they do in both abodes, to indicate that what is meant by these actions is what results from them of recompense, or what arises from the making of the limbs speak to testify against them on the Day of Resurrection, so that is treated as the testimony of Allah against them, as al-Naysaburi mentioned.

﴿And for every nation﴾ among the past nations, at some time, there is a messenger whom Allah sends to them, who makes clear to them what Allah has legislated for them of rulings according to what the interest requires. ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾ to them and conveys to them what Allah sent him with, and they all deny him, ﴿it will be judged between them﴾, i.e., between the nation and its messenger, with justice, i.e., equity, so the messenger is saved and those who denied him are destroyed, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra': 15]. It is possible that what is meant by the pronoun in "between them" is the nation, on the assumption that some of them denied him and others confirmed him, so the deniers are destroyed and the confirmers are saved, and "they will not be wronged" in that judgment, so they are not punished without sin, nor taken to account without proof. From this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And the prophets and witnesses will be brought, and it will be judged between them﴾ [Az-Zumar: 69], and His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [An-Nisa': 41]. What is meant is emphasis on manifesting justice and fairness among the servants.

The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 50–58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. This is from Him, glory be to Him, a repudiation of the view of the disbelievers regarding hastening the punishment, after the first repudiation. That is: tell Me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you at night (bayatan), i.e., at a time of bayat, by which is meant the time in which they spend the night, sleep, and are heedless of taking precautions. Al-bayat, in the sense of al-tabyit (the act of attacking by night), is an ism masdar like al-salam in the sense of al-taslim, and it is in the accusative of time (zarf). Likewise (nahаran), i.e., at the time of being occupied with seeking livelihood and earning. The pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, and it has been said that it refers to Allah. The interrogative in ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ is for denunciation, which implies a prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The ground of the denunciation against them for their hastening is that the punishment is something hateful, from which hearts recoil and natures reject; so what motivates their hastening toward it? The sentence introduced by the interrogative is the answer of the condition with the fa' omitted. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, and the meaning is: you would regret the hastening, or recognize your error in it. It has also been said that the answer is His saying: ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾, and the sentence ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten from it?﴾ would be a parenthetical clause; the meaning being: if His punishment comes upon you, you will believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you. The first is preferable.

He said (what the criminals seek to hasten from it) and did not say (they seek to hasten from it), to indicate what necessitates leaving off hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear the punishment on account of his crime; so how would he hasten it? This is like what is said to one who finds a matter unwholesome and yet seeks it: "What do you bring upon yourself?"

Al-Nahhas related from al-Zajjaj that if the pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, then there are two possible analyses of "mādhā": first, that "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, and "dhā" means "alladhī" (which), and it is the predicate of "mā", with the returning pronoun omitted. The other analysis: that "mādhā" is one single word in the nominative position as a subject, and the predicate is what follows it. If the pronoun in (minhu) is taken to refer to Allah, Exalted, then "mādhā" is one single thing in the accusative position governed by (yastaʿjilu), and the meaning is: what thing do the criminals seek to hasten from Him, i.e., from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The entry of the interrogative hamza into ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾ on "thumma" is like its entry on the waw and the fa'; it is for denouncing their belief at a time when belief does not benefit, and that is after the descent of the punishment. It includes the meaning of terrifying them and making monstrous what they did at a time other than its time, while they abandoned it at the time when benefit and averting are achieved. This sentence falls under the statement commanded, and the word "thumma", which indicates delay, is used to signify remoteness; and "idhā" is used with the addition of "mā" for emphasis, signifying the certainty of the occurrence of belief from them at a time other than its time, so that there is in that an increase in ridiculing them.

The meaning: after the punishment of Allah has befallen you and His wrath and vengeance have descended upon you, do you believe at a time when this belief will not benefit you at all, nor will it avert harm from you? It has been said that this sentence is not included under the statement commanded, and that it is from the words of the angels, mocking them and belittling them. The first is preferable.

It has been said that "thamma" here is with a fatha on the tha', so it is locative, meaning "there". The first is preferable.

His saying: ﴿Now? And you used to seek to hasten it!﴾ It has been said that this is a resumptive sentence with an implied saying, not included under the statement that Allah commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them. That is: it is said to them at the time of their belief after the punishment has occurred: "Now you believe in it, when you used to seek to hasten it?" That is, seeking the punishment in denial and mockery, because their hastening was by way of denial and mockery. The intended purpose of his being commanded, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this to them is rebuke, mockery and belittling of them. The sentence ﴿and you used to seek to hasten it﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause. The word "ālān" was read with the deletion of the hamza after the lam and the transfer of its vowel onto the lam.

His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong: Taste the punishment of eternity﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb, said to be "now" (ālān), and what is meant by it is reproach and rebuke of them: that is, it is said to those who wronged themselves through disbelief and non-belief: this which you seek is pure harm, void of benefit in every respect, and the intelligent person does not seek that. And it is said to them, by way of humiliation: "Taste the punishment of eternity", that is, the lasting punishment that does not cease. The speakers of this statement and the one before it are said to be the angels who are the guardians of Hell; and it is not far-fetched that the speakers of that are the prophets specifically, or the believers generally. ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾ in worldly life, of disbelief and sins. The interrogative is for affirmation, and it is as if this statement is said to them in response to their pleading for relief from the punishment and the descent of retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related of them, after these clear explanations and answers to their false statements, that they asked again about the certainty of the punishment, so He said: ﴿And they ask you: Is it true?﴾ That is, they ask you, in mockery and denial: is what you promise us of punishment, in this world and the next, true? This question from them is pure ignorance and darkness, one layer upon another. Its reply has already been mentioned earlier, so their repetition here is like that of one who does not understand what he says or what is said to him. It has been said that the intended meaning of this questioning from them is about the truth of the Qur'an. The word "ḥaqq" is in the nominative as a predicate placed first, and the subject is the pronoun following it, and the fronting of the predicate is for emphasis; or it is the subject, and the pronoun, raised by it, serves in place of the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by (yastanbiʾūnaka). It was also read "ālḥaqqu huwa", with the lam being for the category, as if it were said: is it the truth, not falsehood?

His saying: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this statement to them in answer to their question, which came out in the form of mockery: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, without turning to what they intend by mockery: ﴿Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾: that is, yes, by my Lord, what I promise you of punishment is true, established, and will occur without doubt.

In this answer there is emphasis in several respects. First: the oath, with the particle specific to oaths placed in the position of "yes". Second: the entry of the emphatic "inna". Third: the lam in "laḥaqq". Fourth: the nominal form of the sentence. This indicates that they had reached the extreme of denial and rebellion beyond which there is no further extreme. Then He threatened them with the most severe threat and frightened them with the greatest fear, saying: ﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you cannot escape the punishment by flight, by trickery that does not benefit, or by obstinacy that does not repel anything of Allah's decree. This sentence is either conjoined to the sentence of the answer to the oath, or is resumed to show that they have no escape from the punishment of Allah in any way.

Then He increased the emphasis, saying: ﴿And if every soul that did wrong had all that is on earth, it would surely ransom itself with it﴾: that is, even if every soul among those characterized as having wronged themselves through disbelief in Allah and non-belief in Him had all that is on earth of every thing contained therein, of precious wealth and superior treasures, it would surely make it a ransom for itself from the punishment. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. And His saying earlier: ﴿And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment﴾ [Saba': 33]. The pronoun refers to the souls implied by "every soul".

The meaning of "asarru" is: they concealed, that is, they did not show regret but concealed it, because of what they had witnessed in that place, which had stripped their minds and taken away their composure. It is possible that there remained in them, in that state, a vestige that draws them toward the tribal partisanship they had in the world, so they concealed the regret lest the believers gloat over them. It has been said: the leaders concealed it among themselves without their followers, fearing their rebuke, because they were the ones who misled them and stood between them and Islam. This occurred when they saw the punishment; but after entering it, they are the ones who ﴿say: Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106]. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru" is: they displayed. It has been said: they found the pain of anguish in their hearts, because regret cannot be displayed. From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"So I concealed the regret on the day the caller called out to return the camels of Ghadirah."

Al-Mubarrad mentioned two meanings for this: first, that the signs of regret appeared on their faces, namely the contraction (inkisar), whose singular is sirar and plural is asarir; and second, what preceded. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru al-nadama" is: they made it sincere, because concealing it is sincerity. As for "lammā" in His saying ﴿when they saw the punishment﴾, it is a temporal adverb meaning "when", in the accusative governed by "asarru", or a conditional particle whose answer is omitted, the preceding indicating it.

﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾: that is, Allah judged between the believers and the disbelievers, or between the leaders and the followers, or between the oppressors among the disbelievers and the oppressed. It has been said: the meaning of judging between them is the sending down of punishment upon them. "Al-qist" is justice. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: Allah does not wrong them in what He does to them of the punishment that has befallen them, for it is because of what they earned.

The clause ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is brought to affirm the perfection of His power, for whoever owns what is in the heavens and the earth disposes of it as he wills. He gave precedence to the non-rational beings, since they are the majority of creatures.

It has been said: when He mentioned the ransoming of the disbelievers with what is on earth, had they possessed it, He clarified that all things belong to Allah, and they have nothing with which they could ransom themselves. It has been said: when He swore to the truth of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought, He wished to accompany that with clear proof that whatever is in the world, in all its varieties, belongs to Him and He disposes of it as He wills. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting serves to alert the heedless and awaken the bewildered. Then He emphasized what preceded with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true﴾: that is, it will certainly occur, and it is general, encompassing what they sought to hasten of the punishment as an initial inclusion. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting, as we said regarding the one before it, is with the indication of the certainty of the content of both sentences. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾: that is, the disbelievers do not know what their welfare lies in so that they might act upon it, nor what their corruption lies in so that they might avoid it.

﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: He grants life and takes it away. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ in the Hereafter, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves, and will bestow favor upon whomever He wills of His servants.

[p. 630]

His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ means the Qur'an, which contains what whoever recites it and understands its meaning will be admonished by. Al-wa'z (admonition), in its original sense, is reminding of consequences, whether by encouragement or by warning. The admonisher is like the physician who forbids the patient what harms him. The "min" in "min Rabbikum" ("from your Lord") is connected to the verb, which is "jā'atkum" ("has come to you"), in which case it is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin). Or it is connected to an omitted element, in which case it is tab'idiyyah (partitive). ﴿And a healing for what is in the breasts﴾ means from the doubts that afflict some of the skeptics, because of what is derived from it of sound beliefs and its inclusion of the refutation of false beliefs. Al-huda (guidance) is direction for whoever follows the Qur'an, reflects upon it, and contemplates its meanings, to the path that leads to Paradise. Al-rahmah (mercy) is what is found in the Mighty Book of matters by which Allah shows mercy to His servants, so whoever wishes it seeks them until he attains them. The Great Qur'an includes these matters.

Then He commanded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and addressed him after His address to people in general, saying: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy—in that let them rejoice"﴾. By "fadl" (bounty) from Allah, glorified is He, is meant His favour upon His servants in both the deferred and the immediate, in what cannot be counted. "Rahmah" (mercy) is His mercy towards them.

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is Islam.

It was narrated from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatadah that the bounty of Allah is faith (iman), and His mercy is the Qur'an.

The more appropriate reading is to take "fadl" and "rahmah" in their generality, and what is in the Qur'an of both enters into that initially. The original wording is: "Say: by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, let them rejoice," then this verb was omitted because the second clause indicates it: ﴿in that let them rejoice﴾. It was said that the fa' (then) in this omitted verb enters into the answer of an implied conditional clause, as if it were said: "If they rejoice in anything, then let them single out the bounty of Allah and His mercy for rejoicing."

The repetition of the ba' (by) in "bi-rahmatihi" (by His mercy) is to indicate that each of the bounty and the mercy is an independent cause for rejoicing. Al-faraḥ (rejoicing) is the pleasure in the heart caused by attaining what is sought. Allah, glorified is He, has condemned rejoicing in several places, such as His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not like the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and He permitted it in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170], and as in this verse. The ba' in ﴿by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy﴾ may be connected to His saying "jā'atkum" (has come to you), and the sense would be: an admonition has come to you by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy; "fa-bi-dhālika" (in that) means: so by its coming, let them rejoice.

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Ya'qub read "fa-l-tafraḥū" (let them rejoice) with the second-person (taa' fawqiyyah). The majority read it with the third-person (yaa' tahtiyyah). The pronoun in "huwa khayrun" (it is better) refers to what was mentioned of bounty and mercy, or to the coming (of the admonition) according to the second aspect, or to the demonstrative in His saying "fa-bi-dhālika." The meaning is that this is better for them than what they gather of the debris of the world.

It has also been read with the taa' fawqiyyah in "yajma'ūn" (they gather), in agreement with the reading of "fa-l-tafraḥū" with it.

It is established in Arabic that the lam of command (lam al-amr) is omitted with the second-person, except in a rare dialect, and this reading came upon it. The majority read "yajma'ūn" with the yaa' tahtiyyah, as they read "fa-l-yafraḥū."

It was narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "yajma'ūn" with the taa' fawqiyyah and "fa-l-yafraḥū" with the yaa' tahtiyyah.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: A man came to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: "My brother complains of his stomach," so he prescribed him wine. He said: "Glory be to Allah! Allah has not placed healing in what is impure. Healing is only in something of the Qur'an and honey, and they are a healing for what is in the breasts and a healing for mankind."

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan who said: "Indeed Allah made the Qur'an a healing for what is in the breasts, and He did not make it a healing for your diseases."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I complain of my chest.' He said: 'Recite the Qur'an, for Allah says: It is a healing for what is in the breasts.'"

Al-Bayhaqi recorded in Shu'ab al-Iman from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' that "a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) of a pain in his throat. He said: 'Upon you is the recitation of the Qur'an and honey, for the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts, and honey is a healing from every disease.'"

Abu Dawud, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ubayy who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me [the reading] with the taa'," meaning the taa' fawqiyyah. Something similar to this has been narrated through other than this chain.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy'—the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you of its people."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat recorded from al-Bara' something like this from his statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri something like this.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the verse, that he said: "By the Book of Allah and by Islam."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him that he said: "His bounty is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him also, that he said: "By the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and by His mercy is when He made them of its people."

Similar to these earlier narrations has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿it is better than what they gather﴾ that it means: better than the wealth, the crops, and the livestock that they gather.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 50–58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. This is from Him, glory be to Him, a repudiation of the view of the disbelievers regarding hastening the punishment, after the first repudiation. That is: tell Me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you at night (bayatan), i.e., at a time of bayat, by which is meant the time in which they spend the night, sleep, and are heedless of taking precautions. Al-bayat, in the sense of al-tabyit (the act of attacking by night), is an ism masdar like al-salam in the sense of al-taslim, and it is in the accusative of time (zarf). Likewise (nahаran), i.e., at the time of being occupied with seeking livelihood and earning. The pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, and it has been said that it refers to Allah. The interrogative in ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ is for denunciation, which implies a prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The ground of the denunciation against them for their hastening is that the punishment is something hateful, from which hearts recoil and natures reject; so what motivates their hastening toward it? The sentence introduced by the interrogative is the answer of the condition with the fa' omitted. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, and the meaning is: you would regret the hastening, or recognize your error in it. It has also been said that the answer is His saying: ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾, and the sentence ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten from it?﴾ would be a parenthetical clause; the meaning being: if His punishment comes upon you, you will believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you. The first is preferable.

He said (what the criminals seek to hasten from it) and did not say (they seek to hasten from it), to indicate what necessitates leaving off hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear the punishment on account of his crime; so how would he hasten it? This is like what is said to one who finds a matter unwholesome and yet seeks it: "What do you bring upon yourself?"

Al-Nahhas related from al-Zajjaj that if the pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, then there are two possible analyses of "mādhā": first, that "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, and "dhā" means "alladhī" (which), and it is the predicate of "mā", with the returning pronoun omitted. The other analysis: that "mādhā" is one single word in the nominative position as a subject, and the predicate is what follows it. If the pronoun in (minhu) is taken to refer to Allah, Exalted, then "mādhā" is one single thing in the accusative position governed by (yastaʿjilu), and the meaning is: what thing do the criminals seek to hasten from Him, i.e., from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The entry of the interrogative hamza into ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾ on "thumma" is like its entry on the waw and the fa'; it is for denouncing their belief at a time when belief does not benefit, and that is after the descent of the punishment. It includes the meaning of terrifying them and making monstrous what they did at a time other than its time, while they abandoned it at the time when benefit and averting are achieved. This sentence falls under the statement commanded, and the word "thumma", which indicates delay, is used to signify remoteness; and "idhā" is used with the addition of "mā" for emphasis, signifying the certainty of the occurrence of belief from them at a time other than its time, so that there is in that an increase in ridiculing them.

The meaning: after the punishment of Allah has befallen you and His wrath and vengeance have descended upon you, do you believe at a time when this belief will not benefit you at all, nor will it avert harm from you? It has been said that this sentence is not included under the statement commanded, and that it is from the words of the angels, mocking them and belittling them. The first is preferable.

It has been said that "thamma" here is with a fatha on the tha', so it is locative, meaning "there". The first is preferable.

His saying: ﴿Now? And you used to seek to hasten it!﴾ It has been said that this is a resumptive sentence with an implied saying, not included under the statement that Allah commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them. That is: it is said to them at the time of their belief after the punishment has occurred: "Now you believe in it, when you used to seek to hasten it?" That is, seeking the punishment in denial and mockery, because their hastening was by way of denial and mockery. The intended purpose of his being commanded, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this to them is rebuke, mockery and belittling of them. The sentence ﴿and you used to seek to hasten it﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause. The word "ālān" was read with the deletion of the hamza after the lam and the transfer of its vowel onto the lam.

His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong: Taste the punishment of eternity﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb, said to be "now" (ālān), and what is meant by it is reproach and rebuke of them: that is, it is said to those who wronged themselves through disbelief and non-belief: this which you seek is pure harm, void of benefit in every respect, and the intelligent person does not seek that. And it is said to them, by way of humiliation: "Taste the punishment of eternity", that is, the lasting punishment that does not cease. The speakers of this statement and the one before it are said to be the angels who are the guardians of Hell; and it is not far-fetched that the speakers of that are the prophets specifically, or the believers generally. ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾ in worldly life, of disbelief and sins. The interrogative is for affirmation, and it is as if this statement is said to them in response to their pleading for relief from the punishment and the descent of retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related of them, after these clear explanations and answers to their false statements, that they asked again about the certainty of the punishment, so He said: ﴿And they ask you: Is it true?﴾ That is, they ask you, in mockery and denial: is what you promise us of punishment, in this world and the next, true? This question from them is pure ignorance and darkness, one layer upon another. Its reply has already been mentioned earlier, so their repetition here is like that of one who does not understand what he says or what is said to him. It has been said that the intended meaning of this questioning from them is about the truth of the Qur'an. The word "ḥaqq" is in the nominative as a predicate placed first, and the subject is the pronoun following it, and the fronting of the predicate is for emphasis; or it is the subject, and the pronoun, raised by it, serves in place of the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by (yastanbiʾūnaka). It was also read "ālḥaqqu huwa", with the lam being for the category, as if it were said: is it the truth, not falsehood?

His saying: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this statement to them in answer to their question, which came out in the form of mockery: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, without turning to what they intend by mockery: ﴿Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾: that is, yes, by my Lord, what I promise you of punishment is true, established, and will occur without doubt.

In this answer there is emphasis in several respects. First: the oath, with the particle specific to oaths placed in the position of "yes". Second: the entry of the emphatic "inna". Third: the lam in "laḥaqq". Fourth: the nominal form of the sentence. This indicates that they had reached the extreme of denial and rebellion beyond which there is no further extreme. Then He threatened them with the most severe threat and frightened them with the greatest fear, saying: ﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you cannot escape the punishment by flight, by trickery that does not benefit, or by obstinacy that does not repel anything of Allah's decree. This sentence is either conjoined to the sentence of the answer to the oath, or is resumed to show that they have no escape from the punishment of Allah in any way.

Then He increased the emphasis, saying: ﴿And if every soul that did wrong had all that is on earth, it would surely ransom itself with it﴾: that is, even if every soul among those characterized as having wronged themselves through disbelief in Allah and non-belief in Him had all that is on earth of every thing contained therein, of precious wealth and superior treasures, it would surely make it a ransom for itself from the punishment. ﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾: that is, Allah judged between the believers and the disbelievers, or between the leaders and the followers, or between the oppressors among the disbelievers and the oppressed. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 50–58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. This is from Him, glory be to Him, a repudiation of the view of the disbelievers regarding hastening the punishment, after the first repudiation. That is: tell Me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you at night (bayatan), i.e., at a time of bayat, by which is meant the time in which they spend the night, sleep, and are heedless of taking precautions. Al-bayat, in the sense of al-tabyit (the act of attacking by night), is an ism masdar like al-salam in the sense of al-taslim, and it is in the accusative of time (zarf). Likewise (nahаran), i.e., at the time of being occupied with seeking livelihood and earning. The pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, and it has been said that it refers to Allah. The interrogative in ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ is for denunciation, which implies a prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The ground of the denunciation against them for their hastening is that the punishment is something hateful, from which hearts recoil and natures reject; so what motivates their hastening toward it? The sentence introduced by the interrogative is the answer of the condition with the fa' omitted. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, and the meaning is: you would regret the hastening, or recognize your error in it. It has also been said that the answer is His saying: ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾, and the sentence ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten from it?﴾ would be a parenthetical clause; the meaning being: if His punishment comes upon you, you will believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you. The first is preferable.

He said (what the criminals seek to hasten from it) and did not say (they seek to hasten from it), to indicate what necessitates leaving off hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear the punishment on account of his crime; so how would he hasten it? This is like what is said to one who finds a matter unwholesome and yet seeks it: "What do you bring upon yourself?"

Al-Nahhas related from al-Zajjaj that if the pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, then there are two possible analyses of "mādhā": first, that "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, and "dhā" means "alladhī" (which), and it is the predicate of "mā", with the returning pronoun omitted. The other analysis: that "mādhā" is one single word in the nominative position as a subject, and the predicate is what follows it. If the pronoun in (minhu) is taken to refer to Allah, Exalted, then "mādhā" is one single thing in the accusative position governed by (yastaʿjilu), and the meaning is: what thing do the criminals seek to hasten from Him, i.e., from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The entry of the interrogative hamza into ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾ on "thumma" is like its entry on the waw and the fa'; it is for denouncing their belief at a time when belief does not benefit, and that is after the descent of the punishment. It includes the meaning of terrifying them and making monstrous what they did at a time other than its time, while they abandoned it at the time when benefit and averting are achieved. This sentence falls under the statement commanded, and the word "thumma", which indicates delay, is used to signify remoteness; and "idhā" is used with the addition of "mā" for emphasis, signifying the certainty of the occurrence of belief from them at a time other than its time, so that there is in that an increase in ridiculing them.

The meaning: after the punishment of Allah has befallen you and His wrath and vengeance have descended upon you, do you believe at a time when this belief will not benefit you at all, nor will it avert harm from you? It has been said that this sentence is not included under the statement commanded, and that it is from the words of the angels, mocking them and belittling them. The first is preferable.

It has been said that "thamma" here is with a fatha on the tha', so it is locative, meaning "there". The first is preferable.

His saying: ﴿Now? And you used to seek to hasten it!﴾ It has been said that this is a resumptive sentence with an implied saying, not included under the statement that Allah commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them. That is: it is said to them at the time of their belief after the punishment has occurred: "Now you believe in it, when you used to seek to hasten it?" That is, seeking the punishment in denial and mockery, because their hastening was by way of denial and mockery. The intended purpose of his being commanded, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this to them is rebuke, mockery and belittling of them. The sentence ﴿and you used to seek to hasten it﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause. The word "ālān" was read with the deletion of the hamza after the lam and the transfer of its vowel onto the lam.

His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong: Taste the punishment of eternity﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb, said to be "now" (ālān), and what is meant by it is reproach and rebuke of them: that is, it is said to those who wronged themselves through disbelief and non-belief: this which you seek is pure harm, void of benefit in every respect, and the intelligent person does not seek that. And it is said to them, by way of humiliation: "Taste the punishment of eternity", that is, the lasting punishment that does not cease. The speakers of this statement and the one before it are said to be the angels who are the guardians of Hell; and it is not far-fetched that the speakers of that are the prophets specifically, or the believers generally. ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾ in worldly life, of disbelief and sins. The interrogative is for affirmation, and it is as if this statement is said to them in response to their pleading for relief from the punishment and the descent of retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related of them, after these clear explanations and answers to their false statements, that they asked again about the certainty of the punishment, so He said: ﴿And they ask you: Is it true?﴾ That is, they ask you, in mockery and denial: is what you promise us of punishment, in this world and the next, true? This question from them is pure ignorance and darkness, one layer upon another. Its reply has already been mentioned earlier, so their repetition here is like that of one who does not understand what he says or what is said to him. It has been said that the intended meaning of this questioning from them is about the truth of the Qur'an. The word "ḥaqq" is in the nominative as a predicate placed first, and the subject is the pronoun following it, and the fronting of the predicate is for emphasis; or it is the subject, and the pronoun, raised by it, serves in place of the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by (yastanbiʾūnaka). It was also read "ālḥaqqu huwa", with the lam being for the category, as if it were said: is it the truth, not falsehood?

His saying: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this statement to them in answer to their question, which came out in the form of mockery: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, without turning to what they intend by mockery: ﴿Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾: that is, yes, by my Lord, what I promise you of punishment is true, established, and will occur without doubt.

In this answer there is emphasis in several respects. First: the oath, with the particle specific to oaths placed in the position of "yes". Second: the entry of the emphatic "inna". Third: the lam in "laḥaqq". Fourth: the nominal form of the sentence. This indicates that they had reached the extreme of denial and rebellion beyond which there is no further extreme. Then He threatened them with the most severe threat and frightened them with the greatest fear, saying: ﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you cannot escape the punishment by flight, by trickery that does not benefit, or by obstinacy that does not repel anything of Allah's decree. This sentence is either conjoined to the sentence of the answer to the oath, or is resumed to show that they have no escape from the punishment of Allah in any way.

Then He increased the emphasis, saying: ﴿And if every soul that did wrong had all that is on earth, it would surely ransom itself with it﴾: that is, even if every soul among those characterized as having wronged themselves through disbelief in Allah and non-belief in Him had all that is on earth of every thing contained therein, of precious wealth and superior treasures, it would surely make it a ransom for itself from the punishment. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. And His saying earlier: ﴿And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment﴾ [Saba': 33]. The pronoun refers to the souls implied by "every soul".

The meaning of "asarru" is: they concealed, that is, they did not show regret but concealed it, because of what they had witnessed in that place, which had stripped their minds and taken away their composure. It is possible that there remained in them, in that state, a vestige that draws them toward the tribal partisanship they had in the world, so they concealed the regret lest the believers gloat over them. It has been said: the leaders concealed it among themselves without their followers, fearing their rebuke, because they were the ones who misled them and stood between them and Islam. This occurred when they saw the punishment; but after entering it, they are the ones who ﴿say: Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106]. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru" is: they displayed. It has been said: they found the pain of anguish in their hearts, because regret cannot be displayed. From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"So I concealed the regret on the day the caller called out to return the camels of Ghadirah."

Al-Mubarrad mentioned two meanings for this: first, that the signs of regret appeared on their faces, namely the contraction (inkisar), whose singular is sirar and plural is asarir; and second, what preceded. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru al-nadama" is: they made it sincere, because concealing it is sincerity. As for "lammā" in His saying ﴿when they saw the punishment﴾, it is a temporal adverb meaning "when", in the accusative governed by "asarru", or a conditional particle whose answer is omitted, the preceding indicating it.

﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾: that is, Allah judged between the believers and the disbelievers, or between the leaders and the followers, or between the oppressors among the disbelievers and the oppressed. It has been said: the meaning of judging between them is the sending down of punishment upon them. "Al-qist" is justice. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: Allah does not wrong them in what He does to them of the punishment that has befallen them, for it is because of what they earned.

The clause ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is brought to affirm the perfection of His power, for whoever owns what is in the heavens and the earth disposes of it as he wills. He gave precedence to the non-rational beings, since they are the majority of creatures.

It has been said: when He mentioned the ransoming of the disbelievers with what is on earth, had they possessed it, He clarified that all things belong to Allah, and they have nothing with which they could ransom themselves. It has been said: when He swore to the truth of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought, He wished to accompany that with clear proof that whatever is in the world, in all its varieties, belongs to Him and He disposes of it as He wills. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting serves to alert the heedless and awaken the bewildered. Then He emphasized what preceded with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true﴾: that is, it will certainly occur, and it is general, encompassing what they sought to hasten of the punishment as an initial inclusion. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting, as we said regarding the one before it, is with the indication of the certainty of the content of both sentences. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾: that is, the disbelievers do not know what their welfare lies in so that they might act upon it, nor what their corruption lies in so that they might avoid it.

﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: He grants life and takes it away. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ in the Hereafter, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves, and will bestow favor upon whomever He wills of His servants.

[p. 630]

His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ means the Qur'an, which contains what whoever recites it and understands its meaning will be admonished by. Al-wa'z (admonition), in its original sense, is reminding of consequences, whether by encouragement or by warning. The admonisher is like the physician who forbids the patient what harms him. The "min" in "min Rabbikum" ("from your Lord") is connected to the verb, which is "jā'atkum" ("has come to you"), in which case it is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin). Or it is connected to an omitted element, in which case it is tab'idiyyah (partitive). ﴿And a healing for what is in the breasts﴾ means from the doubts that afflict some of the skeptics, because of what is derived from it of sound beliefs and its inclusion of the refutation of false beliefs. Al-huda (guidance) is direction for whoever follows the Qur'an, reflects upon it, and contemplates its meanings, to the path that leads to Paradise. Al-rahmah (mercy) is what is found in the Mighty Book of matters by which Allah shows mercy to His servants, so whoever wishes it seeks them until he attains them. The Great Qur'an includes these matters.

Then He commanded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and addressed him after His address to people in general, saying: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy—in that let them rejoice"﴾. By "fadl" (bounty) from Allah, glorified is He, is meant His favour upon His servants in both the deferred and the immediate, in what cannot be counted. "Rahmah" (mercy) is His mercy towards them.

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is Islam.

It was narrated from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatadah that the bounty of Allah is faith (iman), and His mercy is the Qur'an.

The more appropriate reading is to take "fadl" and "rahmah" in their generality, and what is in the Qur'an of both enters into that initially. The original wording is: "Say: by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, let them rejoice," then this verb was omitted because the second clause indicates it: ﴿in that let them rejoice﴾. It was said that the fa' (then) in this omitted verb enters into the answer of an implied conditional clause, as if it were said: "If they rejoice in anything, then let them single out the bounty of Allah and His mercy for rejoicing."

The repetition of the ba' (by) in "bi-rahmatihi" (by His mercy) is to indicate that each of the bounty and the mercy is an independent cause for rejoicing. Al-faraḥ (rejoicing) is the pleasure in the heart caused by attaining what is sought. Allah, glorified is He, has condemned rejoicing in several places, such as His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not like the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and He permitted it in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170], and as in this verse. The ba' in ﴿by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy﴾ may be connected to His saying "jā'atkum" (has come to you), and the sense would be: an admonition has come to you by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy; "fa-bi-dhālika" (in that) means: so by its coming, let them rejoice.

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Ya'qub read "fa-l-tafraḥū" (let them rejoice) with the second-person (taa' fawqiyyah). The majority read it with the third-person (yaa' tahtiyyah). The pronoun in "huwa khayrun" (it is better) refers to what was mentioned of bounty and mercy, or to the coming (of the admonition) according to the second aspect, or to the demonstrative in His saying "fa-bi-dhālika." The meaning is that this is better for them than what they gather of the debris of the world.

It has also been read with the taa' fawqiyyah in "yajma'ūn" (they gather), in agreement with the reading of "fa-l-tafraḥū" with it.

It is established in Arabic that the lam of command (lam al-amr) is omitted with the second-person, except in a rare dialect, and this reading came upon it. The majority read "yajma'ūn" with the yaa' tahtiyyah, as they read "fa-l-yafraḥū."

It was narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "yajma'ūn" with the taa' fawqiyyah and "fa-l-yafraḥū" with the yaa' tahtiyyah.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: A man came to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: "My brother complains of his stomach," so he prescribed him wine. He said: "Glory be to Allah! Allah has not placed healing in what is impure. Healing is only in something of the Qur'an and honey, and they are a healing for what is in the breasts and a healing for mankind."

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan who said: "Indeed Allah made the Qur'an a healing for what is in the breasts, and He did not make it a healing for your diseases."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I complain of my chest.' He said: 'Recite the Qur'an, for Allah says: It is a healing for what is in the breasts.'"

Al-Bayhaqi recorded in Shu'ab al-Iman from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' that "a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) of a pain in his throat. He said: 'Upon you is the recitation of the Qur'an and honey, for the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts, and honey is a healing from every disease.'"

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy'—the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you of its people."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat recorded from al-Bara' something like this from his statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri something like this.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the verse, that he said: "By the Book of Allah and by Islam."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him that he said: "His bounty is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him also, that he said: "By the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and by His mercy is when He made them of its people."

Similar to these earlier narrations has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).
