The original wording is: "Say: by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, let them rejoice," then this verb was omitted because the second clause indicates it: ﴿in that let them rejoice﴾. It was said that the fa' (then) in this omitted verb enters into the answer of an implied conditional clause, as if it were said: "If they rejoice in anything, then let them single out the bounty of Allah and His mercy for rejoicing."

The repetition of the ba' (by) in "bi-rahmatihi" (by His mercy) is to indicate that each of the bounty and the mercy is an independent cause for rejoicing. Al-faraḥ (rejoicing) is the pleasure in the heart caused by attaining what is sought. Allah, glorified is He, has condemned rejoicing in several places, such as His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not like the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and He permitted it in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170], and as in this verse. The ba' in ﴿by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy﴾ may be connected to His saying "jā'atkum" (has come to you), and the sense would be: an admonition has come to you by the bounty of Allah and by His mercy; "fa-bi-dhālika" (in that) means: so by its coming, let them rejoice.

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Ya'qub read "fa-l-tafraḥū" (let them rejoice) with the second-person (taa' fawqiyyah). The majority read it with the third-person (yaa' tahtiyyah). The pronoun in "huwa khayrun" (it is better) refers to what was mentioned of bounty and mercy, or to the coming (of the admonition) according to the second aspect, or to the demonstrative in His saying "fa-bi-dhālika." The meaning is that this is better for them than what they gather of the debris of the world.

It has also been read with the taa' fawqiyyah in "yajma'ūn" (they gather), in agreement with the reading of "fa-l-tafraḥū" with it.

It is established in Arabic that the lam of command (lam al-amr) is omitted with the second-person, except in a rare dialect, and this reading came upon it. The majority read "yajma'ūn" with the yaa' tahtiyyah, as they read "fa-l-yafraḥū."

It was narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "yajma'ūn" with the taa' fawqiyyah and "fa-l-yafraḥū" with the yaa' tahtiyyah.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: A man came to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: "My brother complains of his stomach," so he prescribed him wine. He said: "Glory be to Allah! Allah has not placed healing in what is impure. Healing is only in something of the Qur'an and honey, and they are a healing for what is in the breasts and a healing for mankind."

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan who said: "Indeed Allah made the Qur'an a healing for what is in the breasts, and He did not make it a healing for your diseases."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I complain of my chest.' He said: 'Recite the Qur'an, for Allah says: It is a healing for what is in the breasts.'"

Al-Bayhaqi recorded in Shu'ab al-Iman from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' that "a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) of a pain in his throat. He said: 'Upon you is the recitation of the Qur'an and honey, for the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts, and honey is a healing from every disease.'"

Abu Dawud, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ubayy who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me [the reading] with the taa'," meaning the taa' fawqiyyah. Something similar to this has been narrated through other than this chain.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy'—the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you of its people."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat recorded from al-Bara' something like this from his statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab recorded from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri something like this.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the verse, that he said: "By the Book of Allah and by Islam."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him that he said: "His bounty is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him also, that he said: "By the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and by His mercy is when He made them of its people."

Similar to these earlier narrations has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿it is better than what they gather﴾ that it means: better than the wealth, the crops, and the livestock that they gather.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 50–58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. This is from Him, glory be to Him, a repudiation of the view of the disbelievers regarding hastening the punishment, after the first repudiation. That is: tell Me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you at night (bayatan), i.e., at a time of bayat, by which is meant the time in which they spend the night, sleep, and are heedless of taking precautions. Al-bayat, in the sense of al-tabyit (the act of attacking by night), is an ism masdar like al-salam in the sense of al-taslim, and it is in the accusative of time (zarf). Likewise (nahаran), i.e., at the time of being occupied with seeking livelihood and earning. The pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, and it has been said that it refers to Allah. The interrogative in ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ is for denunciation, which implies a prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The ground of the denunciation against them for their hastening is that the punishment is something hateful, from which hearts recoil and natures reject; so what motivates their hastening toward it? The sentence introduced by the interrogative is the answer of the condition with the fa' omitted. It has also been said that the answer is omitted, and the meaning is: you would regret the hastening, or recognize your error in it. It has also been said that the answer is His saying: ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾, and the sentence ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten from it?﴾ would be a parenthetical clause; the meaning being: if His punishment comes upon you, you will believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you. The first is preferable.

He said (what the criminals seek to hasten from it) and did not say (they seek to hasten from it), to indicate what necessitates leaving off hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear the punishment on account of his crime; so how would he hasten it? This is like what is said to one who finds a matter unwholesome and yet seeks it: "What do you bring upon yourself?"

Al-Nahhas related from al-Zajjaj that if the pronoun in (minhu) refers to the punishment, then there are two possible analyses of "mādhā": first, that "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, and "dhā" means "alladhī" (which), and it is the predicate of "mā", with the returning pronoun omitted. The other analysis: that "mādhā" is one single word in the nominative position as a subject, and the predicate is what follows it. If the pronoun in (minhu) is taken to refer to Allah, Exalted, then "mādhā" is one single thing in the accusative position governed by (yastaʿjilu), and the meaning is: what thing do the criminals seek to hasten from Him, i.e., from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The entry of the interrogative hamza into ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?﴾ on "thumma" is like its entry on the waw and the fa'; it is for denouncing their belief at a time when belief does not benefit, and that is after the descent of the punishment. It includes the meaning of terrifying them and making monstrous what they did at a time other than its time, while they abandoned it at the time when benefit and averting are achieved. This sentence falls under the statement commanded, and the word "thumma", which indicates delay, is used to signify remoteness; and "idhā" is used with the addition of "mā" for emphasis, signifying the certainty of the occurrence of belief from them at a time other than its time, so that there is in that an increase in ridiculing them.

The meaning: after the punishment of Allah has befallen you and His wrath and vengeance have descended upon you, do you believe at a time when this belief will not benefit you at all, nor will it avert harm from you? It has been said that this sentence is not included under the statement commanded, and that it is from the words of the angels, mocking them and belittling them. The first is preferable.

It has been said that "thamma" here is with a fatha on the tha', so it is locative, meaning "there". The first is preferable.

His saying: ﴿Now? And you used to seek to hasten it!﴾ It has been said that this is a resumptive sentence with an implied saying, not included under the statement that Allah commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them. That is: it is said to them at the time of their belief after the punishment has occurred: "Now you believe in it, when you used to seek to hasten it?" That is, seeking the punishment in denial and mockery, because their hastening was by way of denial and mockery. The intended purpose of his being commanded, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this to them is rebuke, mockery and belittling of them. The sentence ﴿and you used to seek to hasten it﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause. The word "ālān" was read with the deletion of the hamza after the lam and the transfer of its vowel onto the lam.

His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong: Taste the punishment of eternity﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb, said to be "now" (ālān), and what is meant by it is reproach and rebuke of them: that is, it is said to those who wronged themselves through disbelief and non-belief: this which you seek is pure harm, void of benefit in every respect, and the intelligent person does not seek that. And it is said to them, by way of humiliation: "Taste the punishment of eternity", that is, the lasting punishment that does not cease. The speakers of this statement and the one before it are said to be the angels who are the guardians of Hell; and it is not far-fetched that the speakers of that are the prophets specifically, or the believers generally. ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾ in worldly life, of disbelief and sins. The interrogative is for affirmation, and it is as if this statement is said to them in response to their pleading for relief from the punishment and the descent of retribution.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, related of them, after these clear explanations and answers to their false statements, that they asked again about the certainty of the punishment, so He said: ﴿And they ask you: Is it true?﴾ That is, they ask you, in mockery and denial: is what you promise us of punishment, in this world and the next, true? This question from them is pure ignorance and darkness, one layer upon another. Its reply has already been mentioned earlier, so their repetition here is like that of one who does not understand what he says or what is said to him. It has been said that the intended meaning of this questioning from them is about the truth of the Qur'an. The word "ḥaqq" is in the nominative as a predicate placed first, and the subject is the pronoun following it, and the fronting of the predicate is for emphasis; or it is the subject, and the pronoun, raised by it, serves in place of the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position governed by (yastanbiʾūnaka). It was also read "ālḥaqqu huwa", with the lam being for the category, as if it were said: is it the truth, not falsehood?

His saying: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say this statement to them in answer to their question, which came out in the form of mockery: that is, say to them, O Muhammad, without turning to what they intend by mockery: ﴿Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾: that is, yes, by my Lord, what I promise you of punishment is true, established, and will occur without doubt.

In this answer there is emphasis in several respects. First: the oath, with the particle specific to oaths placed in the position of "yes". Second: the entry of the emphatic "inna". Third: the lam in "laḥaqq". Fourth: the nominal form of the sentence. This indicates that they had reached the extreme of denial and rebellion beyond which there is no further extreme. Then He threatened them with the most severe threat and frightened them with the greatest fear, saying: ﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you cannot escape the punishment by flight, by trickery that does not benefit, or by obstinacy that does not repel anything of Allah's decree. This sentence is either conjoined to the sentence of the answer to the oath, or is resumed to show that they have no escape from the punishment of Allah in any way.

Then He increased the emphasis, saying: ﴿And if every soul that did wrong had all that is on earth, it would surely ransom itself with it﴾: that is, even if every soul among those characterized as having wronged themselves through disbelief in Allah and non-belief in Him had all that is on earth of every thing contained therein, of precious wealth and superior treasures, it would surely make it a ransom for itself from the punishment. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. And His saying earlier: ﴿And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment﴾ [Saba': 33]. The pronoun refers to the souls implied by "every soul".

The meaning of "asarru" is: they concealed, that is, they did not show regret but concealed it, because of what they had witnessed in that place, which had stripped their minds and taken away their composure. It is possible that there remained in them, in that state, a vestige that draws them toward the tribal partisanship they had in the world, so they concealed the regret lest the believers gloat over them. It has been said: the leaders concealed it among themselves without their followers, fearing their rebuke, because they were the ones who misled them and stood between them and Islam. This occurred when they saw the punishment; but after entering it, they are the ones who ﴿say: Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106]. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru" is: they displayed. It has been said: they found the pain of anguish in their hearts, because regret cannot be displayed. From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"So I concealed the regret on the day the caller called out to return the camels of Ghadirah."

Al-Mubarrad mentioned two meanings for this: first, that the signs of regret appeared on their faces, namely the contraction (inkisar), whose singular is sirar and plural is asarir; and second, what preceded. It has been said: the meaning of "asarru al-nadama" is: they made it sincere, because concealing it is sincerity. As for "lammā" in His saying ﴿when they saw the punishment﴾, it is a temporal adverb meaning "when", in the accusative governed by "asarru", or a conditional particle whose answer is omitted, the preceding indicating it.

﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾: that is, Allah judged between the believers and the disbelievers, or between the leaders and the followers, or between the oppressors among the disbelievers and the oppressed. It has been said: the meaning of judging between them is the sending down of punishment upon them. "Al-qist" is justice. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: Allah does not wrong them in what He does to them of the punishment that has befallen them, for it is because of what they earned.

The clause ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is brought to affirm the perfection of His power, for whoever owns what is in the heavens and the earth disposes of it as he wills. He gave precedence to the non-rational beings, since they are the majority of creatures.

It has been said: when He mentioned the ransoming of the disbelievers with what is on earth, had they possessed it, He clarified that all things belong to Allah, and they have nothing with which they could ransom themselves. It has been said: when He swore to the truth of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought, He wished to accompany that with clear proof that whatever is in the world, in all its varieties, belongs to Him and He disposes of it as He wills. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting serves to alert the heedless and awaken the bewildered. Then He emphasized what preceded with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true﴾: that is, it will certainly occur, and it is general, encompassing what they sought to hasten of the punishment as an initial inclusion. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting, as we said regarding the one before it, is with the indication of the certainty of the content of both sentences. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾: that is, the disbelievers do not know what their welfare lies in so that they might act upon it, nor what their corruption lies in so that they might avoid it.

﴿He gives life and causes death﴾: He grants life and takes it away. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ in the Hereafter, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves, and will bestow favor upon whomever He wills of His servants.

[p. 630]

His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ means the Qur'an, which contains what whoever recites it and understands its meaning will be admonished by. Al-wa'z (admonition), in its original sense, is reminding of consequences, whether by encouragement or by warning. The admonisher is like the physician who forbids the patient what harms him. The "min" in "min Rabbikum" ("from your Lord") is connected to the verb, which is "jā'atkum" ("has come to you"), in which case it is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin). Or it is connected to an omitted element, in which case it is tab'idiyyah (partitive). ﴿And a healing for what is in the breasts﴾ means from the doubts that afflict some of the skeptics, because of what is derived from it of sound beliefs and its inclusion of the refutation of false beliefs. Al-huda (guidance) is direction for whoever follows the Qur'an, reflects upon it, and contemplates its meanings, to the path that leads to Paradise. Al-rahmah (mercy) is what is found in the Mighty Book of matters by which Allah shows mercy to His servants, so whoever wishes it seeks them until he attains them. The Great Qur'an includes these matters.

Then He commanded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and addressed him after His address to people in general, saying: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy—in that let them rejoice"﴾. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 59–64 (part 1 of 2):

By His saying, ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down…"﴾ and so on, He (glory be to Him) points to another path, different from what preceded, for establishing prophethood. The gist of its explanation is this: you judge some things as lawful and some as unlawful. If that is merely by whim and desire, then it is rejected by the agreement of intelligent people, Muslim and disbelieving alike. But if it is because you believe it to be Allah's ruling concerning you and concerning what He has provided for you, then you know that only through a means that connects you to Allah, and there is no means by which the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful except through the Messengers (p-631) whom Allah has sent to His servants. The meaning of "Have you considered" is "Inform me." The phrase "what" (mā) is in a position of accusative governed by "Have you considered" (arara'aytum), which contains the sense of "Inform me."

It has also been said that "what" (mā) is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ The "Say" in His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. The connecting pronoun is omitted, and the subject with its predicate is in the accusative position governed by "Have you considered." The meaning is: "Inform me about what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful; has Allah permitted you to make it lawful and unlawful, or do you invent lies against Allah?" On both views, "min" in "some of it unlawful" is partitive; the implication is: you made part of it unlawful and made part of it lawful. This is like what they used to do with livestock, as has been related about them in the Noble Book. The meaning of the sending down of provision is that rain descends from above, and likewise the matter of the provision of the servants is decreed in the heavens, as is established in the Preserved Tablet, which contains mention of everything by Him (glory be to Him and exalted).

It is narrated from al-Zajjaj that "what" (mā) is in the accusative position governed by "sent down," and "sent down" here means "created," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6] and ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. According to this view and the first view, His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a new (resumptive) statement. It has been said: it is permissible that the interrogative hamza in ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ is for denunciation, and "am" is disjunctive, meaning: "Rather, do you invent lies against Allah?" The mention of the Noble Name and its placement before the verb serves to indicate the completeness of the fabrication.

In this noble verse is something that strikes the ears of those who take the lead in issuing rulings to the servants of Allah concerning His law, declaring things lawful and unlawful, permissible or not, while they are among the imitators who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not comprehend them, and do not know what they are. Their knowledge goes no further than relating the saying of some speaker from this Community whom they have imitated in their religion and made into an independent lawgiver: whatever he acted upon from the Book and the Sunnah is what is acted upon among them; and whatever did not reach him, or reached him but he did not understand it properly, or he understood it and erred from the correct position in his ijtihad and his weighing of evidence, is in their judgment abrogated, its ruling lifted from the servants. Yet those whom they imitate are, like them, obligated by this Law and judged by its rulings, just as they are judged by it. He exerted his own opinion and discharged what was incumbent upon him, and he earns two rewards if he is correct and one reward if he errs. The real problem lies in their making his erroneous opinion into an independent law and an evidence to be acted upon. In this they have erred a clear error and blundered a gross blunder. For the permission granted to the mujtahid in exercising his own opinion is specific to him alone, and no one among the people of Islam whose sayings are considered has said that it is permissible for another to act upon it by imitating him and following his example. What the imitators have brought to establish this falsehood is of idle ignorance. O Allah, just as You have granted us of knowledge by which we distinguish between truth and falsehood, grant us of fairness by which we may attain what is the truth in Your sight, O Giver of good.

Then He said: ﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: what will be their thought on this Day, and what will be done to them therein? This interrogative sentence, which includes the magnification of the threat against them, is not included under the saying which Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them; rather it is an independent sentence, brought to explain what the punishment of Allah will befall them. "On the Day of Resurrection" is in the accusative governed by "thought." The mention of "lying" after "inventing" is, although inventing is only lying, for added emphasis.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "wa-mā ẓanna" as a verb. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, bestowing upon them kinds of blessings in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿but most of them are not grateful﴾ to Allah for His blessings that reach them from Him (glory be to Him) at every time and every moment.

His saying: ﴿And you are not in any matter﴾ — the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "mā" is negative.

Ash-sha'n (the matter) means "affair" in the sense of "intention," and its root is with a hamza; its plural is shu'ūn.

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs say: "mā sha'anta sha'anahu," meaning: "I did not do his deed."

﴿And you recite from it any Qur'an﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in "minhu" refers to "ash-sha'n," and the prepositional phrase is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a recitation proceeding from it, since reciting the Qur'an is among the greatest of his matters (ﷺ). The meaning is: he recites on account of the matter that gave rise to the Qur'an, so he knows its ruling, or he recites the Qur'an that descends concerning that matter.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Book, meaning: whatever is of the Book of Allah of Qur'an; it is repeated for its magnification, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. The address in ﴿and you do no deed﴾ is to the Messenger of Allah and to the Community. It has been said: the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿But We are witnesses over you when you engage in it﴾ is an exceptive construction with an emptied (incomplete) antecedent, of the most general states of the addressees, meaning: witnesses over you regarding your deed. The pronoun in "fīhi" in ﴿when you engage in it﴾ refers to the deed; it is said: "Fulān plunged into the speech and the deed" when he pressed forward into it.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: when you spread lies concerning the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿And not hidden from your Lord is an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven﴾.

Al-Kisā'ī read "yaʿzibu" with a kasra on the zāy, and the rest read it with a ḍamma; both are eloquent dialects. The meaning of "yaʿzubu" is "to be hidden," and it has been said: "to be far." Ibn Kaysan said: "to go away." These meanings are close. The "min" in "min mithqāl" is extra for emphasis, meaning: nor is hidden from your Lord the weight of an atom, i.e., a red ant. He expressed it with "the earth and the heaven" although nothing is hidden from Him (glory be to Him), neither within them nor in what is outside them, because people do not witness anything other than them and what is in them of created things; and He placed "the earth" before "the heaven" because it is the place of the world's settlement, so they witness what is in it from nearby. The "wāw" in ﴿nor what is less than that or greater﴾ is for coordination with the wording of "mithqāl," and both are in the accusative because they are negated. It is permissible for the coordination to be with "dharra" (atom). It has been said: their accusative is governed by "lā" (not) of generic negation, and the "wāw" is for resumption, and it is not among the complements of "wa-mā yaʿzubu." The predicate of "lā" is ﴿except that it is in a clear Record﴾, and the meaning is: "Nor is anything smaller than an atom's weight or greater than it, except that it is in a clear Record; how then could it be hidden from Him?" Yaʿqūb and Ḥamza read "aṣghara" and "akbara" in the nominative. The reasoning for this is that it is coordinated with the position of "min mithqāl," which is in the nominative. The reading in the accusative or nominative as coordination with the wording or the position of "mithqāl," or with the wording of "dharra," has been subject to an objection, namely that the sense of the verse becomes: "Nothing is hidden from Him in the earth or in the heaven except that it is in a Record," which implies that this thing in the Record is outside His knowledge, and that is impossible.

This objection has been answered: created things are of two kinds. One kind Allah brought into existence directly without intermediary, such as the angels, the heavens and the earth. Another kind He brought into existence through the first kind, such as the events of the world of generation and corruption. Without doubt this second kind is remote in the chain of causation from the rank of the first. So the meaning of the verse is that nothing in the earth or in the heaven is remote from the rank of His existence (glory be to Him) except that it is in a clear Record, in which the form of those known things is fixed. The purpose is to refute him who claims that He does not know particulars.

It has also been answered that the exception is disjunctive: i.e., "but rather, it is in a clear Record."

Abū ʿAlī al-Jurjānī mentioned that "illā" here means "wāw" (and), on the basis that the speech is complete at His saying "nor greater," and then a new beginning occurs with "except that it is in a clear Record," meaning: "and it is also in a clear Record."

The Arabs sometimes place "illā" in the position of "wāw," and among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 10–11], meaning "and one who has wronged." And His saying: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against you, except those who have wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], meaning "and those who have wronged." "Huwa" (it) is supposed after the "wāw" that came in the sense of "illā," as in His saying: ﴿And say, "Ḥiṭṭah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], meaning "it is Ḥiṭṭah." Similarly ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisā': 171], and ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry but it is in a clear Record﴾ [al-An'ām: 59].

Al-Zajjaj said: the nominative, for those who read it in the nominative, is by inception, and its predicate is ﴿except in a Record﴾; and the author of al-Kashshāf chose this. For the accusative reading, which the majority recite, he chose that both are in the accusative governed by "lā" of generic negation, and he raised the problem of coordination in the manner we mentioned.

Then, when He (glory be to Him) made clear His encompassing of all things, and this served to strengthen the hearts of the obedient and to break the hearts of the disobedient, He mentioned the state of the obedient, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of Allah—there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ The "walī" (ally) in the language means "near."

What is meant by "the allies of Allah" is the pure believers, as if they had been brought near to Allah (glory be to Him) through their obedience to Him and their avoidance of His disobedience.

He (glory be to Him) explained these allies by His saying: ﴿Those who believed and used to be fearful of Allah﴾, that is, they believe in what must be believed in, and they guard against what they are obligated to guard against of the disobedience of Allah (glory be to Him). The meaning of the negation of fear concerning them is that they never fear as others fear, because they have fulfilled what Allah obligated upon them and refrained from the sins He forbade them; so they are confident in themselves and have good assumption of their Lord. Likewise they do not grieve over the loss of any object of desire, because they know that this is by the decree and destiny of Allah, so they submit to the decree and destiny and relieve their hearts of worry and turbidity. Their breasts are expanded, their limbs are active, and their hearts are joyful. The place of the relative clause is accusative as a substitute for "allies," or nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, or it is itself a subject whose predicate is "for them is good news," in which case it is not connected to what precedes; or it is accusative also in praise, or as a qualifier of "allies."

His saying: ﴿For them is good news in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of their being allies of Allah: that is, for them is good news from Allah while they are alive, through what He reveals to His prophets and sends down in His books, that the state of believers with Him is their entry into Paradise and His good pleasure with them, as many good tidings for the believers occur in the noble Qur'an. Likewise there is what they attain of good dreams, and what Allah graciously bestows upon them of answered supplication, and what they witness of glad tidings at the arrival of their appointed times, through the descent of angels upon them saying: "Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in Paradise." As for good news in the Hereafter, it is the angels' welcoming them, bringing glad tidings of success in bliss and safety from punishment.

The bounty (al-bushra) is a verbal noun (masdar) used to mean the thing announced as glad tidings, and the two adverbial phrases (al-zarfan) are in the accusative position as circumstantial clauses (ḥāl): that is, "during their life in this world" and "during their life in the Hereafter." The meaning of ﴿There is no altering of the words of God﴾ is that there is no change to His statements in general, so it includes what He promised to His righteous servants by way of primary inclusion. The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers back to what was mentioned before it, namely their being given glad tidings in both abodes. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, whose worth cannot be measured and to which nothing else is comparable. The two sentences, ﴿There is no altering of the words of God﴾ and ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, are, according to those who permit it, a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) at the end of the speech, and their benefit is to confirm the good tidings and magnify their importance. Alternatively, the first is a parenthetical insertion and the second is a concluding appendage (tadhyil).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision﴾, that he said: "They are the people of polytheism who would make lawful from the livestock and the tilth whatever they wished, and make unlawful whatever they wished."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿when you engage in it﴾, that he said: "when you do it." Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His words: ﴿Nor is absent from your Lord﴾, that he said: "The weight of an atom is not hidden from Him, ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record﴾." He said: "It is the Record that is with God."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, concerning His words: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God﴾, that it was said: "Who are they, O Lord?" He said: "They are those who believed and used to be mindful of God."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They are those who, when seen, God is remembered."

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated "from Ibn Abbas, both marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and mawquf (stopping at Ibn Abbas), who said: 'They are those who, when seen, God is remembered because of their sight.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, marfu', and it is mursal (a report whose chain omits a companion).

Something similar has been narrated through other routes, both marfu' and mawquf.

Ahmad and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Amr ibn al-Jamuh that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "A servant does not attain the true reality of sincere faith until he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake. When he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake, he has deserved allegiance from God. Indeed, My allies among My servants and My beloved among My creation are those who are remembered by My remembrance, and I am remembered by their remembrance."

Ahmad narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, reaching the Prophet (ﷺ) with it: "The best of God's servants are those who, when seen, God is remembered; and the worst of His servants are those who go about with tale-bearing, who sow discord among loved ones, and who seek the faults of the innocent."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the one whose sight reminds you of God, whose speech increases your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire the Hereafter."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas, marfu', the like of it.

Al-Hakim narrated, and declared sound, from Ibn Umar, marfu': "Indeed, God has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their nearness to Him and their station with Him." A Bedouin then got down on his knees and said: "O Messenger of God, describe them to us, make them clear to us!" He said: "They are a people from the various strangers of mankind, from the scattered tribes, who have become pure with one another for God's sake and love one another for God's sake. On the Day of Resurrection God will set up for them pulpits of light and seat them upon them. People will fear while they will not fear. They are the allies of God, on whom there is no fear, nor will they grieve."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is good.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, marfu', something similar.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, marfu', something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of God: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God﴾, the verse, and he said: 'Those who love one another for God's sake.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, marfu', the like of it.

Traditions have come concerning the virtue of those who love one another for God's sake, none of which states that they are the ones intended by the verse.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ata' ibn Yasar, "from a man of the people of Egypt, who said: I asked Abu al-Darda' about the meaning of His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, and he said: 'No one has asked me about it since I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: No one has asked me about it besides you since it was revealed to me. It is: the righteous dream which a Muslim sees, or which is seen for him. So it is his good news in the life of this world, and his good news in the Hereafter is Paradise.'" In its chain is this unknown man.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, and he said: 'It is the righteous dream which the believer sees, or which is seen for him.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated "from Abd Allah ibn Amr, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, that he said: 'The righteous dream by which the believer is given good news is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood. So whoever sees such, let him inform of it,'" the hadith.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the verse, that he said: "In this world it is the righteous dream which the righteous servant sees, or which is seen for him; and in the Hereafter it is Paradise."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Mandah narrated, by way of Abu Ja'far from Jabir, "that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) interpreted the good news in the life of this world as the beloved dream, and in the Hereafter as the good news to the believer at death: 'Indeed, God has forgiven you and whoever carries you to your grave.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, marfu', the first part of the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas the like of it.

Sound traditions have come that the righteous dream is among the glad tidings and that it is a part of the parts of prophethood, but they have not been restricted to the interpretation of this verse.

It has been narrated that what is meant by the good news in the verse is His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from God a great bounty﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab 33:47).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated that from the route of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, by the route of Miqsam, that it is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾ (Surah Fussilat 41:30).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Nafi', who said: "Al-Hajjaj gave a sermon and said: 'Ibn al-Zubayr has altered the Book of God.' Ibn Umar said: 'Neither you nor Ibn al-Zubayr can do that: ﴿There is no altering of the words of God.﴾'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 59–64 (part 1 of 2):

By His saying, ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down…"﴾ and so on, He (glory be to Him) points to another path, different from what preceded, for establishing prophethood. The gist of its explanation is this: you judge some things as lawful and some as unlawful. If that is merely by whim and desire, then it is rejected by the agreement of intelligent people, Muslim and disbelieving alike. But if it is because you believe it to be Allah's ruling concerning you and concerning what He has provided for you, then you know that only through a means that connects you to Allah, and there is no means by which the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful except through the Messengers (p-631) whom Allah has sent to His servants. The meaning of "Have you considered" is "Inform me." The phrase "what" (mā) is in a position of accusative governed by "Have you considered" (arara'aytum), which contains the sense of "Inform me."

It has also been said that "what" (mā) is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ The "Say" in His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. The connecting pronoun is omitted, and the subject with its predicate is in the accusative position governed by "Have you considered." The meaning is: "Inform me about what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful; has Allah permitted you to make it lawful and unlawful, or do you invent lies against Allah?" On both views, "min" in "some of it unlawful" is partitive; the implication is: you made part of it unlawful and made part of it lawful. This is like what they used to do with livestock, as has been related about them in the Noble Book. The meaning of the sending down of provision is that rain descends from above, and likewise the matter of the provision of the servants is decreed in the heavens, as is established in the Preserved Tablet, which contains mention of everything by Him (glory be to Him and exalted).

It is narrated from al-Zajjaj that "what" (mā) is in the accusative position governed by "sent down," and "sent down" here means "created," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6] and ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. According to this view and the first view, His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a new (resumptive) statement. It has been said: it is permissible that the interrogative hamza in ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ is for denunciation, and "am" is disjunctive, meaning: "Rather, do you invent lies against Allah?" The mention of the Noble Name and its placement before the verb serves to indicate the completeness of the fabrication.

In this noble verse is something that strikes the ears of those who take the lead in issuing rulings to the servants of Allah concerning His law, declaring things lawful and unlawful, permissible or not, while they are among the imitators who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not comprehend them, and do not know what they are. Their knowledge goes no further than relating the saying of some speaker from this Community whom they have imitated in their religion and made into an independent lawgiver: whatever he acted upon from the Book and the Sunnah is what is acted upon among them; and whatever did not reach him, or reached him but he did not understand it properly, or he understood it and erred from the correct position in his ijtihad and his weighing of evidence, is in their judgment abrogated, its ruling lifted from the servants. Yet those whom they imitate are, like them, obligated by this Law and judged by its rulings, just as they are judged by it. He exerted his own opinion and discharged what was incumbent upon him, and he earns two rewards if he is correct and one reward if he errs. The real problem lies in their making his erroneous opinion into an independent law and an evidence to be acted upon. In this they have erred a clear error and blundered a gross blunder. For the permission granted to the mujtahid in exercising his own opinion is specific to him alone, and no one among the people of Islam whose sayings are considered has said that it is permissible for another to act upon it by imitating him and following his example. What the imitators have brought to establish this falsehood is of idle ignorance. O Allah, just as You have granted us of knowledge by which we distinguish between truth and falsehood, grant us of fairness by which we may attain what is the truth in Your sight, O Giver of good.

Then He said: ﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: what will be their thought on this Day, and what will be done to them therein? This interrogative sentence, which includes the magnification of the threat against them, is not included under the saying which Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them; rather it is an independent sentence, brought to explain what the punishment of Allah will befall them. "On the Day of Resurrection" is in the accusative governed by "thought." The mention of "lying" after "inventing" is, although inventing is only lying, for added emphasis.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "wa-mā ẓanna" as a verb. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, bestowing upon them kinds of blessings in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿but most of them are not grateful﴾ to Allah for His blessings that reach them from Him (glory be to Him) at every time and every moment.

His saying: ﴿And you are not in any matter﴾ — the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "mā" is negative.

Ash-sha'n (the matter) means "affair" in the sense of "intention," and its root is with a hamza; its plural is shu'ūn.

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs say: "mā sha'anta sha'anahu," meaning: "I did not do his deed."

﴿And you recite from it any Qur'an﴾. The meaning is: he recites on account of the matter that gave rise to the Qur'an, so he knows its ruling, or he recites the Qur'an that descends concerning that matter.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: when you spread lies concerning the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿And not hidden from your Lord is an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven﴾.

The predicate of "lā" is ﴿except that it is in a clear Record﴾, and the meaning is: "Nor is anything smaller than an atom's weight or greater than it, except that it is in a clear Record; how then could it be hidden from Him?" Another kind He brought into existence through the first kind, such as the events of the world of generation and corruption. Without doubt this second kind is remote in the chain of causation from the rank of the first. So the meaning of the verse is that nothing in the earth or in the heaven is remote from the rank of His existence (glory be to Him) except that it is in a clear Record, in which the form of those known things is fixed. The purpose is to refute him who claims that He does not know particulars.

It has also been answered that the exception is disjunctive: i.e., "but rather, it is in a clear Record."

Abū ʿAlī al-Jurjānī mentioned that "illā" here means "wāw" (and), on the basis that the speech is complete at His saying "nor greater," and then a new beginning occurs with "except that it is in a clear Record," meaning: "and it is also in a clear Record."

The Arabs sometimes place "illā" in the position of "wāw," and among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 10–11], meaning "and one who has wronged." And His saying: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against you, except those who have wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], meaning "and those who have wronged." "Huwa" (it) is supposed after the "wāw" that came in the sense of "illā," as in His saying: ﴿And say, "Ḥiṭṭah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], meaning "it is Ḥiṭṭah." Similarly ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisā': 171], and ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry but it is in a clear Record﴾ [al-An'ām: 59].

Al-Zajjaj said: the nominative, for those who read it in the nominative, is by inception, and its predicate is ﴿except in a Record﴾; and the author of al-Kashshāf chose this. For the accusative reading, which the majority recite, he chose that both are in the accusative governed by "lā" of generic negation, and he raised the problem of coordination in the manner we mentioned.

Then, when He (glory be to Him) made clear His encompassing of all things, and this served to strengthen the hearts of the obedient and to break the hearts of the disobedient, He mentioned the state of the obedient, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of Allah—there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ The "walī" (ally) in the language means "near."

What is meant by "the allies of Allah" is the pure believers, as if they had been brought near to Allah (glory be to Him) through their obedience to Him and their avoidance of His disobedience.

He (glory be to Him) explained these allies by His saying: ﴿Those who believed and used to be fearful of Allah﴾, that is, they believe in what must be believed in, and they guard against what they are obligated to guard against of the disobedience of Allah (glory be to Him). The meaning of the negation of fear concerning them is that they never fear as others fear, because they have fulfilled what Allah obligated upon them and refrained from the sins He forbade them; so they are confident in themselves and have good assumption of their Lord. Likewise they do not grieve over the loss of any object of desire, because they know that this is by the decree and destiny of Allah, so they submit to the decree and destiny and relieve their hearts of worry and turbidity. Their breasts are expanded, their limbs are active, and their hearts are joyful. The place of the relative clause is accusative as a substitute for "allies," or nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, or it is itself a subject whose predicate is "for them is good news," in which case it is not connected to what precedes; or it is accusative also in praise, or as a qualifier of "allies."

His saying: ﴿For them is good news in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of their being allies of Allah: that is, for them is good news from Allah while they are alive, through what He reveals to His prophets and sends down in His books, that the state of believers with Him is their entry into Paradise and His good pleasure with them, as many good tidings for the believers occur in the noble Qur'an. Likewise there is what they attain of good dreams, and what Allah graciously bestows upon them of answered supplication, and what they witness of glad tidings at the arrival of their appointed times, through the descent of angels upon them saying: "Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in Paradise." As for good news in the Hereafter, it is the angels' welcoming them, bringing glad tidings of success in bliss and safety from punishment.

The bounty (al-bushra) is a verbal noun (masdar) used to mean the thing announced as glad tidings, and the two adverbial phrases (al-zarfan) are in the accusative position as circumstantial clauses (ḥāl): that is, "during their life in this world" and "during their life in the Hereafter." The meaning of ﴿There is no altering of the words of God﴾ is that there is no change to His statements in general, so it includes what He promised to His righteous servants by way of primary inclusion. The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers back to what was mentioned before it, namely their being given glad tidings in both abodes. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, whose worth cannot be measured and to which nothing else is comparable. The two sentences, ﴿There is no altering of the words of God﴾ and ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, are, according to those who permit it, a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) at the end of the speech, and their benefit is to confirm the good tidings and magnify their importance. Alternatively, the first is a parenthetical insertion and the second is a concluding appendage (tadhyil).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision﴾, that he said: "They are the people of polytheism who would make lawful from the livestock and the tilth whatever they wished, and make unlawful whatever they wished."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿when you engage in it﴾, that he said: "when you do it." Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His words: ﴿Nor is absent from your Lord﴾, that he said: "The weight of an atom is not hidden from Him, ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record﴾." He said: "It is the Record that is with God."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, concerning His words: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God﴾, that it was said: "Who are they, O Lord?" He said: "They are those who believed and used to be mindful of God."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They are those who, when seen, God is remembered."

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated "from Ibn Abbas, both marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and mawquf (stopping at Ibn Abbas), who said: 'They are those who, when seen, God is remembered because of their sight.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, marfu', and it is mursal (a report whose chain omits a companion).

Something similar has been narrated through other routes, both marfu' and mawquf.

Ahmad and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Amr ibn al-Jamuh that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "A servant does not attain the true reality of sincere faith until he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake. When he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake, he has deserved allegiance from God. Indeed, My allies among My servants and My beloved among My creation are those who are remembered by My remembrance, and I am remembered by their remembrance."

Ahmad narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, reaching the Prophet (ﷺ) with it: "The best of God's servants are those who, when seen, God is remembered; and the worst of His servants are those who go about with tale-bearing, who sow discord among loved ones, and who seek the faults of the innocent."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the one whose sight reminds you of God, whose speech increases your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire the Hereafter."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas, marfu', the like of it.

Al-Hakim narrated, and declared sound, from Ibn Umar, marfu': "Indeed, God has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their nearness to Him and their station with Him." A Bedouin then got down on his knees and said: "O Messenger of God, describe them to us, make them clear to us!" He said: "They are a people from the various strangers of mankind, from the scattered tribes, who have become pure with one another for God's sake and love one another for God's sake. On the Day of Resurrection God will set up for them pulpits of light and seat them upon them. People will fear while they will not fear. They are the allies of God, on whom there is no fear, nor will they grieve."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is good.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, marfu', something similar.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, marfu', something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of God: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God﴾, the verse, and he said: 'Those who love one another for God's sake.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, marfu', the like of it.

Traditions have come concerning the virtue of those who love one another for God's sake, none of which states that they are the ones intended by the verse.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ata' ibn Yasar, "from a man of the people of Egypt, who said: I asked Abu al-Darda' about the meaning of His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, and he said: 'No one has asked me about it since I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: No one has asked me about it besides you since it was revealed to me. It is: the righteous dream which a Muslim sees, or which is seen for him. So it is his good news in the life of this world, and his good news in the Hereafter is Paradise.'" In its chain is this unknown man.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, and he said: 'It is the righteous dream which the believer sees, or which is seen for him.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated "from Abd Allah ibn Amr, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning His words: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, that he said: 'The righteous dream by which the believer is given good news is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood. So whoever sees such, let him inform of it,'" the hadith.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the verse, that he said: "In this world it is the righteous dream which the righteous servant sees, or which is seen for him; and in the Hereafter it is Paradise."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Mandah narrated, by way of Abu Ja'far from Jabir, "that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) interpreted the good news in the life of this world as the beloved dream, and in the Hereafter as the good news to the believer at death: 'Indeed, God has forgiven you and whoever carries you to your grave.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, marfu', the first part of the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas the like of it.

Sound traditions have come that the righteous dream is among the glad tidings and that it is a part of the parts of prophethood, but they have not been restricted to the interpretation of this verse.

It has been narrated that what is meant by the good news in the verse is His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from God a great bounty﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab 33:47).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated that from the route of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, by the route of Miqsam, that it is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾ (Surah Fussilat 41:30).

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Nafi', who said: "Al-Hajjaj gave a sermon and said: 'Ibn al-Zubayr has altered the Book of God.' Ibn Umar said: 'Neither you nor Ibn al-Zubayr can do that: ﴿There is no altering of the words of God.﴾'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 59–64 (part 1 of 2):

By His saying, ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down…"﴾ and so on, He (glory be to Him) points to another path, different from what preceded, for establishing prophethood. The gist of its explanation is this: you judge some things as lawful and some as unlawful. If that is merely by whim and desire, then it is rejected by the agreement of intelligent people, Muslim and disbelieving alike. But if it is because you believe it to be Allah's ruling concerning you and concerning what He has provided for you, then you know that only through a means that connects you to Allah, and there is no means by which the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful except through the Messengers (p-631) whom Allah has sent to His servants. The meaning of "Have you considered" is "Inform me." The phrase "what" (mā) is in a position of accusative governed by "Have you considered" (arara'aytum), which contains the sense of "Inform me."

It has also been said that "what" (mā) is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ The "Say" in His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. The connecting pronoun is omitted, and the subject with its predicate is in the accusative position governed by "Have you considered." The meaning is: "Inform me about what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful; has Allah permitted you to make it lawful and unlawful, or do you invent lies against Allah?" On both views, "min" in "some of it unlawful" is partitive; the implication is: you made part of it unlawful and made part of it lawful. This is like what they used to do with livestock, as has been related about them in the Noble Book. The meaning of the sending down of provision is that rain descends from above, and likewise the matter of the provision of the servants is decreed in the heavens, as is established in the Preserved Tablet, which contains mention of everything by Him (glory be to Him and exalted).

It is narrated from al-Zajjaj that "what" (mā) is in the accusative position governed by "sent down," and "sent down" here means "created," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6] and ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. According to this view and the first view, His saying ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you?"﴾ is a new (resumptive) statement. It has been said: it is permissible that the interrogative hamza in ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ is for denunciation, and "am" is disjunctive, meaning: "Rather, do you invent lies against Allah?" The mention of the Noble Name and its placement before the verb serves to indicate the completeness of the fabrication.

In this noble verse is something that strikes the ears of those who take the lead in issuing rulings to the servants of Allah concerning His law, declaring things lawful and unlawful, permissible or not, while they are among the imitators who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not comprehend them, and do not know what they are. Their knowledge goes no further than relating the saying of some speaker from this Community whom they have imitated in their religion and made into an independent lawgiver: whatever he acted upon from the Book and the Sunnah is what is acted upon among them; and whatever did not reach him, or reached him but he did not understand it properly, or he understood it and erred from the correct position in his ijtihad and his weighing of evidence, is in their judgment abrogated, its ruling lifted from the servants. Yet those whom they imitate are, like them, obligated by this Law and judged by its rulings, just as they are judged by it. He exerted his own opinion and discharged what was incumbent upon him, and he earns two rewards if he is correct and one reward if he errs. The real problem lies in their making his erroneous opinion into an independent law and an evidence to be acted upon. In this they have erred a clear error and blundered a gross blunder. For the permission granted to the mujtahid in exercising his own opinion is specific to him alone, and no one among the people of Islam whose sayings are considered has said that it is permissible for another to act upon it by imitating him and following his example. What the imitators have brought to establish this falsehood is of idle ignorance. O Allah, just as You have granted us of knowledge by which we distinguish between truth and falsehood, grant us of fairness by which we may attain what is the truth in Your sight, O Giver of good.

Then He said: ﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: what will be their thought on this Day, and what will be done to them therein? This interrogative sentence, which includes the magnification of the threat against them, is not included under the saying which Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them; rather it is an independent sentence, brought to explain what the punishment of Allah will befall them. "On the Day of Resurrection" is in the accusative governed by "thought." The mention of "lying" after "inventing" is, although inventing is only lying, for added emphasis.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "wa-mā ẓanna" as a verb. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, bestowing upon them kinds of blessings in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿but most of them are not grateful﴾ to Allah for His blessings that reach them from Him (glory be to Him) at every time and every moment.

His saying: ﴿And you are not in any matter﴾ — the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "mā" is negative.

Ash-sha'n (the matter) means "affair" in the sense of "intention," and its root is with a hamza; its plural is shu'ūn.

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs say: "mā sha'anta sha'anahu," meaning: "I did not do his deed."

﴿And you recite from it any Qur'an﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in "minhu" refers to "ash-sha'n," and the prepositional phrase is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a recitation proceeding from it, since reciting the Qur'an is among the greatest of his matters (ﷺ). The meaning is: he recites on account of the matter that gave rise to the Qur'an, so he knows its ruling, or he recites the Qur'an that descends concerning that matter.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Book, meaning: whatever is of the Book of Allah of Qur'an; it is repeated for its magnification, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. The address in ﴿and you do no deed﴾ is to the Messenger of Allah and to the Community. It has been said: the address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿But We are witnesses over you when you engage in it﴾ is an exceptive construction with an emptied (incomplete) antecedent, of the most general states of the addressees, meaning: witnesses over you regarding your deed. The pronoun in "fīhi" in ﴿when you engage in it﴾ refers to the deed; it is said: "Fulān plunged into the speech and the deed" when he pressed forward into it.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: when you spread lies concerning the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿And not hidden from your Lord is an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven﴾.

Al-Kisā'ī read "yaʿzibu" with a kasra on the zāy, and the rest read it with a ḍamma; both are eloquent dialects. The meaning of "yaʿzubu" is "to be hidden," and it has been said: "to be far." Ibn Kaysan said: "to go away." These meanings are close. The "min" in "min mithqāl" is extra for emphasis, meaning: nor is hidden from your Lord the weight of an atom, i.e., a red ant. He expressed it with "the earth and the heaven" although nothing is hidden from Him (glory be to Him), neither within them nor in what is outside them, because people do not witness anything other than them and what is in them of created things; and He placed "the earth" before "the heaven" because it is the place of the world's settlement, so they witness what is in it from nearby. The "wāw" in ﴿nor what is less than that or greater﴾ is for coordination with the wording of "mithqāl," and both are in the accusative because they are negated. It is permissible for the coordination to be with "dharra" (atom). It has been said: their accusative is governed by "lā" (not) of generic negation, and the "wāw" is for resumption, and it is not among the complements of "wa-mā yaʿzubu." The predicate of "lā" is ﴿except that it is in a clear Record﴾, and the meaning is: "Nor is anything smaller than an atom's weight or greater than it, except that it is in a clear Record; how then could it be hidden from Him?" Yaʿqūb and Ḥamza read "aṣghara" and "akbara" in the nominative. The reasoning for this is that it is coordinated with the position of "min mithqāl," which is in the nominative. The reading in the accusative or nominative as coordination with the wording or the position of "mithqāl," or with the wording of "dharra," has been subject to an objection, namely that the sense of the verse becomes: "Nothing is hidden from Him in the earth or in the heaven except that it is in a Record," which implies that this thing in the Record is outside His knowledge, and that is impossible.

This objection has been answered: created things are of two kinds. One kind Allah brought into existence directly without intermediary, such as the angels, the heavens and the earth. Another kind He brought into existence through the first kind, such as the events of the world of generation and corruption. Without doubt this second kind is remote in the chain of causation from the rank of the first. So the meaning of the verse is that nothing in the earth or in the heaven is remote from the rank of His existence (glory be to Him) except that it is in a clear Record, in which the form of those known things is fixed. The purpose is to refute him who claims that He does not know particulars.

And His saying: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against you, except those who have wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], meaning "and those who have wronged." "Huwa" (it) is supposed after the "wāw" that came in the sense of "illā," as in His saying: ﴿And say, "Ḥiṭṭah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], meaning "it is Ḥiṭṭah." He (glory be to Him) explained these allies by His saying: ﴿Those who believed and used to be fearful of Allah﴾, that is, they believe in what must be believed in, and they guard against what they are obligated to guard against of the disobedience of Allah (glory be to Him). Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿when you engage in it﴾, that he said: "when you do it." Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His words: ﴿Nor is absent from your Lord﴾, that he said: "The weight of an atom is not hidden from Him, ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record﴾." He said: "It is the Record that is with God."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, concerning His words: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God﴾, that it was said: "Who are they, O Lord?" He said: "They are those who believed and used to be mindful of God."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They are those who, when seen, God is remembered."

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara narrated "from Ibn Abbas, both marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and mawquf (stopping at Ibn Abbas), who said: 'They are those who, when seen, God is remembered because of their sight.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, marfu', and it is mursal (a report whose chain omits a companion).

Something similar has been narrated through other routes, both marfu' and mawquf.

Ahmad and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Amr ibn al-Jamuh that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "A servant does not attain the true reality of sincere faith until he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake. When he loves for God's sake and hates for God's sake, he has deserved allegiance from God. Indeed, My allies among My servants and My beloved among My creation are those who are remembered by My remembrance, and I am remembered by their remembrance."

Ahmad narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, reaching the Prophet (ﷺ) with it: "The best of God's servants are those who, when seen, God is remembered; and the worst of His servants are those who go about with tale-bearing, who sow discord among loved ones, and who seek the faults of the innocent."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the one whose sight reminds you of God, whose speech increases your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire the Hereafter."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas, marfu', the like of it.

Al-Hakim narrated, and declared sound, from Ibn Umar, marfu': "Indeed, God has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their nearness to Him and their station with Him." A Bedouin then got down on his knees and said: "O Messenger of God, describe them to us, make them clear to us!" He said: "They are a people from the various strangers of mankind, from the scattered tribes, who have become pure with one another for God's sake and love one another for God's sake. They are the allies of God, on whom there is no fear, nor will they grieve."

So whoever sees such, let him inform of it,'" the hadith.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, marfu', the like of the hadith of Jabir.
