Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, that he said: "You have no authority for this."

**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah Yunus (10), verses 65–70:**

His words, ﴿And let not their speech grieve you﴾, are a prohibition addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) against grief over the speech of the disbelievers, which contained disparagement of him, denial of him, and criticism of his religion. The purpose is to console him and give him good tidings.

Then Allah, glorified is He, resumed speaking to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), giving the reason for the prohibition He had mentioned. He said: ﴿Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾. That is, dominance and subjugation belong to Him in His kingdom and authority, and none of His servants possesses them. If all of that belongs to Him, then how could they harm you so that you would grieve over their false words, when they possess none of the power?

It has been recited as "yuḥznka" (from *aḥzana*).

It has also been recited as "anna al-ʿizzata" with the hamza opened (*fatḥ*), meaning "because honour belongs to Allah." The fact that all honour is Allah's, as stated in this verse, is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], because every honour is through Allah, so all of it belongs to Him. Similarly, His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21], and ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51]. (p. 634)

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth.﴾ Among them are these polytheists, the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ). Since they are within His dominion, and He disposes of them as He wills, how could they be able to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with what Allah has not permitted? The rational beings are given precedence over the others because they are more noble.

In the verse there is a rebuke of those who worship humans, angels, and inanimate objects, because they worshipped that which is owned and abandoned the Owner. This contradicts what reason requires. For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners﴾. The meaning is: although they name their objects of worship "partners" of Allah, they are not truly partners of Him, because that is impossible: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. The "mā" in (wa-mā yattabiʿu) is a negation particle, and "shurakāʾ" (partners) is the object (*mafʿūl*) of *yattabiʿu*. On this reading, the object of *yadʿūna* (they call upon) is elided, and the original sense is: "And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners, [being] partners in reality; they are only names without referents." One of the two (objects) is omitted because the mentioned one indicates it. It is also permissible for the mentioned word to be the object of *yadʿūna*, with the object of *yattabiʿu* omitted because the mentioned word indicates it. It is also permissible for it to be interrogative, meaning "What do those who call upon other than Allah follow as partners?" In this case "shurakāʾ" is in the accusative governed by *yadʿūna*, and the speech is in the form of reproach and disparagement of them.

It is also permissible for "mā" to be a relative pronoun conjoined to (man fī al-samāwāti): that is, "To Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners." The meaning is that Allah owns their objects of worship, since they are among those in the heavens and on the earth.

Then He, glorified is He, increased the emphasis in refuting them and rejecting their claims, and said: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾. That is, they do not follow certainty; they follow only conjecture, and conjecture does not avail against the truth at all. ﴿They are only guessing﴾: that is, they assume that they are partners, an assumption that is false and sheer lies. This verse has already occurred in al-Anʿam.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned a portion of the signs of His power, together with the bestowal of favour upon His servants through some of His blessings. He said: ﴿It is He who made for you the night to rest therein and the day giving sight﴾. That is, He made time for His servants divided into two parts. One is dark, which is the night, so that the servants may rest therein from movement and fatigue, and relieve themselves from toil and earning. The other is illuminated, so that they may strive therein for what benefits them and increases their livelihood, and obtain what they need in a bright, luminous time, in which nothing great or small is hidden from them. His, glorified is He, making the day "giving sight" is a metaphor. The meaning is that it gives sight to its owner, like the saying "his day is fasting."

The reference in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who listen﴾ is to the aforementioned arrangement: wondrous and numerous signs. That is, they hear what is recited to them of the revealed verses, which direct attention to the created signs, both those Allah mentioned here and others He did not mention. Upon hearing these, they reflect and take heed, and this is among the greatest causes of faith.

His saying: ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient.﴾ This is another kind of the falsehoods of the polytheists that they used to utter, namely their claim that Allah, glorified is He, has taken a son. He refuted this by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient﴾. He, exalted is He, is far above what they ascribed to Him of this manifest falsehood, and He made clear that He is free of need of that, and that a son is sought only out of need. The absolutely Self-Sufficient has no need, so that He would have a son to fulfil it. And when need is absent, the son is absent. Furthermore, only one who is on the verge of extinction needs a son to take his place, whereas the Eternal, the Ancient, has no need of that.

The interpretation of this verse has already been given in al-Baqarah.

Then He went further in refuting them with what is like a proof, and said: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Since all of it belongs to Him and is in His dominion, it is not valid for anything in them to be a son of His, because of the incompatibility between ownership and sonship or fatherhood.

Then He nullified their baseless claim and made clear that it has no evidence. He said: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾. That is, do you have any proof or evidence for this statement that you utter? The "min" in ﴿min sultān﴾ is an emphatic extra particle. The prepositional phrase "bihādhā" (for this) is connected either to *sulṭān* (authority), since it means proof and evidence, or to *ʿindakum* (you have), because of the sense of settledness it carries.

Then He rebuked them for this statement, which is empty of evidence and false in the view of rational people, and said: ﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ From this it is deduced that every statement that lacks evidence is not knowledge at all, but pure ignorance.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them words that indicate that what they said is a lie, and that whoever lies against Allah will not prosper. He said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not succeed."﴾ That is, every fabricator whose condition is this, and these are included in it primarily.

The mention of "lie" together with "fabricate" is for emphasis, as has been mentioned before in several places in the Noble Book.

The meaning is that those who lie against their Lord do not attain any of the things they seek.

﴿A brief enjoyment in this world; then to Us will be their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ Then Allah, glorified is He, explained that this fabrication, even if its perpetrator gains something of the immediate aims, is only a little enjoyment in this world. Then death and return to Allah will follow, and He will punish the fabricator with an everlasting punishment.

Thus "matāʿun" (enjoyment) is the predicate of an elided subject, and the sentence is resumptive, clarifying that what the fabricator gains by his fabrication is not a benefit worth counting. Rather, it is a small enjoyment in this world, followed by a severe punishment because of disbelief, which arises from causes among which is lying against Allah.

Al-Akhfash said: the implied meaning is "for them is enjoyment in this world," so the elided element on this view is the predicate.

Al-Kisa'i said: the implied meaning is "that is enjoyment," or "it is enjoyment," so the elided element on this view is the subject.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said regarding His saying: ﴿And let not grieve you﴾: when they did not benefit from what came to them from Allah and persisted in their disbelief, that weighed heavily upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so there came to him from Allah a reproach: ﴿And let not grieve you their saying that honour belongs to Allah entirely. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. He hears what they say and knows it. Had He willed, by His might, He would have taken vengeance upon them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿and the day giving sight﴾, that he said: "illuminating."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, that he said: "You have no authority for this."

(p. 635)

When Allah, glory be to Him, had thoroughly established the clear proofs and repelled the crumbling doubts, He began to mention the stories of the prophets, because in this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: ﴿And recite to them﴾, i.e., to the disbelievers contemporary with you, who oppose what you have brought with their false statements, ﴿the news of Noah﴾, i.e., his account. The *naba'* (news) is the report that has significance and importance. The intended meaning is what befell him with his people, who disbelieved in what he brought, just as the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like have done. ﴿When he said to his people﴾, i.e., at the time he said to his people. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is in the accusative governed by *naba'*, or it is a substitute for it, a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*). The *lam* in *li-qawmihi* is the *lam* of conveyance (*lam al-tabligh*). ﴿O my people, if my position [maqam] is burdensome to you﴾, i.e., if it is great and heavy for you. The word *maqam* with a *fatha* on the *mim* means the place where one stands, and with a *damma* it means the act of standing.

The readers agree on the *fatha*. He used *maqam* as a metonymy for himself, as one says "I did it for the sake of so-and-so," meaning for his sake. From this is Allah's saying: ﴿And for he who fears the position of his Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], i.e., who fears his Lord. It is also permissible that *maqam* means remaining, i.e., my staying among you is burdensome to you. It is also permissible that *maqam* means standing, because the preacher stands while admonishing. The meaning is: if my standing up to preach at your gatherings is burdensome to you, and my reminding you of the signs of Allah, both those of creation (*takwiniyyah*) and those revealed (*tanzili-yyah*), is burdensome to you. ﴿Then upon Allah I have relied﴾. This sentence is the answer to the condition. The meaning is: I do not face that from you except by reliance upon Allah, for that is my custom that I have followed, past and present.

It is also permissible that he intends the establishment of a specific rank among the ranks of reliance. It is also permissible that the answer to the condition is *fa-ajmi'u* (so resolve), and the sentence ﴿upon Allah I have relied﴾ is a parenthetical interjection, like your saying: "If you have objected to something of mine, then Allah is sufficient for me."

The meaning of ﴿So resolve upon your matter﴾ is: determine upon it, from *ajma'a al-amr*, when one intends it and resolves upon it. So said al-Farra'.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: *ajma'a al-shay'* means "he prepared it."

Mu'arraj al-Sadusi said: *ajma'a al-amr* is more eloquent than *ajma'a 'alayhi*. And he recited:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit: will I one day set out while my affair is resolved?"

Abu al-Haytham said: *ajma'a amrahu* means he made it whole (*jamee'an*) after it had been scattered. Its scattering is when you say, once, "I will do such-and-such," and once, "I will do such-and-such." When he resolves upon one matter, he has gathered it, i.e., made it whole. This is the original meaning of *ijma'* (consensus of resolve), and then it came to mean determination.

The majority of readers agree on the accusative of *shurakā'akum* (your partners) and on the *hamzah* of *ajma'u* being pronounced as a cut (*qat' al-hamzah*), i.e., *ajmi'u* with an initial *hamzah* that is pronounced.

Ya'qub, 'Asim al-Jahdari, read *ajma'u* with a connecting *hamzah* (*hamzat wasl*), taking it as from *jama'a yajma'u jam'an*.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Ya'qub read *wa-shurakā'ukum* with the nominative (*raf'*).

Al-Nahhas said: For the accusative of *al-shurakā'* according to the majority reading there are three possibilities. The first: it means "and call upon your partners," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', i.e., call upon them for your support. On this view it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: It is coordinated with the meaning. The poet said:

"Would that your husband in battle were girded with a sword and a spear."

The spear is not girded with, but it is carried like the sword.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "together with your partners," so the *waw* here is the *waw* of accompaniment (*waw ma'a*).

As for the reading *ijmau'* with a connecting *hamzah*, the coordination is evident: i.e., gather your affair and gather your partners.

As for the grammatical justification of the nominative reading, it is by coordinating *al-shurakā'* with the pronoun of subject in *ajmi'u*. This coordination is acceptable even without emphasis by a separate pronoun, which is what is normally required, because the speech has been lengthened.

Al-Nahhas and others said: This reading is weak, because if *shurakā'akum* were nominative it would have been written in the Mushaf with a *waw*, and that is not found in it.

Al-Mahdawi said: It is also permissible that *al-shurakā'* is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*), with the predicate omitted, meaning: and your partners, let them gather their affair. The attribution of this to the partners, even though the idols do not understand, is for the purpose of rebuke and reproach of the one who worships them.

It is related from Ubayy that he read: "and call upon your partners," with the verb made explicit.

His saying: ﴿Then let not your affair be obscured to you﴾. *Ghummah* means covering, from the saying "the crescent was ghumma," when it became hidden, i.e., let your affair be clear and manifest.

Tarafah said:

"By your life, my affair is not obscured to me, neither my day nor my night is hidden from me by a continuous darkness."

Thus said al-Zajjaj.

Al-Haytham said: Its meaning is: let not your affair be ambiguous to you.

It was said: *ghummah* means the narrowness of the matter. This is related from Abu 'Ubaydah.

The meaning is: let not your affair be a severe narrowness for you, by my companionship and my politeness toward you; rather, remove this narrowness and hardship by whatever you wish and are able to do. On the first two interpretations, the meaning of the second "affair" is the first affair; on the third, it means something other than it.

His saying: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite﴾. I.e., carry out that affair which you intend against me. The root of *uqdu* is from *qada'*, which is making firm (*al-ihkam*).

The meaning is: make that affair firm.

Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: It is like ﴿And We conveyed that decree to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66], i.e., We communicated it to him and informed him of it. Then "do not give me respite," i.e., do not delay me, but hasten your affair and do what you see fit. It was said: its meaning is: then proceed toward me and do not delay.

Al-Nahhas said: This is a sound statement in the language, and from it comes *qadā al-mayyit*, meaning he passed away.

Al-Farra' related from some readers that they read "thumma afdu" with the *fa* and a cut *hamzah*, meaning: turn toward me. In these words of Noah, peace be upon him, there is what indicates his confidence in the support of his Lord and his indifference to what his people threaten him with.

Then he explained to them that all that he brought to them of warning, admonition, and conveying the law from Allah was not for a worldly greed nor for a base aim. So he said: ﴿And if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any compensation﴾. I.e., if you turn away from acting upon my advice to you and my reminder to you, then I have not asked you in exchange for that for any reward that you would pay me, so that you might accuse me regarding what I have brought. The *fa'* in *fa-in tawallaytum* marks the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, and the *fa'* in *fa-ma sa'altukum* is the answer particle (*fa' jazā'iyyah*). ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, i.e., my reward for the advice and reminder is only from Him, glory be to Him; He will reward me, whether you believe or (p. 636) turn away.

The people of Medina, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read the *ya'* in *ajriya* with movement (*tahrik*), and the rest read it with sukun.

﴿And I have been commanded to be of the Muslims﴾, those who submit to the judgment of Allah, who make their deeds purely for Allah, glory be to Him, taking no wage for them and not seeking worldly gain.

His saying: ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾. I.e., they persisted in denying him and insisted upon that. The intended meaning is not that they began to deny him after not having denied him before. The intended meaning of "those with him" is those who had responded to him and become upon his religion. *Khala'if* is the plural of *khalifah*, and the meaning is that He, glory be to Him, made them successors dwelling in the land which had belonged to those destroyed by drowning, and succeeding them in it. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, from the stubborn disbelievers opposing Noah, those who did not believe in him; Allah drowned them with the flood. ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned﴾. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a threat to the polytheists and a terrifying warning to them.

﴿Then We sent after him﴾, i.e., after Noah, messengers such as Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, and Shu'ayb. ﴿And they brought them clear proofs﴾, i.e., miracles and what Allah had sent them with of the laws which Allah had legislated for the people of each prophet. ﴿But they were not [such] as to believe﴾, i.e., they did not newly bring about faith, but persisted in disbelief and insisted upon it.

The meaning is: it was not valid nor right for any of those peoples to whom Allah sent His messengers to believe at any time ﴿in that which they had denied before﴾, i.e., before their denial that occurred when the messengers came to them.

Abu al-Haytham said: *ajma'a amrahu* means he made it whole (*jamee'an*) after it had been scattered. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Ya'qub read *wa-shurakā'ukum* with the nominative (*raf'*).

Al-Nahhas said: For the accusative of *al-shurakā'* according to the majority reading there are three possibilities. Thus said al-Zajjaj.

The intended meaning is what befell him with his people, who disbelieved in what he brought, just as the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like have done. ﴿When he said to his people﴾, i.e., at the time he said to his people. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is in the accusative governed by *naba'*, or it is a substitute for it, a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*). The *lam* in *li-qawmihi* is the *lam* of conveyance (*lam al-tabligh*). ﴿O my people, if my position [maqam] is burdensome to you﴾, i.e., if it is great and heavy for you. The word *maqam* with a *fatha* on the *mim* means the place where one stands, and with a *damma* it means the act of standing.

The readers agree on the *fatha*. He used *maqam* as a metonymy for himself, as one says "I did it for the sake of so-and-so," meaning for his sake. From this is Allah's saying: ﴿And for he who fears the position of his Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], i.e., who fears his Lord. It is also permissible that *maqam* means remaining, i.e., my staying among you is burdensome to you. It is also permissible that *maqam* means standing, because the preacher stands while admonishing. The meaning is: if my standing up to preach at your gatherings is burdensome to you, and my reminding you of the signs of Allah, both those of creation (*takwiniyyah*) and those revealed (*tanzili-yyah*), is burdensome to you. ﴿Then upon Allah I have relied﴾. This sentence is the answer to the condition. The meaning is: I do not face that from you except by reliance upon Allah, for that is my custom that I have followed, past and present.

It is also permissible that he intends the establishment of a specific rank among the ranks of reliance. It is also permissible that the answer to the condition is *fa-ajmi'u* (so resolve), and the sentence ﴿upon Allah I have relied﴾ is a parenthetical interjection, like your saying: "If you have objected to something of mine, then Allah is sufficient for me."

The meaning of ﴿So resolve upon your matter﴾ is: determine upon it, from *ajma'a al-amr*, when one intends it and resolves upon it. So said al-Farra'.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: *ajma'a al-shay'* means "he prepared it."

Mu'arraj al-Sadusi said: *ajma'a al-amr* is more eloquent than *ajma'a 'alayhi*. And he recited:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit: will I one day set out while my affair is resolved?"

Abu al-Haytham said: *ajma'a amrahu* means he made it whole (*jamee'an*) after it had been scattered. Its scattering is when you say, once, "I will do such-and-such," and once, "I will do such-and-such." When he resolves upon one matter, he has gathered it, i.e., made it whole. This is the original meaning of *ijma'* (consensus of resolve), and then it came to mean determination.

The majority of readers agree on the accusative of *shurakā'akum* (your partners) and on the *hamzah* of *ajma'u* being pronounced as a cut (*qat' al-hamzah*), i.e., *ajmi'u* with an initial *hamzah* that is pronounced.

Ya'qub, 'Asim al-Jahdari, read *ajma'u* with a connecting *hamzah* (*hamzat wasl*), taking it as from *jama'a yajma'u jam'an*.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Ya'qub read *wa-shurakā'ukum* with the nominative (*raf'*).

Al-Nahhas said: For the accusative of *al-shurakā'* according to the majority reading there are three possibilities. The first: it means "and call upon your partners," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', i.e., call upon them for your support. On this view it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: It is coordinated with the meaning. The poet said:

"Would that your husband in battle were girded with a sword and a spear."

The spear is not girded with, but it is carried like the sword.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "together with your partners," so the *waw* here is the *waw* of accompaniment (*waw ma'a*).

As for the reading *ijmau'* with a connecting *hamzah*, the coordination is evident: i.e., gather your affair and gather your partners.

As for the grammatical justification of the nominative reading, it is by coordinating *al-shurakā'* with the pronoun of subject in *ajmi'u*. This coordination is acceptable even without emphasis by a separate pronoun, which is what is normally required, because the speech has been lengthened.

Al-Nahhas and others said: This reading is weak, because if *shurakā'akum* were nominative it would have been written in the Mushaf with a *waw*, and that is not found in it.

Al-Mahdawi said: It is also permissible that *al-shurakā'* is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*), with the predicate omitted, meaning: and your partners, let them gather their affair. The attribution of this to the partners, even though the idols do not understand, is for the purpose of rebuke and reproach of the one who worships them.

It is related from Ubayy that he read: "and call upon your partners," with the verb made explicit.

His saying: ﴿Then let not your affair be obscured to you﴾. *Ghummah* means covering, from the saying "the crescent was ghumma," when it became hidden, i.e., let your affair be clear and manifest.

Tarafah said:

"By your life, my affair is not obscured to me, neither my day nor my night is hidden from me by a continuous darkness."

Thus said al-Zajjaj.

Al-Haytham said: Its meaning is: let not your affair be ambiguous to you.

It was said: *ghummah* means the narrowness of the matter. This is related from Abu 'Ubaydah.

The meaning is: let not your affair be a severe narrowness for you, by my companionship and my politeness toward you; rather, remove this narrowness and hardship by whatever you wish and are able to do. On the first two interpretations, the meaning of the second "affair" is the first affair; on the third, it means something other than it.

His saying: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite﴾. I.e., carry out that affair which you intend against me. The root of *uqdu* is from *qada'*, which is making firm (*al-ihkam*).

The meaning is: make that affair firm.

Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: It is like ﴿And We conveyed that decree to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66], i.e., We communicated it to him and informed him of it. Then "do not give me respite," i.e., do not delay me, but hasten your affair and do what you see fit. It was said: its meaning is: then proceed toward me and do not delay.

Al-Nahhas said: This is a sound statement in the language, and from it comes *qadā al-mayyit*, meaning he passed away.

Al-Farra' related from some readers that they read "thumma afdu" with the *fa* and a cut *hamzah*, meaning: turn toward me. In these words of Noah, peace be upon him, there is what indicates his confidence in the support of his Lord and his indifference to what his people threaten him with.

Then he explained to them that all that he brought to them of warning, admonition, and conveying the law from Allah was not for a worldly greed nor for a base aim. So he said: ﴿And if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any compensation﴾. I.e., if you turn away from acting upon my advice to you and my reminder to you, then I have not asked you in exchange for that for any reward that you would pay me, so that you might accuse me regarding what I have brought. The *fa'* in *fa-in tawallaytum* marks the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, and the *fa'* in *fa-ma sa'altukum* is the answer particle (*fa' jazā'iyyah*). ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, i.e., my reward for the advice and reminder is only from Him, glory be to Him; He will reward me, whether you believe or (p. 636) turn away.

The people of Medina, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read the *ya'* in *ajriya* with movement (*tahrik*), and the rest read it with sukun.

﴿And I have been commanded to be of the Muslims﴾, those who submit to the judgment of Allah, who make their deeds purely for Allah, glory be to Him, taking no wage for them and not seeking worldly gain.

His saying: ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾. I.e., they persisted in denying him and insisted upon that. The intended meaning is not that they began to deny him after not having denied him before. The intended meaning of "those with him" is those who had responded to him and become upon his religion. *Khala'if* is the plural of *khalifah*, and the meaning is that He, glory be to Him, made them successors dwelling in the land which had belonged to those destroyed by drowning, and succeeding them in it. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, from the stubborn disbelievers opposing Noah, those who did not believe in him; Allah drowned them with the flood. ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned﴾. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a threat to the polytheists and a terrifying warning to them.

﴿Then We sent after him﴾, i.e., after Noah, messengers such as Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, and Shu'ayb. ﴿And they brought them clear proofs﴾, i.e., miracles and what Allah had sent them with of the laws which Allah had legislated for the people of each prophet. ﴿But they were not [such] as to believe﴾, i.e., they did not newly bring about faith, but persisted in disbelief and insisted upon it.

The meaning is: it was not valid nor right for any of those peoples to whom Allah sent His messengers to believe at any time ﴿in that which they had denied before﴾, i.e., before their denial that occurred when the messengers came to them.

The meaning is: every nation of the world did not believe, at the time Allah sent to them the messenger specifically sent to them, in what they had been denying before his coming to them, because they were not believers but deniers of the religion. Had they been believers, He would not have sent a messenger to them. This is based on the view that the pronoun in *fa-ma kanu li-yu'minu* and in *bi-ma kadhdhabu* refers to the people mentioned in His saying "to their people." It was also said: the pronoun in "they denied" refers to the people of Noah: i.e., the people of the messengers were not to believe in what the people of Noah had denied before these peoples came who came after them. ﴿And their messengers brought them clear proofs﴾. It was also said: the *ba'* in ﴿in that which they had denied before﴾ is causal (*sababiyyah*): i.e., they were not to believe at the coming of the messengers because of what they had become accustomed to of denying the truth before their coming. In this there is consideration.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿in that which they had denied before﴾ is: in the realm of atoms (*'alam al-dharr*), for among them is he who denied with his heart, even if he outwardly believed.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the best of what has been said is that it refers to specific people. ﴿Thus We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾, i.e., with a sealing like that great sealing, We seal the hearts of those who exceed the known limit in disbelief.

The explanation of this has preceded in more than one place.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-A'raj, regarding His saying ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾, that he said: "Make firm your affair and call upon your partners."

He also related from al-Hasan regarding the verse, i.e., "let them gather their affair together with you."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Then let not your affair be obscured to you﴾, that he said: "Let your affair not be burdensome to you." ﴿Then carry out﴾ what you are going to carry out.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Then carry out﴾, that he said: "Rise up," ﴿against me and give me no respite﴾, he says: "and do not delay me."

[p. 637] **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 10, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ is conjunctive with His saying: ﴿Then after him We sent Messengers﴾ (Yunus: 74). The pronoun in "after them" refers to the Messengers mentioned earlier. He singled out Musa and Harun for mention, although they are included among the Messengers, because of their greater nobility and the great importance of what took place between them and Fir'awn. "The chiefs" (al-mala') means the nobles. "The signs" (al-ayat) means the miracles, namely the nine mentioned in the Noble Book. They were arrogant and refused to accept them, and did not humble themselves before them or submit to what they contained of miracles that necessitated believing in the one who brought them. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ means they were people of great crime and grave sins. Because of that, they dared to reject them, for sins prevent their possessor from recognizing the truth and seeing what is right. It has been said that this clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), confirming the meaning of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Indeed this is clear magic﴾ means: when the truth, which is the miracles, came from Allah to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they did not believe in them, but called them magic, out of obstinate denial.

Musa responded to them, saying: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you: Is this magic?﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic? Then do not say that." Then he resumed with another denial from himself, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He omitted their first statement, relying on the second. What compels this interpretation is that they did not ask him whether it was magic, so that he would repeat what they said with the words "Is this magic?" Rather, they affirmed definitively that it was magic, for they said: ﴿Indeed this is clear magic﴾. Thus the words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ would not be from their saying. Al-Akhfash said that they are from their saying, but this is open to question for what we have already mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning of "Do you say" is "Do you find fault with the truth and slander it?" and it was incumbent upon you to submit to it. Then he said, "Is this magic?!", rejecting what they had said. It has also been said that the object of "Do you say" is omitted, and it is what their saying "Indeed this is magic" indicates. The sense is: "Do you say what you say, namely your saying 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" Then he said, "Is this magic?" According to this interpretation and the first one, the clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a resumptive statement from Musa, peace be upon him, and the interrogation is for rebuke and reproach, following the first resumptive clause, which answers an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did Musa say to them when they said: 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you…﴾ in the manner of a rhetorical question of denial. The meaning is: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is clear magic? It is the furthest thing from magic."

Then he denied and rebuked and reproached them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ So Musa, peace be upon him, came with denial after denial, reproach after reproach, and accusation of ignorance after accusation of ignorance. The clause ﴿and sorcerers do not prosper﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, when the state is that sorcerers do not prosper, so they do not attain their aim, do not win any good, and are not saved from any harm? How then could one who is sent from Allah fall into this, when He has supported him with miracles and clear proofs?"

The clause ﴿They said: Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾ is a resumptive clause, answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after Musa had said what he said?" This indicates that they were cut off from proof and unable to produce an argument. They did not deny what he had put to them, but resorted to what the people of ignorance and dullness resort to, which is arguing from the disbelief their fathers had been upon. To this they added what was really their aim, the goal of their desire and the cause of their obstinacy against the truth and their rejection of clear signs, namely worldly leadership, which they feared losing and thought would depart from them if they believed. How many people have remained upon falsehood while knowing it to be falsehood, by this pretext, among the groups of this world, in past and future times! Some of them were held back by it from leaving disbelief, and some of them were held back from leaving innovation for the Sunnah, and from sound transmission for mere personal opinion.

It is said: "He turned him (lafataha) with a turning (laftan)" when he diverted him from a thing and twisted him away from it. From this the poet said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*aching from listening, in the neck and the nape.*

That is, you wish to divert us from the thing upon which we found our fathers, which is the worship of idols. By "greatness" (al-kibriya') is meant kingship. Al-Zajjaj said: kingship was called greatness because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It has also been said that it was so called because the king is proud (yatakabbar).

The summary is that they gave two reasons for not accepting Musa's call: clinging to the imitation of their fathers, and greed for worldly leadership. For if they answered the Prophet and confirmed him, the reins of their community's affairs would pass to him, and the king would have no complete leadership left, because governing people by religion removes the rule of kings over them by policies and customs. Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. The address was singular to Musa in their saying "Have you come to us to turn us away," but then they combined him with Harun in address in their saying: ﴿And that greatness might be yours two in the land. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer﴾. He said this when he saw the white hand and the staff, because he believed them to be of sorcery. So he commanded his people to bring him every knowing sorcerer. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash read it as *sahhar* (a sorcerer of intensive form). The rest read *sahir*. This has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

*Sahhar* is an intensive form: that is, one who practices sorcery much, with much knowledge of its work and its kinds.

﴿So when the sorcerers came﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is as follows: "And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer," and they brought them to him. So when the sorcerers came, the *fa'* (so) is conjunctive to the implied, omitted clause.

His saying: ﴿Musa said to them: Cast what you are casting﴾ means: he said this to them after they had said to him: "Either you cast, or we will be the casters." That is: throw on the ground what you have of your ropes and staffs.

﴿So when they cast﴾ what they cast of that, Musa said to them: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "magic." The meaning is that it is sorcery, not one of the signs of Allah.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *sihr* (magic) governed by *ji'tum* (you brought), with *ma* as a conditional particle, the condition being *ji'tum* and the response being ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, with an implied *fa'* (then): that is, "then indeed Allah will nullify it." It has also been said that *al-sihr* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): that is, "what you have brought is sorcery." Then the alif and lam entered (making it definite). On this view, there is no need to omit the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by most grammarians except in poetic necessity.

Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read *ā-ssiḥru* (with the interrogative hamzah), so that the hamzah is interrogative, and the sense is: "Is it magic?" On this reading, *ma* is interrogative.

Ubayy read: *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun, inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will nullify it). That is, He will annihilate it, so that it becomes false by what He manifests of miraculous signs at my hands. ﴿Indeed Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾: that is, the work of this kind. It includes everyone to whom the description "corrupter" truly applies, and it primarily enters sorcery and sorcerers.

The *wāw* in ﴿and Allah establishes the truth﴾ is conjunctive to "will nullify": that is, He will make it clear and manifest by His words which He sent down in His books upon His prophets, because they contain proofs and evidences. ﴿Even if the guilty disliked it﴾: the guilty are either from the family of Fir'awn, or the guilty in general, and the family of Fir'awn enter among them primarily. *Ijram* means sins.

His saying: ﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun returns to Musa, that is, "from the people of Musa," and they were a group of the descendants of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a group of the descendants of Fir'awn, so the pronoun returns to Fir'awn. It has been said that among them were the believer of the family of Fir'awn, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer. It has also been said that they were a people whose fathers were of the Copts and whose mothers were of the Children of Israel. This was narrated from al-Farra'. "Out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs": the pronoun refers to Fir'awn, but it is in the plural because, since he was a tyrant, they used plural pronouns for him out of glorification. It has also been said that the people of Fir'awn were named after Fir'awn, like Thamud, so the pronoun returned to them in this sense. It has also been said that it returns to an omitted noun, and the sense is "out of fear of the family of Fir'awn." This was narrated from al-Farra'. But al-Khalil and Sibawayh prohibited this, so according to them it is not permitted to say: "Hind stood up," while you mean "her boy."

It was narrated from al-Akhfash that the pronoun returns to "offspring." Al-Nahhas supported that. ﴿That he might turn them away from their religion﴾: that is, that he might divert them from their religion by the punishment which he used to inflict on them. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (masdar) of "fear."

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

His saying: ﴿And Musa said: O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾. It has been said that this belongs to the category of repeating the condition: he made reliance on Allah conditional upon belief in Him and submission, that is, surrender to His decree and destiny. It has also been said that this is not a case of making the ruling conditional on two conditions. Rather, what is conditional upon belief is the obligation of reliance, and what is conditional upon submission is its existence. The meaning is: they should surrender themselves to Allah, that is, make themselves wholly sincere to Him, with no share for Satan in them, because reliance does not exist alongside mixing.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its parallel in speech is: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him, if you have strength against him."

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." According to the first meaning, "trial" is in the sense of "one who is tempted."

When they had put first the humble supplication to Allah, that He preserve their religion from corruption, they followed it with asking for the protection of their own selves, and said: ﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾. In this there is evidence that they were more concerned with the matter of religion than with the safety of their own selves.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. One says: "I settled Zayd in a place" and "I settled a place for Zayd." The *mubawwa'* is the dwelling where one is kept (al-manzil al-mal-zum). From this comes "Allah settled him a dwelling," meaning He made him stay in it and lodged him in it. From this is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*
*glory and kingship have settled upon us.*

Egypt in this verse is said by some to be Alexandria, and others say it is Egypt as it is well known, not Alexandria. ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, meaning facing toward the direction of the qiblah. It is said that the houses here refer to mosques, and a group of the early generation (al-salaf) went to this view. It is also said that the houses meant are those in which they dwell, and they were commanded to make them a qiblah for us. The qiblah, according to the first view, is the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. It is also said that the meaning is that they should make their houses face the qiblah so that they might pray in them secretly, lest some harm from the disbelievers befall them because of the prayer. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer He commanded you to establish, for it indicates that the qiblah is the qiblah of prayer, whether in mosques or in houses, not the making of the houses face one another. He addressed Musa and Harun at the beginning of the speech, then made it addressed to both of them and their people in His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah and establish the prayer﴾. Then He addressed Musa alone after that, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, because the choice of place is entrusted to the prophets. Then it was made general in facing the qiblah and establishing the prayer, because that is obligatory upon everyone and is not specific to the prophets. Then it was made specific to Musa, because he is the principal in the message and Harun follows him. So this was a magnification of the good tidings and of the one to whom they were given. It is also said that the address in ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by way of iltifat (turning of address) and i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion). The first view is preferred.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿to mislead us﴾, that he said: "to turn us away."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: "to divert us from our gods."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and that greatness in the land may belong to you both﴾, that he said: "the majesty, the kingship and the authority."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a small group (dhurriyyah)﴾, that he said: "dhurriyyah means a few."

These same narrators related from him regarding His saying: ﴿a group from his people﴾, that he said: "from the children of Israel."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, who said: "They were the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent, after a long time had passed and their fathers had died."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The dhurriyyah who believed in Musa were people other than the children of Israel, from the people of Pharaoh, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believing man of Pharaoh's family, the treasurer of Pharaoh, and the wife of his treasurer."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾, that he said: "Do not let them dominate us, lest they tempt us."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said in explaining the verse: "Do not punish us at the hands of the people of Pharaoh, nor with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not be punished nor would we have been given power over them, so they would be tempted by us.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Qilabah regarding the verse, who said: "He asked his Lord not to let our enemy prevail over us, for they would then reckon that they were more deserving of justice and would be tempted by that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Mijlaz something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Pharaoh prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to make their places of prayer in their houses and to face them toward the qiblah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿that you both settle your people in Egypt﴾, that he said: "Egypt is Alexandria."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding the verse, who said: "They did not pray except in churches until they feared the family of Pharaoh, so they were commanded to pray in their houses."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, who said: "They were commanded to take mosques in their houses."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Sinan, who said: "The qiblah is the Ka'bah, and it is mentioned that Adam and those after him used to pray facing the Ka'bah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, that he said: "that some of them face others."

[p. 637] **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 10, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ is conjunctive with His saying: ﴿Then after him We sent Messengers﴾ (Yunus: 74). The pronoun in "after them" refers to the Messengers mentioned earlier. He singled out Musa and Harun for mention, although they are included among the Messengers, because of their greater nobility and the great importance of what took place between them and Fir'awn. "The chiefs" (al-mala') means the nobles. "The signs" (al-ayat) means the miracles, namely the nine mentioned in the Noble Book. They were arrogant and refused to accept them, and did not humble themselves before them or submit to what they contained of miracles that necessitated believing in the one who brought them. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ means they were people of great crime and grave sins. Because of that, they dared to reject them, for sins prevent their possessor from recognizing the truth and seeing what is right. It has been said that this clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), confirming the meaning of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Indeed this is clear magic﴾ means: when the truth, which is the miracles, came from Allah to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they did not believe in them, but called them magic, out of obstinate denial.

Musa responded to them, saying: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you: Is this magic?﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic? Then do not say that." Then he resumed with another denial from himself, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He omitted their first statement, relying on the second. What compels this interpretation is that they did not ask him whether it was magic, so that he would repeat what they said with the words "Is this magic?" Rather, they affirmed definitively that it was magic, for they said: ﴿Indeed this is clear magic﴾. Thus the words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ would not be from their saying. Al-Akhfash said that they are from their saying, but this is open to question for what we have already mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning of "Do you say" is "Do you find fault with the truth and slander it?" and it was incumbent upon you to submit to it. Then he said, "Is this magic?!", rejecting what they had said. It has also been said that the object of "Do you say" is omitted, and it is what their saying "Indeed this is magic" indicates. The sense is: "Do you say what you say, namely your saying 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" Then he said, "Is this magic?" According to this interpretation and the first one, the clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a resumptive statement from Musa, peace be upon him, and the interrogation is for rebuke and reproach, following the first resumptive clause, which answers an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did Musa say to them when they said: 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you…﴾ in the manner of a rhetorical question of denial. The meaning is: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is clear magic? It is the furthest thing from magic."

Then he denied and rebuked and reproached them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ So Musa, peace be upon him, came with denial after denial, reproach after reproach, and accusation of ignorance after accusation of ignorance. The clause ﴿and sorcerers do not prosper﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, when the state is that sorcerers do not prosper, so they do not attain their aim, do not win any good, and are not saved from any harm? How then could one who is sent from Allah fall into this, when He has supported him with miracles and clear proofs?"

The clause ﴿They said: Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾ is a resumptive clause, answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after Musa had said what he said?" This indicates that they were cut off from proof and unable to produce an argument. They did not deny what he had put to them, but resorted to what the people of ignorance and dullness resort to, which is arguing from the disbelief their fathers had been upon. To this they added what was really their aim, the goal of their desire and the cause of their obstinacy against the truth and their rejection of clear signs, namely worldly leadership, which they feared losing and thought would depart from them if they believed. How many people have remained upon falsehood while knowing it to be falsehood, by this pretext, among the groups of this world, in past and future times! Some of them were held back by it from leaving disbelief, and some of them were held back from leaving innovation for the Sunnah, and from sound transmission for mere personal opinion.

It is said: "He turned him (lafataha) with a turning (laftan)" when he diverted him from a thing and twisted him away from it. From this the poet said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*aching from listening, in the neck and the nape.*

That is, you wish to divert us from the thing upon which we found our fathers, which is the worship of idols. By "greatness" (al-kibriya') is meant kingship. Al-Zajjaj said: kingship was called greatness because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It has also been said that it was so called because the king is proud (yatakabbar).

The summary is that they gave two reasons for not accepting Musa's call: clinging to the imitation of their fathers, and greed for worldly leadership. For if they answered the Prophet and confirmed him, the reins of their community's affairs would pass to him, and the king would have no complete leadership left, because governing people by religion removes the rule of kings over them by policies and customs. Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. The address was singular to Musa in their saying "Have you come to us to turn us away," but then they combined him with Harun in address in their saying: ﴿And that greatness might be yours two in the land. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer﴾. He said this when he saw the white hand and the staff, because he believed them to be of sorcery. So he commanded his people to bring him every knowing sorcerer. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash read it as *sahhar* (a sorcerer of intensive form). The rest read *sahir*. This has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

*Sahhar* is an intensive form: that is, one who practices sorcery much, with much knowledge of its work and its kinds.

﴿So when the sorcerers came﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is as follows: "And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer," and they brought them to him. So when the sorcerers came, the *fa'* (so) is conjunctive to the implied, omitted clause.

His saying: ﴿Musa said to them: Cast what you are casting﴾ means: he said this to them after they had said to him: "Either you cast, or we will be the casters." That is: throw on the ground what you have of your ropes and staffs.

﴿So when they cast﴾ what they cast of that, Musa said to them: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "magic." The meaning is that it is sorcery, not one of the signs of Allah.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *sihr* (magic) governed by *ji'tum* (you brought), with *ma* as a conditional particle, the condition being *ji'tum* and the response being ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, with an implied *fa'* (then): that is, "then indeed Allah will nullify it." It has also been said that *al-sihr* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): that is, "what you have brought is sorcery." Then the alif and lam entered (making it definite). On this view, there is no need to omit the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by most grammarians except in poetic necessity.

Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read *ā-ssiḥru* (with the interrogative hamzah), so that the hamzah is interrogative, and the sense is: "Is it magic?" On this reading, *ma* is interrogative.

Ubayy read: *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun, inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will nullify it). That is, He will annihilate it, so that it becomes false by what He manifests of miraculous signs at my hands. ﴿Indeed Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾: that is, the work of this kind. It includes everyone to whom the description "corrupter" truly applies, and it primarily enters sorcery and sorcerers.

The *wāw* in ﴿and Allah establishes the truth﴾ is conjunctive to "will nullify": that is, He will make it clear and manifest by His words which He sent down in His books upon His prophets, because they contain proofs and evidences. ﴿Even if the guilty disliked it﴾: the guilty are either from the family of Fir'awn, or the guilty in general, and the family of Fir'awn enter among them primarily. *Ijram* means sins.

His saying: ﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun returns to Musa, that is, "from the people of Musa," and they were a group of the descendants of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a group of the descendants of Fir'awn, so the pronoun returns to Fir'awn. It has been said that among them were the believer of the family of Fir'awn, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer. It has also been said that they were a people whose fathers were of the Copts and whose mothers were of the Children of Israel. This was narrated from al-Farra'. "Out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs": the pronoun refers to Fir'awn, but it is in the plural because, since he was a tyrant, they used plural pronouns for him out of glorification. It has also been said that the people of Fir'awn were named after Fir'awn, like Thamud, so the pronoun returned to them in this sense. It has also been said that it returns to an omitted noun, and the sense is "out of fear of the family of Fir'awn." This was narrated from al-Farra'. But al-Khalil and Sibawayh prohibited this, so according to them it is not permitted to say: "Hind stood up," while you mean "her boy."

It was narrated from al-Akhfash that the pronoun returns to "offspring." Al-Nahhas supported that. ﴿That he might turn them away from their religion﴾: that is, that he might divert them from their religion by the punishment which he used to inflict on them. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (masdar) of "fear."

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

His saying: ﴿And Musa said: O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾. It has been said that this belongs to the category of repeating the condition: he made reliance on Allah conditional upon belief in Him and submission, that is, surrender to His decree and destiny. It has also been said that this is not a case of making the ruling conditional on two conditions. Rather, what is conditional upon belief is the obligation of reliance, and what is conditional upon submission is its existence. The meaning is: they should surrender themselves to Allah, that is, make themselves wholly sincere to Him, with no share for Satan in them, because reliance does not exist alongside mixing.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its parallel in speech is: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him, if you have strength against him."

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." According to the first meaning, "trial" is in the sense of "one who is tempted."

When they had put first the humble supplication to Allah, that He preserve their religion from corruption, they followed it with asking for the protection of their own selves, and said: ﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾. In this there is evidence that they were more concerned with the matter of religion than with the safety of their own selves.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. One says: "I settled Zayd in a place" and "I settled a place for Zayd." The *mubawwa'* is the dwelling where one is kept (al-manzil al-mal-zum). From this comes "Allah settled him a dwelling," meaning He made him stay in it and lodged him in it. From this is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*
*glory and kingship have settled upon us.*

Egypt in this verse is said by some to be Alexandria, and others say it is Egypt as it is well known, not Alexandria. ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, meaning facing toward the direction of the qiblah. It is said that the houses here refer to mosques, and a group of the early generation (al-salaf) went to this view. It is also said that the houses meant are those in which they dwell, and they were commanded to make them a qiblah for us. The qiblah, according to the first view, is the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. It is also said that the meaning is that they should make their houses face the qiblah so that they might pray in them secretly, lest some harm from the disbelievers befall them because of the prayer. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer He commanded you to establish, for it indicates that the qiblah is the qiblah of prayer, whether in mosques or in houses, not the making of the houses face one another. He addressed Musa and Harun at the beginning of the speech, then made it addressed to both of them and their people in His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah and establish the prayer﴾. Then He addressed Musa alone after that, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, because the choice of place is entrusted to the prophets. Then it was made general in facing the qiblah and establishing the prayer, because that is obligatory upon everyone and is not specific to the prophets. Then it was made specific to Musa, because he is the principal in the message and Harun follows him. So this was a magnification of the good tidings and of the one to whom they were given. It is also said that the address in ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by way of iltifat (turning of address) and i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion). The first view is preferred.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: "to divert us from our gods."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and that greatness in the land may belong to you both﴾, that he said: "the majesty, the kingship and the authority."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a small group (dhurriyyah)﴾, that he said: "dhurriyyah means a few."

These same narrators related from him regarding His saying: ﴿a group from his people﴾, that he said: "from the children of Israel."

So he commanded his people to bring him every knowing sorcerer. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash read it as *sahhar* (a sorcerer of intensive form). The rest read *sahir*.
