*Sahhar* is an intensive form: that is, one who practices sorcery much, with much knowledge of its work and its kinds.

﴿So when the sorcerers came﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is as follows: "And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer," and they brought them to him. So when the sorcerers came, the *fa'* (so) is conjunctive to the implied, omitted clause.

His saying: ﴿Musa said to them: Cast what you are casting﴾ means: he said this to them after they had said to him: "Either you cast, or we will be the casters." That is: throw on the ground what you have of your ropes and staffs.

﴿So when they cast﴾ what they cast of that, Musa said to them: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "magic." The meaning is that it is sorcery, not one of the signs of Allah.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *sihr* (magic) governed by *ji'tum* (you brought), with *ma* as a conditional particle, the condition being *ji'tum* and the response being ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, with an implied *fa'* (then): that is, "then indeed Allah will nullify it." It has also been said that *al-sihr* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): that is, "what you have brought is sorcery." Then the alif and lam entered (making it definite). On this view, there is no need to omit the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by most grammarians except in poetic necessity.

Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read *ā-ssiḥru* (with the interrogative hamzah), so that the hamzah is interrogative, and the sense is: "Is it magic?" On this reading, *ma* is interrogative.

Ubayy read: *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun, inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will nullify it). That is, He will annihilate it, so that it becomes false by what He manifests of miraculous signs at my hands. ﴿Indeed Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾: that is, the work of this kind. It includes everyone to whom the description "corrupter" truly applies, and it primarily enters sorcery and sorcerers.

The *wāw* in ﴿and Allah establishes the truth﴾ is conjunctive to "will nullify": that is, He will make it clear and manifest by His words which He sent down in His books upon His prophets, because they contain proofs and evidences. ﴿Even if the guilty disliked it﴾: the guilty are either from the family of Fir'awn, or the guilty in general, and the family of Fir'awn enter among them primarily. *Ijram* means sins.

His saying: ﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun returns to Musa, that is, "from the people of Musa," and they were a group of the descendants of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a group of the descendants of Fir'awn, so the pronoun returns to Fir'awn. It has been said that among them were the believer of the family of Fir'awn, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer. It has also been said that they were a people whose fathers were of the Copts and whose mothers were of the Children of Israel. This was narrated from al-Farra'. "Out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs": the pronoun refers to Fir'awn, but it is in the plural because, since he was a tyrant, they used plural pronouns for him out of glorification. It has also been said that the people of Fir'awn were named after Fir'awn, like Thamud, so the pronoun returned to them in this sense. It has also been said that it returns to an omitted noun, and the sense is "out of fear of the family of Fir'awn." This was narrated from al-Farra'. But al-Khalil and Sibawayh prohibited this, so according to them it is not permitted to say: "Hind stood up," while you mean "her boy."

It was narrated from al-Akhfash that the pronoun returns to "offspring." Al-Nahhas supported that. ﴿That he might turn them away from their religion﴾: that is, that he might divert them from their religion by the punishment which he used to inflict on them. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (masdar) of "fear."

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

His saying: ﴿And Musa said: O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾. It has been said that this belongs to the category of repeating the condition: he made reliance on Allah conditional upon belief in Him and submission, that is, surrender to His decree and destiny. It has also been said that this is not a case of making the ruling conditional on two conditions. Rather, what is conditional upon belief is the obligation of reliance, and what is conditional upon submission is its existence. The meaning is: they should surrender themselves to Allah, that is, make themselves wholly sincere to Him, with no share for Satan in them, because reliance does not exist alongside mixing.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its parallel in speech is: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him, if you have strength against him."

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." According to the first meaning, "trial" is in the sense of "one who is tempted."

When they had put first the humble supplication to Allah, that He preserve their religion from corruption, they followed it with asking for the protection of their own selves, and said: ﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾. In this there is evidence that they were more concerned with the matter of religion than with the safety of their own selves.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. One says: "I settled Zayd in a place" and "I settled a place for Zayd." The *mubawwa'* is the dwelling where one is kept (al-manzil al-mal-zum). From this comes "Allah settled him a dwelling," meaning He made him stay in it and lodged him in it. From this is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*
*glory and kingship have settled upon us.*

Egypt in this verse is said by some to be Alexandria, and others say it is Egypt as it is well known, not Alexandria. ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, meaning facing toward the direction of the qiblah. It is said that the houses here refer to mosques, and a group of the early generation (al-salaf) went to this view. It is also said that the houses meant are those in which they dwell, and they were commanded to make them a qiblah for us. The qiblah, according to the first view, is the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. It is also said that the meaning is that they should make their houses face the qiblah so that they might pray in them secretly, lest some harm from the disbelievers befall them because of the prayer. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer He commanded you to establish, for it indicates that the qiblah is the qiblah of prayer, whether in mosques or in houses, not the making of the houses face one another. He addressed Musa and Harun at the beginning of the speech, then made it addressed to both of them and their people in His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah and establish the prayer﴾. Then He addressed Musa alone after that, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, because the choice of place is entrusted to the prophets. Then it was made general in facing the qiblah and establishing the prayer, because that is obligatory upon everyone and is not specific to the prophets. Then it was made specific to Musa, because he is the principal in the message and Harun follows him. So this was a magnification of the good tidings and of the one to whom they were given. It is also said that the address in ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by way of iltifat (turning of address) and i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion). The first view is preferred.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿to mislead us﴾, that he said: "to turn us away."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: "to divert us from our gods."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and that greatness in the land may belong to you both﴾, that he said: "the majesty, the kingship and the authority."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a small group (dhurriyyah)﴾, that he said: "dhurriyyah means a few."

These same narrators related from him regarding His saying: ﴿a group from his people﴾, that he said: "from the children of Israel."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, who said: "They were the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent, after a long time had passed and their fathers had died."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The dhurriyyah who believed in Musa were people other than the children of Israel, from the people of Pharaoh, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believing man of Pharaoh's family, the treasurer of Pharaoh, and the wife of his treasurer."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾, that he said: "Do not let them dominate us, lest they tempt us."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said in explaining the verse: "Do not punish us at the hands of the people of Pharaoh, nor with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not be punished nor would we have been given power over them, so they would be tempted by us.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Qilabah regarding the verse, who said: "He asked his Lord not to let our enemy prevail over us, for they would then reckon that they were more deserving of justice and would be tempted by that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Mijlaz something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Pharaoh prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to make their places of prayer in their houses and to face them toward the qiblah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿that you both settle your people in Egypt﴾, that he said: "Egypt is Alexandria."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding the verse, who said: "They did not pray except in churches until they feared the family of Pharaoh, so they were commanded to pray in their houses."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, who said: "They were commanded to take mosques in their houses."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Sinan, who said: "The qiblah is the Ka'bah, and it is mentioned that Adam and those after him used to pray facing the Ka'bah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, that he said: "that some of them face others."

[p. 637] **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 10, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ is conjunctive with His saying: ﴿Then after him We sent Messengers﴾ (Yunus: 74). The pronoun in "after them" refers to the Messengers mentioned earlier. He singled out Musa and Harun for mention, although they are included among the Messengers, because of their greater nobility and the great importance of what took place between them and Fir'awn. "The chiefs" (al-mala') means the nobles. "The signs" (al-ayat) means the miracles, namely the nine mentioned in the Noble Book. They were arrogant and refused to accept them, and did not humble themselves before them or submit to what they contained of miracles that necessitated believing in the one who brought them. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ means they were people of great crime and grave sins. Because of that, they dared to reject them, for sins prevent their possessor from recognizing the truth and seeing what is right. It has been said that this clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), confirming the meaning of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Indeed this is clear magic﴾ means: when the truth, which is the miracles, came from Allah to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they did not believe in them, but called them magic, out of obstinate denial.

Musa responded to them, saying: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you: Is this magic?﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic? Then do not say that." Then he resumed with another denial from himself, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He omitted their first statement, relying on the second. What compels this interpretation is that they did not ask him whether it was magic, so that he would repeat what they said with the words "Is this magic?" Rather, they affirmed definitively that it was magic, for they said: ﴿Indeed this is clear magic﴾. Thus the words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ would not be from their saying. Al-Akhfash said that they are from their saying, but this is open to question for what we have already mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning of "Do you say" is "Do you find fault with the truth and slander it?" and it was incumbent upon you to submit to it. Then he said, "Is this magic?!", rejecting what they had said. It has also been said that the object of "Do you say" is omitted, and it is what their saying "Indeed this is magic" indicates. The sense is: "Do you say what you say, namely your saying 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" Then he said, "Is this magic?" According to this interpretation and the first one, the clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a resumptive statement from Musa, peace be upon him, and the interrogation is for rebuke and reproach, following the first resumptive clause, which answers an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did Musa say to them when they said: 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you…﴾ in the manner of a rhetorical question of denial. The meaning is: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is clear magic? It is the furthest thing from magic."

Then he denied and rebuked and reproached them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ So Musa, peace be upon him, came with denial after denial, reproach after reproach, and accusation of ignorance after accusation of ignorance. The clause ﴿and sorcerers do not prosper﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, when the state is that sorcerers do not prosper, so they do not attain their aim, do not win any good, and are not saved from any harm? How then could one who is sent from Allah fall into this, when He has supported him with miracles and clear proofs?"

The clause ﴿They said: Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾ is a resumptive clause, answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after Musa had said what he said?" This indicates that they were cut off from proof and unable to produce an argument. They did not deny what he had put to them, but resorted to what the people of ignorance and dullness resort to, which is arguing from the disbelief their fathers had been upon. To this they added what was really their aim, the goal of their desire and the cause of their obstinacy against the truth and their rejection of clear signs, namely worldly leadership, which they feared losing and thought would depart from them if they believed. How many people have remained upon falsehood while knowing it to be falsehood, by this pretext, among the groups of this world, in past and future times! Some of them were held back by it from leaving disbelief, and some of them were held back from leaving innovation for the Sunnah, and from sound transmission for mere personal opinion.

It is said: "He turned him (lafataha) with a turning (laftan)" when he diverted him from a thing and twisted him away from it. From this the poet said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*aching from listening, in the neck and the nape.*

That is, you wish to divert us from the thing upon which we found our fathers, which is the worship of idols. By "greatness" (al-kibriya') is meant kingship. Al-Zajjaj said: kingship was called greatness because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It has also been said that it was so called because the king is proud (yatakabbar).

The summary is that they gave two reasons for not accepting Musa's call: clinging to the imitation of their fathers, and greed for worldly leadership. For if they answered the Prophet and confirmed him, the reins of their community's affairs would pass to him, and the king would have no complete leadership left, because governing people by religion removes the rule of kings over them by policies and customs. Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. The address was singular to Musa in their saying "Have you come to us to turn us away," but then they combined him with Harun in address in their saying: ﴿And that greatness might be yours two in the land. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer﴾. He said this when he saw the white hand and the staff, because he believed them to be of sorcery. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and that greatness in the land may belong to you both﴾, that he said: "the majesty, the kingship and the authority."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a small group (dhurriyyah)﴾, that he said: "dhurriyyah means a few."

These same narrators related from him regarding His saying: ﴿a group from his people﴾, that he said: "from the children of Israel."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, who said: "They were the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent, after a long time had passed and their fathers had died."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The dhurriyyah who believed in Musa were people other than the children of Israel, from the people of Pharaoh, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believing man of Pharaoh's family, the treasurer of Pharaoh, and the wife of his treasurer."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾, that he said: "Do not let them dominate us, lest they tempt us."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said in explaining the verse: "Do not punish us at the hands of the people of Pharaoh, nor with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not be punished nor would we have been given power over them, so they would be tempted by us.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Qilabah regarding the verse, who said: "He asked his Lord not to let our enemy prevail over us, for they would then reckon that they were more deserving of justice and would be tempted by that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Mijlaz something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Pharaoh prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to make their places of prayer in their houses and to face them toward the qiblah."

[p. 637] **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 10, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ is conjunctive with His saying: ﴿Then after him We sent Messengers﴾ (Yunus: 74). The pronoun in "after them" refers to the Messengers mentioned earlier. He singled out Musa and Harun for mention, although they are included among the Messengers, because of their greater nobility and the great importance of what took place between them and Fir'awn. "The chiefs" (al-mala') means the nobles. "The signs" (al-ayat) means the miracles, namely the nine mentioned in the Noble Book. They were arrogant and refused to accept them, and did not humble themselves before them or submit to what they contained of miracles that necessitated believing in the one who brought them. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ means they were people of great crime and grave sins. Because of that, they dared to reject them, for sins prevent their possessor from recognizing the truth and seeing what is right. It has been said that this clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), confirming the meaning of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Indeed this is clear magic﴾ means: when the truth, which is the miracles, came from Allah to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they did not believe in them, but called them magic, out of obstinate denial.

Musa responded to them, saying: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you: Is this magic?﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic? Then do not say that." Then he resumed with another denial from himself, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He omitted their first statement, relying on the second. What compels this interpretation is that they did not ask him whether it was magic, so that he would repeat what they said with the words "Is this magic?" Rather, they affirmed definitively that it was magic, for they said: ﴿Indeed this is clear magic﴾. Thus the words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ would not be from their saying. Al-Akhfash said that they are from their saying, but this is open to question for what we have already mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning of "Do you say" is "Do you find fault with the truth and slander it?" and it was incumbent upon you to submit to it. Then he said, "Is this magic?!", rejecting what they had said. It has also been said that the object of "Do you say" is omitted, and it is what their saying "Indeed this is magic" indicates. The sense is: "Do you say what you say, namely your saying 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" Then he said, "Is this magic?" According to this interpretation and the first one, the clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a resumptive statement from Musa, peace be upon him, and the interrogation is for rebuke and reproach, following the first resumptive clause, which answers an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did Musa say to them when they said: 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you…﴾ in the manner of a rhetorical question of denial. The meaning is: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is clear magic? It is the furthest thing from magic."

Then he denied and rebuked and reproached them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ So Musa, peace be upon him, came with denial after denial, reproach after reproach, and accusation of ignorance after accusation of ignorance. The clause ﴿and sorcerers do not prosper﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, when the state is that sorcerers do not prosper, so they do not attain their aim, do not win any good, and are not saved from any harm? How then could one who is sent from Allah fall into this, when He has supported him with miracles and clear proofs?"

The clause ﴿They said: Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾ is a resumptive clause, answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after Musa had said what he said?" This indicates that they were cut off from proof and unable to produce an argument. They did not deny what he had put to them, but resorted to what the people of ignorance and dullness resort to, which is arguing from the disbelief their fathers had been upon. To this they added what was really their aim, the goal of their desire and the cause of their obstinacy against the truth and their rejection of clear signs, namely worldly leadership, which they feared losing and thought would depart from them if they believed. How many people have remained upon falsehood while knowing it to be falsehood, by this pretext, among the groups of this world, in past and future times! Some of them were held back by it from leaving disbelief, and some of them were held back from leaving innovation for the Sunnah, and from sound transmission for mere personal opinion.

It is said: "He turned him (lafataha) with a turning (laftan)" when he diverted him from a thing and twisted him away from it. From this the poet said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*aching from listening, in the neck and the nape.*

That is, you wish to divert us from the thing upon which we found our fathers, which is the worship of idols. By "greatness" (al-kibriya') is meant kingship. Al-Zajjaj said: kingship was called greatness because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It has also been said that it was so called because the king is proud (yatakabbar).

The summary is that they gave two reasons for not accepting Musa's call: clinging to the imitation of their fathers, and greed for worldly leadership. For if they answered the Prophet and confirmed him, the reins of their community's affairs would pass to him, and the king would have no complete leadership left, because governing people by religion removes the rule of kings over them by policies and customs. Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. The address was singular to Musa in their saying "Have you come to us to turn us away," but then they combined him with Harun in address in their saying: ﴿And that greatness might be yours two in the land. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer﴾. He said this when he saw the white hand and the staff, because he believed them to be of sorcery. So he commanded his people to bring him every knowing sorcerer. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash read it as *sahhar* (a sorcerer of intensive form). The rest read *sahir*. This has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

*Sahhar* is an intensive form: that is, one who practices sorcery much, with much knowledge of its work and its kinds.

﴿So when the sorcerers came﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is as follows: "And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer," and they brought them to him. So when the sorcerers came, the *fa'* (so) is conjunctive to the implied, omitted clause.

His saying: ﴿Musa said to them: Cast what you are casting﴾ means: he said this to them after they had said to him: "Either you cast, or we will be the casters." That is: throw on the ground what you have of your ropes and staffs.

﴿So when they cast﴾ what they cast of that, Musa said to them: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "magic." The meaning is that it is sorcery, not one of the signs of Allah.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *sihr* (magic) governed by *ji'tum* (you brought), with *ma* as a conditional particle, the condition being *ji'tum* and the response being ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, with an implied *fa'* (then): that is, "then indeed Allah will nullify it." It has also been said that *al-sihr* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): that is, "what you have brought is sorcery." Then the alif and lam entered (making it definite). On this view, there is no need to omit the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by most grammarians except in poetic necessity.

Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read *ā-ssiḥru* (with the interrogative hamzah), so that the hamzah is interrogative, and the sense is: "Is it magic?" On this reading, *ma* is interrogative.

Ubayy read: *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun, inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will nullify it). That is, He will annihilate it, so that it becomes false by what He manifests of miraculous signs at my hands. ﴿Indeed Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾: that is, the work of this kind. It includes everyone to whom the description "corrupter" truly applies, and it primarily enters sorcery and sorcerers.

The *wāw* in ﴿and Allah establishes the truth﴾ is conjunctive to "will nullify": that is, He will make it clear and manifest by His words which He sent down in His books upon His prophets, because they contain proofs and evidences. ﴿Even if the guilty disliked it﴾: the guilty are either from the family of Fir'awn, or the guilty in general, and the family of Fir'awn enter among them primarily. *Ijram* means sins.

His saying: ﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun returns to Musa, that is, "from the people of Musa," and they were a group of the descendants of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a group of the descendants of Fir'awn, so the pronoun returns to Fir'awn. It has been said that among them were the believer of the family of Fir'awn, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer. It has also been said that they were a people whose fathers were of the Copts and whose mothers were of the Children of Israel. This was narrated from al-Farra'. "Out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs": the pronoun refers to Fir'awn, but it is in the plural because, since he was a tyrant, they used plural pronouns for him out of glorification. It has also been said that the people of Fir'awn were named after Fir'awn, like Thamud, so the pronoun returned to them in this sense. It has also been said that it returns to an omitted noun, and the sense is "out of fear of the family of Fir'awn." This was narrated from al-Farra'. But al-Khalil and Sibawayh prohibited this, so according to them it is not permitted to say: "Hind stood up," while you mean "her boy."

It was narrated from al-Akhfash that the pronoun returns to "offspring." Al-Nahhas supported that. ﴿That he might turn them away from their religion﴾: that is, that he might divert them from their religion by the punishment which he used to inflict on them. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (masdar) of "fear."

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

His saying: ﴿And Musa said: O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾. It has been said that this belongs to the category of repeating the condition: he made reliance on Allah conditional upon belief in Him and submission, that is, surrender to His decree and destiny. It has also been said that this is not a case of making the ruling conditional on two conditions. Rather, what is conditional upon belief is the obligation of reliance, and what is conditional upon submission is its existence. The meaning is: they should surrender themselves to Allah, that is, make themselves wholly sincere to Him, with no share for Satan in them, because reliance does not exist alongside mixing.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its parallel in speech is: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him, if you have strength against him."

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." According to the first meaning, "trial" is in the sense of "one who is tempted."

When they had put first the humble supplication to Allah, that He preserve their religion from corruption, they followed it with asking for the protection of their own selves, and said: ﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾. In this there is evidence that they were more concerned with the matter of religion than with the safety of their own selves.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. One says: "I settled Zayd in a place" and "I settled a place for Zayd." The *mubawwa'* is the dwelling where one is kept (al-manzil al-mal-zum). From this comes "Allah settled him a dwelling," meaning He made him stay in it and lodged him in it. From this is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*
*glory and kingship have settled upon us.*

Egypt in this verse is said by some to be Alexandria, and others say it is Egypt as it is well known, not Alexandria. ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, meaning facing toward the direction of the qiblah. It is said that the houses here refer to mosques, and a group of the early generation (al-salaf) went to this view. It is also said that the houses meant are those in which they dwell, and they were commanded to make them a qiblah for us. The qiblah, according to the first view, is the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. It is also said that the meaning is that they should make their houses face the qiblah so that they might pray in them secretly, lest some harm from the disbelievers befall them because of the prayer. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer He commanded you to establish, for it indicates that the qiblah is the qiblah of prayer, whether in mosques or in houses, not the making of the houses face one another. He addressed Musa and Harun at the beginning of the speech, then made it addressed to both of them and their people in His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah and establish the prayer﴾. Then He addressed Musa alone after that, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, because the choice of place is entrusted to the prophets. Then it was made general in facing the qiblah and establishing the prayer, because that is obligatory upon everyone and is not specific to the prophets. Then it was made specific to Musa, because he is the principal in the message and Harun follows him. So this was a magnification of the good tidings and of the one to whom they were given. It is also said that the address in ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by way of iltifat (turning of address) and i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion). The first view is preferred.

Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer﴾. He said this when he saw the white hand and the staff, because he believed them to be of sorcery. So he commanded his people to bring him every knowing sorcerer. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash read it as *sahhar* (a sorcerer of intensive form). The rest read *sahir*. This has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

*Sahhar* is an intensive form: that is, one who practices sorcery much, with much knowledge of its work and its kinds.

﴿So when the sorcerers came﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is as follows: "And Fir'awn said: Bring me every knowing sorcerer," and they brought them to him. So when the sorcerers came, the *fa'* (so) is conjunctive to the implied, omitted clause.

His saying: ﴿Musa said to them: Cast what you are casting﴾ means: he said this to them after they had said to him: "Either you cast, or we will be the casters." That is: throw on the ground what you have of your ropes and staffs.

﴿So when they cast﴾ what they cast of that, Musa said to them: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "magic." The meaning is that it is sorcery, not one of the signs of Allah.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *sihr* (magic) governed by *ji'tum* (you brought), with *ma* as a conditional particle, the condition being *ji'tum* and the response being ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, with an implied *fa'* (then): that is, "then indeed Allah will nullify it." It has also been said that *al-sihr* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): that is, "what you have brought is sorcery." Then the alif and lam entered (making it definite). On this view, there is no need to omit the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by most grammarians except in poetic necessity.

Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read *ā-ssiḥru* (with the interrogative hamzah), so that the hamzah is interrogative, and the sense is: "Is it magic?" On this reading, *ma* is interrogative.

Ubayy read: *mā ataytum bihi siḥrun, inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (What you have brought is sorcery; indeed Allah will nullify it). That is, He will annihilate it, so that it becomes false by what He manifests of miraculous signs at my hands. ﴿Indeed Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾: that is, the work of this kind. It includes everyone to whom the description "corrupter" truly applies, and it primarily enters sorcery and sorcerers.

The *wāw* in ﴿and Allah establishes the truth﴾ is conjunctive to "will nullify": that is, He will make it clear and manifest by His words which He sent down in His books upon His prophets, because they contain proofs and evidences. ﴿Even if the guilty disliked it﴾: the guilty are either from the family of Fir'awn, or the guilty in general, and the family of Fir'awn enter among them primarily. *Ijram* means sins.

His saying: ﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun returns to Musa, that is, "from the people of Musa," and they were a group of the descendants of the Children of Israel. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a group of the descendants of Fir'awn, so the pronoun returns to Fir'awn. It has been said that among them were the believer of the family of Fir'awn, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer. It has also been said that they were a people whose fathers were of the Copts and whose mothers were of the Children of Israel. This was narrated from al-Farra'. "Out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs": the pronoun refers to Fir'awn, but it is in the plural because, since he was a tyrant, they used plural pronouns for him out of glorification. It has also been said that the people of Fir'awn were named after Fir'awn, like Thamud, so the pronoun returned to them in this sense. It has also been said that it returns to an omitted noun, and the sense is "out of fear of the family of Fir'awn." This was narrated from al-Farra'. But al-Khalil and Sibawayh prohibited this, so according to them it is not permitted to say: "Hind stood up," while you mean "her boy."

It was narrated from al-Akhfash that the pronoun returns to "offspring." Al-Nahhas supported that. ﴿That he might turn them away from their religion﴾: that is, that he might divert them from their religion by the punishment which he used to inflict on them. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative governed by the verbal noun (masdar) of "fear."

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

His saying: ﴿And Musa said: O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾. It has been said that this belongs to the category of repeating the condition: he made reliance on Allah conditional upon belief in Him and submission, that is, surrender to His decree and destiny. It has also been said that this is not a case of making the ruling conditional on two conditions. Rather, what is conditional upon belief is the obligation of reliance, and what is conditional upon submission is its existence. The meaning is: they should surrender themselves to Allah, that is, make themselves wholly sincere to Him, with no share for Satan in them, because reliance does not exist alongside mixing.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its parallel in speech is: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him, if you have strength against him."

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." According to the first meaning, "trial" is in the sense of "one who is tempted."

When they had put first the humble supplication to Allah, that He preserve their religion from corruption, they followed it with asking for the protection of their own selves, and said: ﴿And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾. In this there is evidence that they were more concerned with the matter of religion than with the safety of their own selves.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. One says: "I settled Zayd in a place" and "I settled a place for Zayd." The *mubawwa'* is the dwelling where one is kept (al-manzil al-mal-zum). From this comes "Allah settled him a dwelling," meaning He made him stay in it and lodged him in it. From this is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire." From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*
*glory and kingship have settled upon us.*

Egypt in this verse is said by some to be Alexandria, and others say it is Egypt as it is well known, not Alexandria. ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, meaning facing toward the direction of the qiblah. It is said that the houses here refer to mosques, and a group of the early generation (al-salaf) went to this view. It is also said that the houses meant are those in which they dwell, and they were commanded to make them a qiblah for us. The qiblah, according to the first view, is the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. It is also said that the meaning is that they should make their houses face the qiblah so that they might pray in them secretly, lest some harm from the disbelievers befall them because of the prayer. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning the prayer He commanded you to establish, for it indicates that the qiblah is the qiblah of prayer, whether in mosques or in houses, not the making of the houses face one another. He addressed Musa and Harun at the beginning of the speech, then made it addressed to both of them and their people in His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah and establish the prayer﴾. Then He addressed Musa alone after that, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, because the choice of place is entrusted to the prophets. Then it was made general in facing the qiblah and establishing the prayer, because that is obligatory upon everyone and is not specific to the prophets. Then it was made specific to Musa, because he is the principal in the message and Harun follows him. So this was a magnification of the good tidings and of the one to whom they were given. It is also said that the address in ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by way of iltifat (turning of address) and i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion). The first view is preferred.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿to mislead us﴾, that he said: "to turn us away."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: "to divert us from our gods."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and that greatness in the land may belong to you both﴾, that he said: "the majesty, the kingship and the authority."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a small group (dhurriyyah)﴾, that he said: "dhurriyyah means a few."

These same narrators related from him regarding His saying: ﴿a group from his people﴾, that he said: "from the children of Israel."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, who said: "They were the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent, after a long time had passed and their fathers had died."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The dhurriyyah who believed in Musa were people other than the children of Israel, from the people of Pharaoh, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believing man of Pharaoh's family, the treasurer of Pharaoh, and the wife of his treasurer."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾, that he said: "Do not let them dominate us, lest they tempt us."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said in explaining the verse: "Do not punish us at the hands of the people of Pharaoh, nor with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not be punished nor would we have been given power over them, so they would be tempted by us.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Qilabah regarding the verse, who said: "He asked his Lord not to let our enemy prevail over us, for they would then reckon that they were more deserving of justice and would be tempted by that."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Mijlaz something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Pharaoh prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to make their places of prayer in their houses and to face them toward the qiblah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿that you both settle your people in Egypt﴾, that he said: "Egypt is Alexandria."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding the verse, who said: "They did not pray except in churches until they feared the family of Pharaoh, so they were commanded to pray in their houses."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, who said: "They were commanded to take mosques in their houses."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Sinan, who said: "The qiblah is the Ka'bah, and it is mentioned that Adam and those after him used to pray facing the Ka'bah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And make your houses into a qiblah﴾, that he said: "that some of them face others."

[p. 637] **Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 10, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ is conjunctive with His saying: ﴿Then after him We sent Messengers﴾ (Yunus: 74). The pronoun in "after them" refers to the Messengers mentioned earlier. He singled out Musa and Harun for mention, although they are included among the Messengers, because of their greater nobility and the great importance of what took place between them and Fir'awn. "The chiefs" (al-mala') means the nobles. "The signs" (al-ayat) means the miracles, namely the nine mentioned in the Noble Book. They were arrogant and refused to accept them, and did not humble themselves before them or submit to what they contained of miracles that necessitated believing in the one who brought them. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ means they were people of great crime and grave sins. Because of that, they dared to reject them, for sins prevent their possessor from recognizing the truth and seeing what is right. It has been said that this clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), confirming the meaning of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: Indeed this is clear magic﴾ means: when the truth, which is the miracles, came from Allah to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they did not believe in them, but called them magic, out of obstinate denial.

Musa responded to them, saying: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you: Is this magic?﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic? Then do not say that." Then he resumed with another denial from himself, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He omitted their first statement, relying on the second. What compels this interpretation is that they did not ask him whether it was magic, so that he would repeat what they said with the words "Is this magic?" Rather, they affirmed definitively that it was magic, for they said: ﴿Indeed this is clear magic﴾. Thus the words ﴿Is this magic?﴾ would not be from their saying. Al-Akhfash said that they are from their saying, but this is open to question for what we have already mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning of "Do you say" is "Do you find fault with the truth and slander it?" and it was incumbent upon you to submit to it. Then he said, "Is this magic?!", rejecting what they had said. It has also been said that the object of "Do you say" is omitted, and it is what their saying "Indeed this is magic" indicates. The sense is: "Do you say what you say, namely your saying 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" Then he said, "Is this magic?" According to this interpretation and the first one, the clause ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a resumptive statement from Musa, peace be upon him, and the interrogation is for rebuke and reproach, following the first resumptive clause, which answers an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did Musa say to them when they said: 'Indeed this is clear magic'?" So it was said: He said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you…﴾ in the manner of a rhetorical question of denial. The meaning is: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is clear magic? It is the furthest thing from magic."

Then he denied and rebuked and reproached them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ So Musa, peace be upon him, came with denial after denial, reproach after reproach, and accusation of ignorance after accusation of ignorance. The clause ﴿and sorcerers do not prosper﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, when the state is that sorcerers do not prosper, so they do not attain their aim, do not win any good, and are not saved from any harm? How then could one who is sent from Allah fall into this, when He has supported him with miracles and clear proofs?"

The clause ﴿They said: Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾ is a resumptive clause, answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after Musa had said what he said?" This indicates that they were cut off from proof and unable to produce an argument. They did not deny what he had put to them, but resorted to what the people of ignorance and dullness resort to, which is arguing from the disbelief their fathers had been upon. To this they added what was really their aim, the goal of their desire and the cause of their obstinacy against the truth and their rejection of clear signs, namely worldly leadership, which they feared losing and thought would depart from them if they believed. How many people have remained upon falsehood while knowing it to be falsehood, by this pretext, among the groups of this world, in past and future times! Some of them were held back by it from leaving disbelief, and some of them were held back from leaving innovation for the Sunnah, and from sound transmission for mere personal opinion.

It is said: "He turned him (lafataha) with a turning (laftan)" when he diverted him from a thing and twisted him away from it. From this the poet said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*aching from listening, in the neck and the nape.*

That is, you wish to divert us from the thing upon which we found our fathers, which is the worship of idols. By "greatness" (al-kibriya') is meant kingship. Al-Zajjaj said: kingship was called greatness because it is the greatest thing sought in worldly affairs. It has also been said that it was so called because the king is proud (yatakabbar).

The summary is that they gave two reasons for not accepting Musa's call: clinging to the imitation of their fathers, and greed for worldly leadership. For if they answered the Prophet and confirmed him, the reins of their community's affairs would pass to him, and the king would have no complete leadership left, because governing people by religion removes the rule of kings over them by policies and customs. Then they said: ﴿And we will not believe you two﴾, openly declaring their denial and cutting off any hope of their belief. The address was singular to Musa in their saying "Have you come to us to turn us away," but then they combined him with Harun in address in their saying: ﴿And that greatness might be yours two in the land. And we will not believe you two.﴾ The reason is that they attributed the coming and the turning away from the way of their fathers to Musa, because he was the intended one of the mission, the one who conveyed from Allah what He had legislated for them. They combined both in the two later pronouns, because in their supposition greatness encompassed both of them, and because abandoning belief in Musa entails abandoning belief in Harun. The story has already passed in Surat al-A'raf.

﴿And indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land﴾: that is, arrogant, proud, dominant over the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the extravagant﴾: those who exceed the limit in disbelief, and in what he did of killing, crucifixion, and varying punishments.

﴿So they said﴾: that is, the people of Musa, answering him, ﴿In Allah we have relied﴾. Then they called upon Allah sincerely, and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, that is, a place of trial for the wrongdoing people. The meaning is: do not empower them over us so that they punish us until they tempt us away from our religion, and do not make us a trial for them, so that they tempt others through us, saying to them: "If these people were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them and punished them." His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The *an* (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah), because in the revelation there is the meaning of "settle": that is, take for your people houses in Egypt. *We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt,*

It is also said that it is the direction of the Ka'bah, and that it was the qiblah of Musa and those with him.
