Al-Asma'i said: it is said atba'ahu, with a cut alif, when one catches up with and overtakes him, and ittaba'ahu, with a connected alif, when one follows his trail, whether he overtakes him or not.

Abu Zayd said likewise. Abu 'Amr said: ittaba'ahu with a connected alif means he imitated him.

The accusative of baghyan and ʿadwan is adverbial (ḥāl). Al-baghy is injustice, and al-ʿadw is aggression. It is also permissible that their accusative is for causation, that is: for the sake of transgression and enmity.

Al-Hasan read ʿudūwan with a ḍamma on the ʿayn and the dāl and a doubled wāw, like ʿalā yaʿlū ʿulūwan. It was also said that al-baghy is seeking to exalt oneself in speech without right, and al-ʿadw is in deed.

﴿Until, when the drowning overtook him﴾, that is, reached him, arrived at him, and seized him.

This is because Musa went out with the Children of Israel at a moment of heedlessness on Pharaoh's part. When Pharaoh heard of this, he pursued them with his hosts. Allah split the sea for Musa and the Children of Israel, and they walked through it until they came out on the other side. Pharaoh followed them while the sea remained in the state it had been in when Musa and those with him passed through. When Pharaoh's hosts had fully entered and were about to come out on the other side, it closed over them and they drowned, as Allah, glorified is He, related.

﴿He said: I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe.⁠﴾ That is: I affirm that— with the hamza fatḥa on the premise that the original is bi-annahu, and the bā' was dropped, and the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n).

It was also read with a kasra on inna, as a fresh resumption (isti'nāf). Abu Hatim claimed that there is an elided verb of speech: "I believe," so I said: "Indeed He..." This faith did not benefit him because it occurred after the drowning had fully overtaken him, as was discussed earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. The accursed one did not say "I believe in Allah" or "in the Lord of the worlds," but said: "I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe," because a vestige of the claim to divinity remained in him.

His words: ﴿And I am of the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to Allah's command, who are obedient to Him, who affirm His oneness and negate whatever is other than Him. This clause is either in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or conjoined to āmantu (I believe).

His words: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters?⁠﴾ It is the speech of an implied verb of speech conjoined to "he said: I believe," that is: it was said to him, "Do you believe now?"

It has been disputed who said this statement to Pharaoh. It was said: it is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He. It was said: it is from the speech of Jibril. It was said: it is from the speech of Mika'il. It was said: it is from the speech of Pharaoh himself, who said it within himself to himself.

The clause ﴿And you had disobeyed before﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of the implied verb following the implied speech, which is "Do you believe now?" The meaning is a denial of faith from him at the moment when drowning seized him, while he had disobeyed Allah before. The purpose is reproach and rebuke.

The clause ﴿And you were among the corrupters⁠﴾ is conjoined to "you had disobeyed" and included in the circumstantial sense: that is, you were among the corrupters in the land by your straying from the truth and your leading others astray.

His words: ﴿So today We will save you with your body⁠﴾. It is read nunajjīka with lightening (nunjīka), but the majority read it with doubling.

Al-Yazidi read nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed ḥā' from al-tanḥiya (removal), and 'Alqama narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud. The meaning of nunajjīka with the jīm: We cast you upon a height of the earth. That is because the Children of Israel did not believe that Pharaoh had drowned, and they said: he is greater in importance than that. So Allah cast him upon a height of the earth, that is, an elevated place on the earth, until they saw him. It was also said the meaning is: We bring you out of what your people have fallen into, sinking to the bottom of the sea, and We make you float so that they may see you dead by drowning. The meaning of nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed letter is: We throw you onto one side of the earth.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read bi-abdānika (with your bodies).

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of bi-badanika. It was said: its meaning is with your body after the soul has been removed from it. It was said: its meaning is with your coat of mail, since a coat of mail is called a badan. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You see the abdān (coats of mail) on them, fully covering, on the heroes, and the sturdy helmet."

He meant by abdān the coats of mail. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"Their women went forth with every full-length, tight-fitting coat of mail, and with abdān."

That is, with full-length coats of mail and short coats of mail, which are called abdān, as Abu 'Ubayda said.

Al-Akhfash said: as for the saying of one who says "with your coat of mail," it is nothing, and he preferred that the badan meant here is the body.

His words: ﴿So that you may be a sign for those after you⁠﴾. This is the reason for casting him out with his body. It indicates that he did not expose his body apart from his people except for this reason and no other. The sign (āya) here means the mark: so that for those among mankind who come after you, it is a mark by which they recognize your destruction, and that you are not as you claimed, and the doubt is removed from them about whether you have become dead by drowning. It was also said: the meaning is that your being cast onto the shore alone, apart from your drowned people, is a sign from the signs of Allah by which people may take a lesson, or by which those nations that will come later may take a lesson when they hear of it, so that they beware of arrogance, tyranny, and rebellion against Allah, glorified is He. For this one who reached what he reached of the claim to divinity and persisted in it for a long time had this shameful end.

It was read liman khalafaka (for those who succeeded you) in the past tense form, that is: for those who come after you of the generations, or those who succeeded you in leadership, or in dwelling in the residence you used to inhabit. ﴿And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs⁠﴾, which require reflection and contemplation and awaken one from the slumber of heedlessness. This clause is a concluding remark (tadhyīl).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth⁠﴾, that he said: destroy their wealth and annihilate it. ﴿And harden their hearts⁠﴾: he said: seal them. ﴿So they will not believe until they see the painful punishment⁠﴾, which is drowning. (p. 640)

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked me about His words, ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾. I informed him that God had obliterated the wealth of Pharaoh and the family of Pharaoh until it turned into stones. Umar said: "Stay as you are until I come to you." He then called for a sealed bag and opened it, and inside was silver cut into pieces, like stones, and dinars and dirhams and similar kinds of wealth, all of them stones.

It has also been related that their wealth turned into stones, through a group of the early generations (al-salaf, the righteous predecessors).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Your supplication has been answered." He said: So He answered him, and He placed a barrier between Pharaoh and faith.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Whenever Musa supplicated, Harun would say "Amin" to his supplication. Abu Hurayrah said: "Amin" is one of the names of God. This is His words, ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They claim that Pharaoh remained for forty years after this supplication.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj something similar.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿So go straight and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾, that "go straight" means "proceed according to My command," and this is the istiqamah (steadfastness).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "al-adw" (transgression), "al-utuww" (arrogance) and "al-uluww" (haughtiness) in the Book of God all mean tajabbur (tyranny).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the last of Musa's companions had left, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, God revealed to the sea: 'Close over them.' Then the finger of Pharaoh emerged, saying: 'There is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believed.' Jibril said: 'I knew that the Lord is merciful, and I feared that mercy would reach him, so I covered him with my wing and said: Now, after you disobeyed before?' When Musa and his companions had come out, those among the people of Pharaoh who had stayed behind said: 'Pharaoh and his companions did not drown, but they are in the islands of the sea hunting.' So God revealed to the sea: 'Cast out Pharaoh naked.' It cast him out naked, bald, short and reddish-yellow (akhyanis), and this is His words: ﴿Today We will save you in your body, so that you may be a sign to those who come after you﴾, against the one who said that Pharaoh had not drowned. It was as if the salvation of others had not been a salvation of wellbeing. Then God revealed to the sea: 'Cast out what is in you,' and it cast them out onto the shore. The sea would not cast out a drowned person from its belly until the fish had eaten him, and the sea will never accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God drowned Pharaoh, and he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾. Jibril said to me: 'O Muhammad, if you had seen me as I took mud from the bottom of the sea and pushed it into his mouth, for fear that mercy would reach him.'"

Al-Tirmidhi narrated this hadith through more than one chain and said: "hasan sahih gharib" (good, sound, strange). Al-Hakim also declared it sahih.

It was also related from Ibn Abbas as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report through other routes.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Jibril said to me: 'There was nothing on earth more hateful to me than Pharaoh. When he believed, I began to stuff his mouth with black mud, while I was covering him, for fear that mercy would reach him.'"

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Ibn Umar as a marfu' report as well.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar from Abu Umamah as a marfu' report as well. In the isnad of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah there is an unknown man (majhul), while the rest of its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat).

It is most astonishing that some of the exegetes who have no knowledge of the science of narration (fann al-riwayah) and can barely distinguish between the most authentic of the sound hadiths and the most false of the lies, how they venture to speak about the hadiths of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), refuting what is authentic among them, and letting their tongues and pens run with pure ignorance and shameful deficiency that anyone with even slight practice in the science of hadith would laugh at. So, O poor one, what have you to do with this matter, of which you have no part at all? Would you not conceal yourself and keep to your place, and recognize that in this science you are among the most ignorant of the ignorant? Occupy yourself with what is your knowledge, beyond which you cannot go, and what is your entire portion, which is nothing other than it: the science of the Arabic language and its auxiliary instrumental sciences (al-ulum al-alatiyyah, the tools-sciences serving the Qur'an and hadith). The author of al-Kashshaf, may God have mercy on him, became, because of what he touches upon in his tafsir from the science of hadith, which is not part of his field, neither in his path nor in his breast, a mockery for the mockers and a lesson for those who take heed. Sometimes he narrates in his book fabricated reports (mawdu'at) while he does not know that they are fabricated, and sometimes he attempts to reject what is authentic, asserting with certainty that it is a lie upon the Messenger of God and a slander against him, while it may be found in the Two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and other collections, and in what is attached to them, through the narration of a group of the Companions, with chains whose narrators are all imams, trustworthy, firmly established and authoritative proofs. The least portion of intellect would restrain its possessor from speaking on a science he does not know and of which he has even the slightest understanding, even if that science is one of the technical sciences (ulum al-istilah) upon which a group of people agree and establish conventions among themselves. So what then of the science of the Sunnah, which is the counterpart of the Book of God, whose speaker is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and whose transmitter from him is the best of generations, then those who follow them, then those who follow them, and every letter of it and every word of it establishes a general law for all the people of Islam.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: God saved Pharaoh for the Children of Israel from the sea, so they looked at him after he had drowned.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "In your body." Some of the Children of Israel denied the death of Pharaoh, so he was cast onto the shore of the sea until the Children of Israel saw him, reddish and short, as if he were a bull.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: "In your armour." His armour was made of pearl, in which he used to meet wars.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 88–92 (part 1 of 2):

When Musa (peace be upon him) exceeded in displaying the miracles and establishing the clear proofs, and this had no effect on those to whom he was sent, he invoked (a curse) against them after explaining the cause of their persistence in disbelief and their clinging to denial and obstinacy. So he said, first explaining the cause: ﴿Our Lord, You have indeed given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world.﴾ It has already been mentioned that al-mala' (the chiefs) are the nobles. Zina (adornment) is the name for everything one adorns oneself with: clothing, mounts, jewelry, furnishings, weapons and other things. Then he repeated the address for emphasis, saying: ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way.﴾

Scholars differ regarding this lam (the particle "that") entering the verb. Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh said that it is lam al-'aqiba wa al-sayrura (the lam of consequence and outcome). The meaning is that, since the outcome of their affair was misguidance, it was as if Allah, glorified is He, gave them what He gave them of blessings so that they would go astray. On this view the lam is connected to ātayta (You have given). It was also said that it is lam kay (the lam of purpose), meaning: You gave them so that they would go astray.

Others said the meaning is: You gave them that so they would not go astray, and the particle "not" (lā) was dropped, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176].

Al-Nahhas said: the apparent sense of this answer is good, except that the Arabs do not drop lā except together with an (anna). The proponent of this interpretation obscured the matter by citing His words ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176]. It was also said that the lam is for supplication against them. The meaning is: test them with destruction away from Your way. The one who holds this view cites His words after this: ﴿Obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts﴾.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) went to great lengths in establishing this view with what is of no benefit. The first view is the preferable one.

The Kufans read liyudillū with a ḍamma on the initial letter of the imperfect verb, meaning that they cause others to be led astray. The rest read it with a fatḥa, meaning that they themselves go astray.

﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth.﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: ṭams (obliteration) of a thing is removing it from its form. The meaning is a supplication against them that Allah erase their wealth and destroy it. It was also read with a ḍamma on the mīm of iṭmus ( it is recited as iṭmus).

﴿And harden their hearts﴾, that is, make them hard and sealed, not accepting the truth and not opening up to faith.

His words: ﴿So they will not believe.﴾

Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to liyudillū, and the meaning is: You gave them blessings so that they would go astray and not believe. The material between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ).

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda said: it is a supplication in the form of a prohibition, and the implied sense is: O Allah, let them not believe. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"So let there not expand between your two eyes what has withdrawn, and do not meet me except with your nose humbled."

Al-Akhfash said: it is the answer to the imperative, that is: obliterate and harden, so that they will not believe; and so it is in the accusative. This is also narrated from al-Farra'. From this is the saying:

"O she-camel, march with a wide, long stride, to Sulayman, so that we may rest."

﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾, that is, faith will not come from them except when they witness what Allah will punish them with, and at that time their faith will not benefit them.

Some scholars have raised a difficulty concerning this verse's supplication against these people, saying: the Messengers only seek the guidance and faith of their peoples. It was answered: it is not permissible for a prophet to invoke against his people except by Allah's permission, glorified is He. Allah only grants this permission because He knows that none among them will believe. This is why, when Allah informed Nuh (peace be upon him) that none of his people would believe except those who had already believed, he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers as a dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26].

﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered, so go straight.﴾ Here He attributes the supplication to Musa and Harun, whereas earlier He attributed it to Musa alone. It was said: Harun used to say "Amin" to Musa's supplication, so he is here called a supplicant. Even if the one supplicating was Musa alone, at the beginning of the speech He attributed the supplication to Musa because he was the one who supplicated, while here He attributed it to both of them, treating the one who says "Amin" as the one who supplicates. It is also permissible that both of them were supplicants, but He attributed the supplication to Musa at the beginning of the speech because of his primacy in the message.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: the proof that the supplication was for both of them is Musa's saying "our Lord" (rabbanā) and not "my Lord" (rabbi).

'Ali and al-Sulami read du'ā'ukumā (your supplication), and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read da'wākumā (your supplication). Istiqāma (going straight) is steadfastness in what they were upon of calling to Allah.

Al-Farra' and others said: they were commanded to go straight in their affair and to persist in it, in calling Pharaoh and his people to faith, until the fulfilment (ta'wīl) of the answer comes to them, forty years later, after which they were destroyed. It was also said: the meaning of istiqāma is leaving off haste, adhering to tranquility, contentment, and submission to what Allah, glorified is He, decrees.

His words: ﴿And do not follow the path of those who do not know.﴾ It is read with a doubled nūn for emphasis (nūn al-ta'kīd), and it is vocalized with a kasra because that is the original form, and because it resembles the nūn of the dual.

Ibn Dhakwan read it with a single nūn, as a negation and not as a prohibition.

It was also read with the second tā' of tattabi'ānn lightened.

The meaning: a prohibition to them from adopting the way of one who does not know Allah's custom, glorified is He, in the conduct of affairs according to what the interests require, in hastening and deferring.

His words: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea.﴾ It is from jāwaza al-makān (he crossed the place), when one leaves it behind and passes beyond it. The bā' is for transitivity, that is: We made them cross the sea until they reached the shore, because Allah, glorified is He, made the sea dry, and they passed through it until they came out onto the land.

This has already been explained in Surat al-Baqara in His words: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 50].

Al-Hasan read wa-jawwaznā, and both are dialects. ﴿So Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them.﴾ It is said: tabiʿa and atbaʿa have the same meaning, when one catches up with someone.

Al-Asma'i said: it is said atba'ahu, with a cut alif, when one catches up with and overtakes him, and ittaba'ahu, with a connected alif, when one follows his trail, whether he overtakes him or not.

Abu Zayd said likewise. Abu 'Amr said: ittaba'ahu with a connected alif means he imitated him.

The accusative of baghyan and ʿadwan is adverbial (ḥāl). Al-baghy is injustice, and al-ʿadw is aggression. It is also permissible that their accusative is for causation, that is: for the sake of transgression and enmity.

Al-Hasan read ʿudūwan with a ḍamma on the ʿayn and the dāl and a doubled wāw, like ʿalā yaʿlū ʿulūwan. It was also said that al-baghy is seeking to exalt oneself in speech without right, and al-ʿadw is in deed.

﴿Until, when the drowning overtook him﴾, that is, reached him, arrived at him, and seized him.

This is because Musa went out with the Children of Israel at a moment of heedlessness on Pharaoh's part. When Pharaoh heard of this, he pursued them with his hosts. Allah split the sea for Musa and the Children of Israel, and they walked through it until they came out on the other side. Pharaoh followed them while the sea remained in the state it had been in when Musa and those with him passed through. When Pharaoh's hosts had fully entered and were about to come out on the other side, it closed over them and they drowned, as Allah, glorified is He, related.

﴿He said: I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe.⁠﴾ That is: I affirm that— with the hamza fatḥa on the premise that the original is bi-annahu, and the bā' was dropped, and the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n).

It was also read with a kasra on inna, as a fresh resumption (isti'nāf). Abu Hatim claimed that there is an elided verb of speech: "I believe," so I said: "Indeed He..." This faith did not benefit him because it occurred after the drowning had fully overtaken him, as was discussed earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. The accursed one did not say "I believe in Allah" or "in the Lord of the worlds," but said: "I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe," because a vestige of the claim to divinity remained in him.

His words: ﴿And I am of the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to Allah's command, who are obedient to Him, who affirm His oneness and negate whatever is other than Him. This clause is either in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or conjoined to āmantu (I believe).

His words: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters?⁠﴾ It is the speech of an implied verb of speech conjoined to "he said: I believe," that is: it was said to him, "Do you believe now?"

It has been disputed who said this statement to Pharaoh. It was said: it is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He. It was said: it is from the speech of Jibril. It was said: it is from the speech of Mika'il. It was said: it is from the speech of Pharaoh himself, who said it within himself to himself.

The clause ﴿And you had disobeyed before﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of the implied verb following the implied speech, which is "Do you believe now?" The meaning is a denial of faith from him at the moment when drowning seized him, while he had disobeyed Allah before. The purpose is reproach and rebuke.

The clause ﴿And you were among the corrupters⁠﴾ is conjoined to "you had disobeyed" and included in the circumstantial sense: that is, you were among the corrupters in the land by your straying from the truth and your leading others astray.

His words: ﴿So today We will save you with your body⁠﴾. It is read nunajjīka with lightening (nunjīka), but the majority read it with doubling.

Al-Yazidi read nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed ḥā' from al-tanḥiya (removal), and 'Alqama narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud. The meaning of nunajjīka with the jīm: We cast you upon a height of the earth. That is because the Children of Israel did not believe that Pharaoh had drowned, and they said: he is greater in importance than that. So Allah cast him upon a height of the earth, that is, an elevated place on the earth, until they saw him. It was also said the meaning is: We bring you out of what your people have fallen into, sinking to the bottom of the sea, and We make you float so that they may see you dead by drowning. The meaning of nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed letter is: We throw you onto one side of the earth.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read bi-abdānika (with your bodies).

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of bi-badanika. It was said: its meaning is with your body after the soul has been removed from it. It was said: its meaning is with your coat of mail, since a coat of mail is called a badan. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You see the abdān (coats of mail) on them, fully covering, on the heroes, and the sturdy helmet."

He meant by abdān the coats of mail. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

That is, with full-length coats of mail and short coats of mail, which are called abdān, as Abu 'Ubayda said.

Al-Akhfash said: as for the saying of one who says "with your coat of mail," it is nothing, and he preferred that the badan meant here is the body.

His words: ﴿So that you may be a sign for those after you⁠﴾. This is the reason for casting him out with his body. It indicates that he did not expose his body apart from his people except for this reason and no other. The sign (āya) here means the mark: so that for those among mankind who come after you, it is a mark by which they recognize your destruction, and that you are not as you claimed, and the doubt is removed from them about whether you have become dead by drowning. It was also said: the meaning is that your being cast onto the shore alone, apart from your drowned people, is a sign from the signs of Allah by which people may take a lesson, or by which those nations that will come later may take a lesson when they hear of it, so that they beware of arrogance, tyranny, and rebellion against Allah, glorified is He. This clause is a concluding remark (tadhyīl).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth⁠﴾, that he said: destroy their wealth and annihilate it. ﴿And harden their hearts⁠﴾: he said: seal them. ﴿So they will not believe until they see the painful punishment⁠﴾, which is drowning. (p. 640)

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked me about His words, ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾. I informed him that God had obliterated the wealth of Pharaoh and the family of Pharaoh until it turned into stones. Umar said: "Stay as you are until I come to you." He then called for a sealed bag and opened it, and inside was silver cut into pieces, like stones, and dinars and dirhams and similar kinds of wealth, all of them stones.

It has also been related that their wealth turned into stones, through a group of the early generations (al-salaf, the righteous predecessors).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Your supplication has been answered." He said: So He answered him, and He placed a barrier between Pharaoh and faith.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Whenever Musa supplicated, Harun would say "Amin" to his supplication. Abu Hurayrah said: "Amin" is one of the names of God. This is His words, ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They claim that Pharaoh remained for forty years after this supplication.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj something similar.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿So go straight and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾, that "go straight" means "proceed according to My command," and this is the istiqamah (steadfastness).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "al-adw" (transgression), "al-utuww" (arrogance) and "al-uluww" (haughtiness) in the Book of God all mean tajabbur (tyranny).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the last of Musa's companions had left, and the last of Pharaoh's companions had entered, God revealed to the sea: 'Close over them.' Then the finger of Pharaoh emerged, saying: 'There is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believed.' Jibril said: 'I knew that the Lord is merciful, and I feared that mercy would reach him, so I covered him with my wing and said: Now, after you disobeyed before?' When Musa and his companions had come out, those among the people of Pharaoh who had stayed behind said: 'Pharaoh and his companions did not drown, but they are in the islands of the sea hunting.' So God revealed to the sea: 'Cast out Pharaoh naked.' It cast him out naked, bald, short and reddish-yellow (akhyanis), and this is His words: ﴿Today We will save you in your body, so that you may be a sign to those who come after you﴾, against the one who said that Pharaoh had not drowned. It was as if the salvation of others had not been a salvation of wellbeing. Then God revealed to the sea: 'Cast out what is in you,' and it cast them out onto the shore. The sea would not cast out a drowned person from its belly until the fish had eaten him, and the sea will never accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God drowned Pharaoh, and he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾. Jibril said to me: 'O Muhammad, if you had seen me as I took mud from the bottom of the sea and pushed it into his mouth, for fear that mercy would reach him.'"

Al-Tirmidhi narrated this hadith through more than one chain and said: "hasan sahih gharib" (good, sound, strange). Al-Hakim also declared it sahih.

It was also related from Ibn Abbas as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report through other routes.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Jibril said to me: 'There was nothing on earth more hateful to me than Pharaoh. When he believed, I began to stuff his mouth with black mud, while I was covering him, for fear that mercy would reach him.'"

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Ibn Umar as a marfu' report as well.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar from Abu Umamah as a marfu' report as well. In the isnad of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah there is an unknown man (majhul), while the rest of its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat).

So, O poor one, what have you to do with this matter, of which you have no part at all? Would you not conceal yourself and keep to your place, and recognize that in this science you are among the most ignorant of the ignorant? Occupy yourself with what is your knowledge, beyond which you cannot go, and what is your entire portion, which is nothing other than it: the science of the Arabic language and its auxiliary instrumental sciences (al-ulum al-alatiyyah, the tools-sciences serving the Qur'an and hadith). The author of al-Kashshaf, may God have mercy on him, became, because of what he touches upon in his tafsir from the science of hadith, which is not part of his field, neither in his path nor in his breast, a mockery for the mockers and a lesson for those who take heed. Sometimes he narrates in his book fabricated reports (mawdu'at) while he does not know that they are fabricated, and sometimes he attempts to reject what is authentic, asserting with certainty that it is a lie upon the Messenger of God and a slander against him, while it may be found in the Two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and other collections, and in what is attached to them, through the narration of a group of the Companions, with chains whose narrators are all imams, trustworthy, firmly established and authoritative proofs. The least portion of intellect would restrain its possessor from speaking on a science he does not know and of which he has even the slightest understanding, even if that science is one of the technical sciences (ulum al-istilah) upon which a group of people agree and establish conventions among themselves. So what then of the science of the Sunnah, which is the counterpart of the Book of God, whose speaker is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and whose transmitter from him is the best of generations, then those who follow them, then those who follow them, and every letter of it and every word of it establishes a general law for all the people of Islam.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: God saved Pharaoh for the Children of Israel from the sea, so they looked at him after he had drowned.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "In your body." Some of the Children of Israel denied the death of Pharaoh, so he was cast onto the shore of the sea until the Children of Israel saw him, reddish and short, as if he were a bull.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: "In your armour." His armour was made of pearl, in which he used to meet wars.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 10, verses 88–92 (part 1 of 2):

When Musa (peace be upon him) exceeded in displaying the miracles and establishing the clear proofs, and this had no effect on those to whom he was sent, he invoked (a curse) against them after explaining the cause of their persistence in disbelief and their clinging to denial and obstinacy. So he said, first explaining the cause: ﴿Our Lord, You have indeed given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world.﴾ It has already been mentioned that al-mala' (the chiefs) are the nobles. Zina (adornment) is the name for everything one adorns oneself with: clothing, mounts, jewelry, furnishings, weapons and other things. Then he repeated the address for emphasis, saying: ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way.﴾

Scholars differ regarding this lam (the particle "that") entering the verb. Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh said that it is lam al-'aqiba wa al-sayrura (the lam of consequence and outcome). The meaning is that, since the outcome of their affair was misguidance, it was as if Allah, glorified is He, gave them what He gave them of blessings so that they would go astray. On this view the lam is connected to ātayta (You have given). It was also said that it is lam kay (the lam of purpose), meaning: You gave them so that they would go astray.

Others said the meaning is: You gave them that so they would not go astray, and the particle "not" (lā) was dropped, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176].

Al-Nahhas said: the apparent sense of this answer is good, except that the Arabs do not drop lā except together with an (anna). The proponent of this interpretation obscured the matter by citing His words ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176]. It was also said that the lam is for supplication against them. The meaning is: test them with destruction away from Your way. The one who holds this view cites His words after this: ﴿Obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts﴾.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) went to great lengths in establishing this view with what is of no benefit. The first view is the preferable one.

The Kufans read liyudillū with a ḍamma on the initial letter of the imperfect verb, meaning that they cause others to be led astray. The rest read it with a fatḥa, meaning that they themselves go astray.

﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth.﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: ṭams (obliteration) of a thing is removing it from its form. The meaning is a supplication against them that Allah erase their wealth and destroy it. It was also read with a ḍamma on the mīm of iṭmus ( it is recited as iṭmus).

﴿And harden their hearts﴾, that is, make them hard and sealed, not accepting the truth and not opening up to faith.

His words: ﴿So they will not believe.﴾

Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to liyudillū, and the meaning is: You gave them blessings so that they would go astray and not believe. The material between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ).

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda said: it is a supplication in the form of a prohibition, and the implied sense is: O Allah, let them not believe. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"So let there not expand between your two eyes what has withdrawn, and do not meet me except with your nose humbled."

Al-Akhfash said: it is the answer to the imperative, that is: obliterate and harden, so that they will not believe; and so it is in the accusative. This is also narrated from al-Farra'. From this is the saying:

"O she-camel, march with a wide, long stride, to Sulayman, so that we may rest."

﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾, that is, faith will not come from them except when they witness what Allah will punish them with, and at that time their faith will not benefit them.

Some scholars have raised a difficulty concerning this verse's supplication against these people, saying: the Messengers only seek the guidance and faith of their peoples. It was answered: it is not permissible for a prophet to invoke against his people except by Allah's permission, glorified is He. Allah only grants this permission because He knows that none among them will believe. This is why, when Allah informed Nuh (peace be upon him) that none of his people would believe except those who had already believed, he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers as a dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26].

﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered, so go straight.﴾ Here He attributes the supplication to Musa and Harun, whereas earlier He attributed it to Musa alone. It was said: Harun used to say "Amin" to Musa's supplication, so he is here called a supplicant. Even if the one supplicating was Musa alone, at the beginning of the speech He attributed the supplication to Musa because he was the one who supplicated, while here He attributed it to both of them, treating the one who says "Amin" as the one who supplicates. It is also permissible that both of them were supplicants, but He attributed the supplication to Musa at the beginning of the speech because of his primacy in the message.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: the proof that the supplication was for both of them is Musa's saying "our Lord" (rabbanā) and not "my Lord" (rabbi).

'Ali and al-Sulami read du'ā'ukumā (your supplication), and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read da'wākumā (your supplication). Istiqāma (going straight) is steadfastness in what they were upon of calling to Allah.

Al-Farra' and others said: they were commanded to go straight in their affair and to persist in it, in calling Pharaoh and his people to faith, until the fulfilment (ta'wīl) of the answer comes to them, forty years later, after which they were destroyed. It was also said: the meaning of istiqāma is leaving off haste, adhering to tranquility, contentment, and submission to what Allah, glorified is He, decrees.

His words: ﴿And do not follow the path of those who do not know.﴾ It is read with a doubled nūn for emphasis (nūn al-ta'kīd), and it is vocalized with a kasra because that is the original form, and because it resembles the nūn of the dual.

Ibn Dhakwan read it with a single nūn, as a negation and not as a prohibition.

It was also read with the second tā' of tattabi'ānn lightened.

The meaning: a prohibition to them from adopting the way of one who does not know Allah's custom, glorified is He, in the conduct of affairs according to what the interests require, in hastening and deferring.

His words: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea.﴾ It is from jāwaza al-makān (he crossed the place), when one leaves it behind and passes beyond it. The bā' is for transitivity, that is: We made them cross the sea until they reached the shore, because Allah, glorified is He, made the sea dry, and they passed through it until they came out onto the land.

This has already been explained in Surat al-Baqara in His words: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 50].

Al-Hasan read wa-jawwaznā, and both are dialects. ﴿So Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them.﴾ It is said: tabiʿa and atbaʿa have the same meaning, when one catches up with someone.

Al-Asma'i said: it is said atba'ahu, with a cut alif, when one catches up with and overtakes him, and ittaba'ahu, with a connected alif, when one follows his trail, whether he overtakes him or not.

Abu Zayd said likewise. Abu 'Amr said: ittaba'ahu with a connected alif means he imitated him.

The accusative of baghyan and ʿadwan is adverbial (ḥāl). Al-baghy is injustice, and al-ʿadw is aggression. It is also permissible that their accusative is for causation, that is: for the sake of transgression and enmity.

Al-Hasan read ʿudūwan with a ḍamma on the ʿayn and the dāl and a doubled wāw, like ʿalā yaʿlū ʿulūwan. It was also said that al-baghy is seeking to exalt oneself in speech without right, and al-ʿadw is in deed.

﴿Until, when the drowning overtook him﴾, that is, reached him, arrived at him, and seized him.

This is because Musa went out with the Children of Israel at a moment of heedlessness on Pharaoh's part. When Pharaoh heard of this, he pursued them with his hosts. Allah split the sea for Musa and the Children of Israel, and they walked through it until they came out on the other side. Pharaoh followed them while the sea remained in the state it had been in when Musa and those with him passed through. When Pharaoh's hosts had fully entered and were about to come out on the other side, it closed over them and they drowned, as Allah, glorified is He, related.

﴿He said: I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe.⁠﴾ That is: I affirm that— with the hamza fatḥa on the premise that the original is bi-annahu, and the bā' was dropped, and the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n).

It was also read with a kasra on inna, as a fresh resumption (isti'nāf). Abu Hatim claimed that there is an elided verb of speech: "I believe," so I said: "Indeed He..." This faith did not benefit him because it occurred after the drowning had fully overtaken him, as was discussed earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. The accursed one did not say "I believe in Allah" or "in the Lord of the worlds," but said: "I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe," because a vestige of the claim to divinity remained in him.

His words: ﴿And I am of the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to Allah's command, who are obedient to Him, who affirm His oneness and negate whatever is other than Him. This clause is either in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or conjoined to āmantu (I believe).

His words: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters?⁠﴾ It is the speech of an implied verb of speech conjoined to "he said: I believe," that is: it was said to him, "Do you believe now?"

It has been disputed who said this statement to Pharaoh. It was said: it is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He. It was said: it is from the speech of Jibril. It was said: it is from the speech of Mika'il. It was said: it is from the speech of Pharaoh himself, who said it within himself to himself.

The clause ﴿And you had disobeyed before﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of the implied verb following the implied speech, which is "Do you believe now?" The meaning is a denial of faith from him at the moment when drowning seized him, while he had disobeyed Allah before. The purpose is reproach and rebuke.

The clause ﴿And you were among the corrupters⁠﴾ is conjoined to "you had disobeyed" and included in the circumstantial sense: that is, you were among the corrupters in the land by your straying from the truth and your leading others astray.

His words: ﴿So today We will save you with your body⁠﴾. It is read nunajjīka with lightening (nunjīka), but the majority read it with doubling.

Al-Yazidi read nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed ḥā' from al-tanḥiya (removal), and 'Alqama narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud. The meaning of nunajjīka with the jīm: We cast you upon a height of the earth. That is because the Children of Israel did not believe that Pharaoh had drowned, and they said: he is greater in importance than that. So Allah cast him upon a height of the earth, that is, an elevated place on the earth, until they saw him. It was also said the meaning is: We bring you out of what your people have fallen into, sinking to the bottom of the sea, and We make you float so that they may see you dead by drowning. The meaning of nunaḥḥīka with the unpointed letter is: We throw you onto one side of the earth.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read bi-abdānika (with your bodies).

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of bi-badanika. It was said: its meaning is with your body after the soul has been removed from it. It was said: its meaning is with your coat of mail, since a coat of mail is called a badan. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You see the abdān (coats of mail) on them, fully covering, on the heroes, and the sturdy helmet."

He meant by abdān the coats of mail. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"Their women went forth with every full-length, tight-fitting coat of mail, and with abdān."

That is, with full-length coats of mail and short coats of mail, which are called abdān, as Abu 'Ubayda said.

Al-Akhfash said: as for the saying of one who says "with your coat of mail," it is nothing, and he preferred that the badan meant here is the body.

His words: ﴿So that you may be a sign for those after you⁠﴾. This is the reason for casting him out with his body. It indicates that he did not expose his body apart from his people except for this reason and no other. The sign (āya) here means the mark: so that for those among mankind who come after you, it is a mark by which they recognize your destruction, and that you are not as you claimed, and the doubt is removed from them about whether you have become dead by drowning. It was also said: the meaning is that your being cast onto the shore alone, apart from your drowned people, is a sign from the signs of Allah by which people may take a lesson, or by which those nations that will come later may take a lesson when they hear of it, so that they beware of arrogance, tyranny, and rebellion against Allah, glorified is He. For this one who reached what he reached of the claim to divinity and persisted in it for a long time had this shameful end.

It was read liman khalafaka (for those who succeeded you) in the past tense form, that is: for those who come after you of the generations, or those who succeeded you in leadership, or in dwelling in the residence you used to inhabit. ﴿And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs⁠﴾, which require reflection and contemplation and awaken one from the slumber of heedlessness. This clause is a concluding remark (tadhyīl).

The least portion of intellect would restrain its possessor from speaking on a science he does not know and of which he has even the slightest understanding, even if that science is one of the technical sciences (ulum al-istilah) upon which a group of people agree and establish conventions among themselves. So what then of the science of the Sunnah, which is the counterpart of the Book of God, whose speaker is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and whose transmitter from him is the best of generations, then those who follow them, then those who follow them, and every letter of it and every word of it establishes a general law for all the people of Islam.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: God saved Pharaoh for the Children of Israel from the sea, so they looked at him after he had drowned.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "In your body." Some of the Children of Israel denied the death of Pharaoh, so he was cast onto the shore of the sea until the Children of Israel saw him, reddish and short, as if he were a bull.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding His words, ﴿Today We will save you in your body﴾, that he said: "In your armour." His armour was made of pearl, in which he used to meet wars.

(p. 642) His saying: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling-place﴾ This is part of the blessings that Allah, glorified is He, enumerated among the favours He bestowed upon the Children of Israel. The meaning of *bawwa'na* is "We settled," as in the saying, "I *bawwa'tu* Zayd a dwelling": I settled him in it. *Al-mubawwa'* is either a noun of place or a verbal noun. Its attribution to *al-sidq* (truthfulness) follows the usage of the Arabs, for when they praised something they attributed it to *al-sidq*. What is meant here is the praiseworthy and chosen dwelling. It is said to be the land of Egypt; it is said to be the Jordan and Palestine; it is said to be Syria. ﴿And We provided them with good things﴾, that is, the most delightful of provisions. ﴿Yet they did not differ﴾ concerning the matter of their religion, and they did not split into sects regarding it, after having been upon one way without disagreement, ﴿until knowledge came to them﴾. That is, disagreement in religion did not occur among them except after knowledge had come to them, through their reading of the Torah and their knowledge of its rulings, and of what it contained of reports about the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also said that the meaning is: they did not differ until knowledge came to them, which is the Qur'an revealed to our Prophet (ﷺ), and so they differed concerning its description and attributes; some of them believed in it, and some of them disbelieved in it.

According to the first view, the ones who differed are the Jews after the Torah was revealed to them and they had knowledge of it. According to the second view, they are the Jews contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, so He will reward the doer of good for his good, and the doer of evil for his evil, and the one upon truth for his deed in accordance with truth, and the one upon falsehood for his deed in accordance with falsehood.

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. *Al-shakk* (doubt) in its original linguistic sense is the joining of one thing to another, and from it comes *shakk al-jawhar fi al-'iqd* (the threading of a jewel onto a necklace). The doubter, as it were, joins to what he imagines something else opposite to it, so he wavers and is bewildered. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the intended meaning is others, as occurs in the Qur'an in more than one place.

Abu 'Umar Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahid al-Zahid said: I heard the two imams Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad say: the meaning of ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ is: say, O Muhammad, to the disbeliever, "If you are in doubt, then ask those who read the Book before you," meaning the Muslims among the People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those like him. The idol-worshippers used to acknowledge the Jews' knowledge and admit that they were more knowledgeable than them. So Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet to guide the doubters concerning what Allah had sent down to him of the Qur'an: that they should ask the People of the Book who had embraced Islam, for they would inform them that it is the Book of Allah in truth, that this is His Messenger, and that the Torah bears witness to that and speaks of it. In this interpretation, despite its goodness, there is a departure from the apparent meaning.

Al-Qutaybi said: what is meant by this verse is one of the disbelievers who was not decisive in denying the Prophet (ﷺ) nor in affirming him, but was in doubt.

It is also said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) himself and no one else. The meaning: "If you were of those who are subject to doubt about what We have informed you, and you asked the People of the Book, they would remove the doubt from you."

It is also said that doubt here means constriction of the breast, that is: if your breast is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who read the Book before you, and they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you against the harm of their peoples.

It is also said that the meaning of the verse is supposition and hypothetical assumption, as if He said to him: "If doubt happens to you, for example, and Satan conjures up to you an imagining of it, hypothetically, then ask those who read the Book, for they will inform you about your prophethood and what was sent down to you, and they will acknowledge that, because they find it written in their possession, and what had necessitated their concealing what was with them has ceased among those of them who embraced Islam."

His saying: ﴿Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾. In this is a clarification of what uproots doubt from its root and removes it entirely: it is the testimony of Allah, glorified is He, that this which doubt has befallen—despite the differences of interpretation concerning the doubter—is the truth which no falsehood mixes with and no ambiguity taints. Then He followed it with a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) against disputing about what Allah had sent down to him, rather he should persist in what he is upon of certainty and the absence of doubt.

It is possible that this prohibition addressed to him is an indirect address to others, as in various passages of the Noble Book. The same applies to His prohibiting the Prophet (ﷺ) from denying the signs of Allah, for the apparent meaning in it is indirect address, especially after it was followed by His saying: ﴿Otherwise you would be among the losers﴾. In this indirect address there is a rebuke to the doubters and deniers that is more eloquent and more effective than prohibiting them directly, for if one is prohibited from something of which the one addressed cannot conceivably be guilty, then how much more so is one who is capable of it.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾. A similar expression occurred earlier in this surah. The meaning is that it is decreed upon them by Allah's decree and predestination that they will persist in disbelief and die upon it; faith will never come from them in any state. And if something occurs from them whose form resembles faith, such as one who believes at the witnessing of the punishment, then it is in the ruling of non-existence.

﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ of the created (*takwiniyya*) and revealed (*tanzîliyya*) signs, that would not benefit them, because Allah, glorified is He, has sealed their hearts and the word has been justified against them, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, whereupon there occurs from them what resembles faith but is not faith, and nothing of its rulings follows from it.

His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it?﴾ *Lawla* here is the exhortative *lawla*, meaning *hallā* (why not), as al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i and others said. This is indicated by what is in the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud: "*fa-halla qaryatun*" (so why was there not a town). The meaning: "So why was there not one town out of these towns We destroyed that believed with a faith that is valid, meaning sincerely for Allah before witnessing His punishment, and did not delay it as Pharaoh delayed it?" The exception in His saying ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ is disjunctive (*munqati'*), and it is an exception from "towns," because what is meant is their inhabitants. The meaning: "But the people of Yunus, when they believed with a valid faith before witnessing the punishment, or at the first witnessing before it descended upon them, ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾." A group of imams, among them al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra', held that this exception is disjunctive. It was also said that it may be connected (*muttasil*), the sentence being in the sense of negation, as if it were said: "No town of the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus." Its case-ending is accusative on the basic principle of exception, and it was read in the nominative as a substitute (*badal*).

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the justification of the nominative: the meaning is "other than the people of Yunus," but *illa* was given the sense of it, and it was impossible to make the case-ending depend on it, so the noun following it was inflected like its equivalent.

Ibn Jarir said: the people of Yunus were singled out among the nations in that repentance was accepted from them (p. 643) after witnessing the punishment, and this is reported from a group of exegetes.

Al-Zajjaj said: the punishment did not actually befall them; rather they saw the sign that indicates the punishment. Had they seen the very punishment, faith would not have benefited them. This view is better than the view of Ibn Jarir.

The "punishment of disgrace" that Allah removed from them is the punishment that Yunus had promised them would descend upon them, and they did not see it, or it is that whose signs they had seen without seeing it directly.

﴿And We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾, that is, after the punishment was removed from them, Allah granted them enjoyment in this world for a known term that He had decreed for them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that faith and its opposite are both by the will and decree of Allah. So He said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on the earth would all have believed﴾ — all of them together, such that not one of them would be left out, all united upon faith, not scattering in it and differing. But He did not will that, because it would contradict the wisdom that Allah, glorified is He, intended. The accusative of *jami'an* is circumstantial (*hal*), as Sibawayh said.

Al-Akhfash said: He brought *jami'an* after *kulluhum* for emphasis, like His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods﴾ (al-Nahl: 51). Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of all people, Allah informed him that this would not happen, because His will, which operates according to perfect wisdom and preponderant interests, does not necessitate that. So He said: ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ — for that is not within your power, O Muhammad, nor within your capacity. In this there is consolation to him (ﷺ) and removal of what constricts his breast from seeking the welfare of all, which, were it to occur, would not be a realized welfare but would be closer to corruption. To Allah belongs perfect wisdom.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what preceded with His saying: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is: it is not valid or proper for any soul among souls to believe in Allah except by His permission, meaning by His facilitation, His making it easy, and His will for that. Thus nothing occurs other than what He wills, whatever it may be. ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾, that is, the punishment, or disbelief, or the abandonment (*khidhlan*) which is the cause of punishment.

Al-Hasan, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read *wa-najʿalu* with *nūn*.

For *al-rijs* there are two dialects: with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and with a *kasra*. Those who do not reason are the disbelievers who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not reflect upon His signs, and do not ponder the evidences He has set up for them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Qatada, concerning His saying: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling-place﴾, that he said: Allah settled them in Syria and Bayt al-Maqdis.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "Good dwelling-places" means Egypt and Syria.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying: ﴿Yet they did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾, that he said: "Knowledge" is the Book of Allah which He revealed, and His command which He commanded them with.

It has been related in a hadith that "the Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians split into seventy-two sects, and this Ummah will split into seventy-three sects," and it is in the Sunan and the Musnads, and discussion of it is lengthy.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not doubt, and did not ask.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I do not doubt and I do not ask." This is a *mursal* report.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Ask those who read the Book before you﴾, he said: the Torah and the Gospel. "Those who read the Book before you" are the People of the Book who met Muhammad and believed in him. The meaning: ask them, if you are in doubt, that you are written about among them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾, that he said: the wrath of Allah was justified against them for what they disobeyed Him in.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik concerning His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed﴾, that he said: meaning, "there was no town that believed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada concerning the verse, that he said: This did not occur among the nations before the people of Yunus. No town that disbelieved and then believed at the moment of witnessing the punishment benefited, except the people of Yunus; so Allah made an exception for the people of Yunus.

He said: It has been related to us that the people of Yunus (Jonah) lived at Nineveh, in the land of al-Mawsil (Mosul). When they lost their prophet, Allah cast repentance into their hearts. They wore coarse woolen garments (al-masuh), drove out their livestock, and separated every beast from its young. Then they cried out to Allah for forty mornings. When Allah knew the sincerity in their hearts, their repentance, and their regret for what had passed, He removed the punishment from them after it had hung over them. There was no more than a mile between them and the punishment.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yunus called his people, but when they refused to respond to him, he threatened them with punishment and said: 'It will come upon you on such and such a day.' Then he left them. The prophets, when they threatened their people with punishment, would leave. When the punishment overshadowed them, they went out, separated the mother from her child and the young goat from its young, and went out crying to Allah. Allah knew their sincerity, so He accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. Yunus sat on the road asking for news. A man passed by him and asked: 'What did the people of Yunus do?' He told him what they had done. Yunus said: 'I will not return to a people who have called me a liar,' and he set off in anger (mughadiban), meaning defiant (muraghiman)."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The punishment enveloped the people of Yunus as a grave is covered by a garment when its occupant enters it, and the sky rained blood.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that the punishment had descended upon the people of Yunus, with no more than two-thirds of a mile between them and it. When they called upon Allah, He removed it from them.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Jald, who said: When the punishment enveloped the people of Yunus, they went to an elder from among the remaining scholars of their people and said to him: "What do you advise?" He said: "Say: 'O Ever-Living when there is no living one, O Ever-Living who gives life to the dead, O Ever-Living, there is no god but You.'" They said it, and the punishment was removed from them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and He places the defilement﴾ that it means wrath (al-sukhṭ).

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, who said: "Ar-rijs" is the devil, and "ar-rijs" is also the punishment.
