Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not doubt, and did not ask.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I do not doubt and I do not ask." This is a *mursal* report.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Ask those who read the Book before you﴾, he said: the Torah and the Gospel. "Those who read the Book before you" are the People of the Book who met Muhammad and believed in him. The meaning: ask them, if you are in doubt, that you are written about among them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾, that he said: the wrath of Allah was justified against them for what they disobeyed Him in.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik concerning His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed﴾, that he said: meaning, "there was no town that believed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada concerning the verse, that he said: This did not occur among the nations before the people of Yunus. No town that disbelieved and then believed at the moment of witnessing the punishment benefited, except the people of Yunus; so Allah made an exception for the people of Yunus.

He said: It has been related to us that the people of Yunus (Jonah) lived at Nineveh, in the land of al-Mawsil (Mosul). When they lost their prophet, Allah cast repentance into their hearts. They wore coarse woolen garments (al-masuh), drove out their livestock, and separated every beast from its young. Then they cried out to Allah for forty mornings. When Allah knew the sincerity in their hearts, their repentance, and their regret for what had passed, He removed the punishment from them after it had hung over them. There was no more than a mile between them and the punishment.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yunus called his people, but when they refused to respond to him, he threatened them with punishment and said: 'It will come upon you on such and such a day.' Then he left them. The prophets, when they threatened their people with punishment, would leave. When the punishment overshadowed them, they went out, separated the mother from her child and the young goat from its young, and went out crying to Allah. Allah knew their sincerity, so He accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. Yunus sat on the road asking for news. A man passed by him and asked: 'What did the people of Yunus do?' He told him what they had done. Yunus said: 'I will not return to a people who have called me a liar,' and he set off in anger (mughadiban), meaning defiant (muraghiman)."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The punishment enveloped the people of Yunus as a grave is covered by a garment when its occupant enters it, and the sky rained blood.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that the punishment had descended upon the people of Yunus, with no more than two-thirds of a mile between them and it. When they called upon Allah, He removed it from them.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Jald, who said: When the punishment enveloped the people of Yunus, they went to an elder from among the remaining scholars of their people and said to him: "What do you advise?" He said: "Say: 'O Ever-Living when there is no living one, O Ever-Living who gives life to the dead, O Ever-Living, there is no god but You.'" They said it, and the punishment was removed from them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and He places the defilement﴾ that it means wrath (al-sukhṭ).

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, who said: "Ar-rijs" is the devil, and "ar-rijs" is also the punishment.

(p. 642) His saying: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling-place﴾ This is part of the blessings that Allah, glorified is He, enumerated among the favours He bestowed upon the Children of Israel. The meaning of *bawwa'na* is "We settled," as in the saying, "I *bawwa'tu* Zayd a dwelling": I settled him in it. *Al-mubawwa'* is either a noun of place or a verbal noun. Its attribution to *al-sidq* (truthfulness) follows the usage of the Arabs, for when they praised something they attributed it to *al-sidq*. What is meant here is the praiseworthy and chosen dwelling. It is said to be the land of Egypt; it is said to be the Jordan and Palestine; it is said to be Syria. ﴿And We provided them with good things﴾, that is, the most delightful of provisions. ﴿Yet they did not differ﴾ concerning the matter of their religion, and they did not split into sects regarding it, after having been upon one way without disagreement, ﴿until knowledge came to them﴾. That is, disagreement in religion did not occur among them except after knowledge had come to them, through their reading of the Torah and their knowledge of its rulings, and of what it contained of reports about the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also said that the meaning is: they did not differ until knowledge came to them, which is the Qur'an revealed to our Prophet (ﷺ), and so they differed concerning its description and attributes; some of them believed in it, and some of them disbelieved in it.

According to the first view, the ones who differed are the Jews after the Torah was revealed to them and they had knowledge of it. According to the second view, they are the Jews contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, so He will reward the doer of good for his good, and the doer of evil for his evil, and the one upon truth for his deed in accordance with truth, and the one upon falsehood for his deed in accordance with falsehood.

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. *Al-shakk* (doubt) in its original linguistic sense is the joining of one thing to another, and from it comes *shakk al-jawhar fi al-'iqd* (the threading of a jewel onto a necklace). The doubter, as it were, joins to what he imagines something else opposite to it, so he wavers and is bewildered. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the intended meaning is others, as occurs in the Qur'an in more than one place.

Abu 'Umar Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahid al-Zahid said: I heard the two imams Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad say: the meaning of ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ is: say, O Muhammad, to the disbeliever, "If you are in doubt, then ask those who read the Book before you," meaning the Muslims among the People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those like him. The idol-worshippers used to acknowledge the Jews' knowledge and admit that they were more knowledgeable than them. So Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet to guide the doubters concerning what Allah had sent down to him of the Qur'an: that they should ask the People of the Book who had embraced Islam, for they would inform them that it is the Book of Allah in truth, that this is His Messenger, and that the Torah bears witness to that and speaks of it. In this interpretation, despite its goodness, there is a departure from the apparent meaning.

Al-Qutaybi said: what is meant by this verse is one of the disbelievers who was not decisive in denying the Prophet (ﷺ) nor in affirming him, but was in doubt.

It is also said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) himself and no one else. The meaning: "If you were of those who are subject to doubt about what We have informed you, and you asked the People of the Book, they would remove the doubt from you."

It is also said that doubt here means constriction of the breast, that is: if your breast is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who read the Book before you, and they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you against the harm of their peoples.

It is also said that the meaning of the verse is supposition and hypothetical assumption, as if He said to him: "If doubt happens to you, for example, and Satan conjures up to you an imagining of it, hypothetically, then ask those who read the Book, for they will inform you about your prophethood and what was sent down to you, and they will acknowledge that, because they find it written in their possession, and what had necessitated their concealing what was with them has ceased among those of them who embraced Islam."

His saying: ﴿Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾. In this is a clarification of what uproots doubt from its root and removes it entirely: it is the testimony of Allah, glorified is He, that this which doubt has befallen—despite the differences of interpretation concerning the doubter—is the truth which no falsehood mixes with and no ambiguity taints. Then He followed it with a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) against disputing about what Allah had sent down to him, rather he should persist in what he is upon of certainty and the absence of doubt.

It is possible that this prohibition addressed to him is an indirect address to others, as in various passages of the Noble Book. The same applies to His prohibiting the Prophet (ﷺ) from denying the signs of Allah, for the apparent meaning in it is indirect address, especially after it was followed by His saying: ﴿Otherwise you would be among the losers﴾. In this indirect address there is a rebuke to the doubters and deniers that is more eloquent and more effective than prohibiting them directly, for if one is prohibited from something of which the one addressed cannot conceivably be guilty, then how much more so is one who is capable of it.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾. A similar expression occurred earlier in this surah. The meaning is that it is decreed upon them by Allah's decree and predestination that they will persist in disbelief and die upon it; faith will never come from them in any state. And if something occurs from them whose form resembles faith, such as one who believes at the witnessing of the punishment, then it is in the ruling of non-existence.

﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ of the created (*takwiniyya*) and revealed (*tanzîliyya*) signs, that would not benefit them, because Allah, glorified is He, has sealed their hearts and the word has been justified against them, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, whereupon there occurs from them what resembles faith but is not faith, and nothing of its rulings follows from it.

His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it?﴾ *Lawla* here is the exhortative *lawla*, meaning *hallā* (why not), as al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i and others said. This is indicated by what is in the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud: "*fa-halla qaryatun*" (so why was there not a town). The meaning: "So why was there not one town out of these towns We destroyed that believed with a faith that is valid, meaning sincerely for Allah before witnessing His punishment, and did not delay it as Pharaoh delayed it?" The exception in His saying ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ is disjunctive (*munqati'*), and it is an exception from "towns," because what is meant is their inhabitants. The meaning: "But the people of Yunus, when they believed with a valid faith before witnessing the punishment, or at the first witnessing before it descended upon them, ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾." A group of imams, among them al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra', held that this exception is disjunctive. It was also said that it may be connected (*muttasil*), the sentence being in the sense of negation, as if it were said: "No town of the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus." Its case-ending is accusative on the basic principle of exception, and it was read in the nominative as a substitute (*badal*).

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the justification of the nominative: the meaning is "other than the people of Yunus," but *illa* was given the sense of it, and it was impossible to make the case-ending depend on it, so the noun following it was inflected like its equivalent.

Ibn Jarir said: the people of Yunus were singled out among the nations in that repentance was accepted from them (p. 643) after witnessing the punishment, and this is reported from a group of exegetes.

Al-Zajjaj said: the punishment did not actually befall them; rather they saw the sign that indicates the punishment. Had they seen the very punishment, faith would not have benefited them. This view is better than the view of Ibn Jarir.

The "punishment of disgrace" that Allah removed from them is the punishment that Yunus had promised them would descend upon them, and they did not see it, or it is that whose signs they had seen without seeing it directly.

﴿And We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾, that is, after the punishment was removed from them, Allah granted them enjoyment in this world for a known term that He had decreed for them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that faith and its opposite are both by the will and decree of Allah. So He said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on the earth would all have believed﴾ — all of them together, such that not one of them would be left out, all united upon faith, not scattering in it and differing. But He did not will that, because it would contradict the wisdom that Allah, glorified is He, intended. The accusative of *jami'an* is circumstantial (*hal*), as Sibawayh said.

Al-Akhfash said: He brought *jami'an* after *kulluhum* for emphasis, like His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods﴾ (al-Nahl: 51). Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of all people, Allah informed him that this would not happen, because His will, which operates according to perfect wisdom and preponderant interests, does not necessitate that. So He said: ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ — for that is not within your power, O Muhammad, nor within your capacity. In this there is consolation to him (ﷺ) and removal of what constricts his breast from seeking the welfare of all, which, were it to occur, would not be a realized welfare but would be closer to corruption. To Allah belongs perfect wisdom.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what preceded with His saying: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is: it is not valid or proper for any soul among souls to believe in Allah except by His permission, meaning by His facilitation, His making it easy, and His will for that. Thus nothing occurs other than what He wills, whatever it may be. ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾, that is, the punishment, or disbelief, or the abandonment (*khidhlan*) which is the cause of punishment.

Al-Hasan, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read *wa-najʿalu* with *nūn*.

For *al-rijs* there are two dialects: with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and with a *kasra*. Those who do not reason are the disbelievers who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not reflect upon His signs, and do not ponder the evidences He has set up for them.

So Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet to guide the doubters concerning what Allah had sent down to him of the Qur'an: that they should ask the People of the Book who had embraced Islam, for they would inform them that it is the Book of Allah in truth, that this is His Messenger, and that the Torah bears witness to that and speaks of it. In this interpretation, despite its goodness, there is a departure from the apparent meaning.

Al-Qutaybi said: what is meant by this verse is one of the disbelievers who was not decisive in denying the Prophet (ﷺ) nor in affirming him, but was in doubt.

It is also said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) himself and no one else. The meaning: "If you were of those who are subject to doubt about what We have informed you, and you asked the People of the Book, they would remove the doubt from you."

It is also said that doubt here means constriction of the breast, that is: if your breast is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who read the Book before you, and they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you against the harm of their peoples.

It is also said that the meaning of the verse is supposition and hypothetical assumption, as if He said to him: "If doubt happens to you, for example, and Satan conjures up to you an imagining of it, hypothetically, then ask those who read the Book, for they will inform you about your prophethood and what was sent down to you, and they will acknowledge that, because they find it written in their possession, and what had necessitated their concealing what was with them has ceased among those of them who embraced Islam."

His saying: ﴿Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾. In this is a clarification of what uproots doubt from its root and removes it entirely: it is the testimony of Allah, glorified is He, that this which doubt has befallen—despite the differences of interpretation concerning the doubter—is the truth which no falsehood mixes with and no ambiguity taints. Then He followed it with a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) against disputing about what Allah had sent down to him, rather he should persist in what he is upon of certainty and the absence of doubt.

It is possible that this prohibition addressed to him is an indirect address to others, as in various passages of the Noble Book. The same applies to His prohibiting the Prophet (ﷺ) from denying the signs of Allah, for the apparent meaning in it is indirect address, especially after it was followed by His saying: ﴿Otherwise you would be among the losers﴾. In this indirect address there is a rebuke to the doubters and deniers that is more eloquent and more effective than prohibiting them directly, for if one is prohibited from something of which the one addressed cannot conceivably be guilty, then how much more so is one who is capable of it.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾. A similar expression occurred earlier in this surah. The meaning is that it is decreed upon them by Allah's decree and predestination that they will persist in disbelief and die upon it; faith will never come from them in any state. And if something occurs from them whose form resembles faith, such as one who believes at the witnessing of the punishment, then it is in the ruling of non-existence.

﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ of the created (*takwiniyya*) and revealed (*tanzîliyya*) signs, that would not benefit them, because Allah, glorified is He, has sealed their hearts and the word has been justified against them, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, whereupon there occurs from them what resembles faith but is not faith, and nothing of its rulings follows from it.

His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it?﴾ *Lawla* here is the exhortative *lawla*, meaning *hallā* (why not), as al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i and others said. This is indicated by what is in the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud: "*fa-halla qaryatun*" (so why was there not a town). The meaning: "So why was there not one town out of these towns We destroyed that believed with a faith that is valid, meaning sincerely for Allah before witnessing His punishment, and did not delay it as Pharaoh delayed it?" The exception in His saying ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ is disjunctive (*munqati'*), and it is an exception from "towns," because what is meant is their inhabitants. The meaning: "But the people of Yunus, when they believed with a valid faith before witnessing the punishment, or at the first witnessing before it descended upon them, ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾." A group of imams, among them al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra', held that this exception is disjunctive. It was also said that it may be connected (*muttasil*), the sentence being in the sense of negation, as if it were said: "No town of the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus." Its case-ending is accusative on the basic principle of exception, and it was read in the nominative as a substitute (*badal*).

Al-Zajjaj said, regarding the justification of the nominative: the meaning is "other than the people of Yunus," but *illa* was given the sense of it, and it was impossible to make the case-ending depend on it, so the noun following it was inflected like its equivalent.

Ibn Jarir said: the people of Yunus were singled out among the nations in that repentance was accepted from them (p. 643) after witnessing the punishment, and this is reported from a group of exegetes.

Al-Zajjaj said: the punishment did not actually befall them; rather they saw the sign that indicates the punishment. Had they seen the very punishment, faith would not have benefited them. This view is better than the view of Ibn Jarir.

The "punishment of disgrace" that Allah removed from them is the punishment that Yunus had promised them would descend upon them, and they did not see it, or it is that whose signs they had seen without seeing it directly.

﴿And We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾, that is, after the punishment was removed from them, Allah granted them enjoyment in this world for a known term that He had decreed for them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, made clear that faith and its opposite are both by the will and decree of Allah. So He said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on the earth would all have believed﴾ — all of them together, such that not one of them would be left out, all united upon faith, not scattering in it and differing. But He did not will that, because it would contradict the wisdom that Allah, glorified is He, intended. The accusative of *jami'an* is circumstantial (*hal*), as Sibawayh said.

Al-Akhfash said: He brought *jami'an* after *kulluhum* for emphasis, like His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods﴾ (al-Nahl: 51). Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of all people, Allah informed him that this would not happen, because His will, which operates according to perfect wisdom and preponderant interests, does not necessitate that. So He said: ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ — for that is not within your power, O Muhammad, nor within your capacity. In this there is consolation to him (ﷺ) and removal of what constricts his breast from seeking the welfare of all, which, were it to occur, would not be a realized welfare but would be closer to corruption. To Allah belongs perfect wisdom.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what preceded with His saying: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is: it is not valid or proper for any soul among souls to believe in Allah except by His permission, meaning by His facilitation, His making it easy, and His will for that. Thus nothing occurs other than what He wills, whatever it may be. ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾, that is, the punishment, or disbelief, or the abandonment (*khidhlan*) which is the cause of punishment.

Al-Hasan, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read *wa-najʿalu* with *nūn*.

For *al-rijs* there are two dialects: with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and with a *kasra*. Those who do not reason are the disbelievers who do not understand the proofs of Allah, do not reflect upon His signs, and do not ponder the evidences He has set up for them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Qatada, concerning His saying: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling-place﴾, that he said: Allah settled them in Syria and Bayt al-Maqdis.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "Good dwelling-places" means Egypt and Syria.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying: ﴿Yet they did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾, that he said: "Knowledge" is the Book of Allah which He revealed, and His command which He commanded them with.

It has been related in a hadith that "the Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians split into seventy-two sects, and this Ummah will split into seventy-three sects," and it is in the Sunan and the Musnads, and discussion of it is lengthy.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not doubt, and did not ask.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I do not doubt and I do not ask." This is a *mursal* report.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Ask those who read the Book before you﴾, he said: the Torah and the Gospel. "Those who read the Book before you" are the People of the Book who met Muhammad and believed in him. The meaning: ask them, if you are in doubt, that you are written about among them.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾, that he said: the wrath of Allah was justified against them for what they disobeyed Him in.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik concerning His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed﴾, that he said: meaning, "there was no town that believed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada concerning the verse, that he said: This did not occur among the nations before the people of Yunus. No town that disbelieved and then believed at the moment of witnessing the punishment benefited, except the people of Yunus; so Allah made an exception for the people of Yunus.

He said: It has been related to us that the people of Yunus (Jonah) lived at Nineveh, in the land of al-Mawsil (Mosul). When they lost their prophet, Allah cast repentance into their hearts. They wore coarse woolen garments (al-masuh), drove out their livestock, and separated every beast from its young. Then they cried out to Allah for forty mornings. When Allah knew the sincerity in their hearts, their repentance, and their regret for what had passed, He removed the punishment from them after it had hung over them. There was no more than a mile between them and the punishment.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yunus called his people, but when they refused to respond to him, he threatened them with punishment and said: 'It will come upon you on such and such a day.' Then he left them. The prophets, when they threatened their people with punishment, would leave. When the punishment overshadowed them, they went out, separated the mother from her child and the young goat from its young, and went out crying to Allah. Allah knew their sincerity, so He accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. Yunus sat on the road asking for news. A man passed by him and asked: 'What did the people of Yunus do?' He told him what they had done. Yunus said: 'I will not return to a people who have called me a liar,' and he set off in anger (mughadiban), meaning defiant (muraghiman)."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The punishment enveloped the people of Yunus as a grave is covered by a garment when its occupant enters it, and the sky rained blood.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that the punishment had descended upon the people of Yunus, with no more than two-thirds of a mile between them and it. When they called upon Allah, He removed it from them.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Jald, who said: When the punishment enveloped the people of Yunus, they went to an elder from among the remaining scholars of their people and said to him: "What do you advise?" He said: "Say: 'O Ever-Living when there is no living one, O Ever-Living who gives life to the dead, O Ever-Living, there is no god but You.'" They said it, and the punishment was removed from them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and He places the defilement﴾ that it means wrath (al-sukhṭ).

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, who said: "Ar-rijs" is the devil, and "ar-rijs" is also the punishment.

[p. 644] His saying: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth."﴾ When He, glory be to Him, had explained that faith only comes about by the will of Allah, He commanded them to reflect and to reason from the signs in the heavens and the earth. What is meant by "looking" (al-nazar) is reflection (al-tafakkur) and taking heed (al-i'tibar). That is: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers: "Reflect and take heed of what is in the heavens and the earth of created things, which point to the Creator, His oneness, and the perfection of His power."

Wa-madha is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "in the heavens and the earth." Or the subject is "ma," and "dha" means "alladhi" (which), and "in the heavens and the earth" is its relative clause (silah). The relative pronoun with its clause is the predicate of the subject. That is: "What is it that is in the heavens and the earth?" In both analyses, the clause is in the accusative position, governed by the verb that precedes it.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that reflection and contemplation upon these signs do not benefit one whose wretchedness has become firmly established. So He said: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not﴾. That is: they do not benefit. Here "ma" is a negation particle. It may also be interrogative, meaning: "What benefit is there?" "The signs" are those He referred to with His saying: ﴿what is in the heavens and the earth﴾. "Warnings" is the plural of "nadhir" (warner), who are the messengers, or it is the plural of "indhar" (warning), which is a verbal noun. ﴿for a people who do not believe﴾ in the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him. The meaning is that whoever is like this, nothing benefits him, and no one can prevent him from disbelief.

His saying: ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ That is: do these disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ) await anything but the like of the events of Allah, glory be to Him, against those disbelievers who passed away before them? The earlier prophets used to threaten the disbelievers of their time with days containing various kinds of punishment, while those people denied them and persisted in disbelief until Allah sent down His punishment upon them and brought His vengeance upon them. Then He said: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers contemporary with you: ﴿So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾, that is: await the promise of your Lord, and I am waiting for the promise of my Lord with you. In this there is a severe threat and an emphatic warning that what befell those people of destruction will befall these.

The "then" (thumma) in His saying: ﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ is for coordination with an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it were said: "We destroyed the nations, then We saved Our messengers who were sent to them."

Ya'qub read "thumma nunji" (with the verb in the form nunji, lightly pronounced), and he read likewise in "Haqqan 'alayna nunji al-mu'minin" (It is incumbent upon Us to save the believers). This is also transmitted from al-Kisa'i and from Hafs in the second instance. The rest read it with the doubled letter (shaddah). Both are eloquent dialects: anja yunji injaa'an, and najja yunajji tanjiyah, with one meaning. ﴿And those who believed﴾ is conjoined to "Our messengers": that is, We saved them and We saved those who believed. Expressing it with the verb in the present (imperfect) tense is to bring before the mind the image of a past situation, to magnify its matter. ﴿Thus, it is incumbent upon Us﴾, that is: that obligation is incumbent upon Us as a binding duty, or a saving like that saving is a binding duty ﴿to save the believers﴾ from Our punishment for the disbelievers. By "the believers" is meant the category, so that the messengers and their followers enter into it. Or it is specific to the believers, who are the followers of the messengers, since the messengers are included in it all the more.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion"﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to make clear the distinction between his way and the way of the polytheists, addressing all people, or the disbelievers among them, or specifically the people of Makkah, with His saying: "If you are in doubt about my religion, which I am upon, which is the worship of Allah alone, with no partner, and you have not known its reality or recognized its validity, and that it is the true religion, besides which there is no other religion, then know that I am innocent of your religions that you are upon." ﴿So I do not worship those you worship besides Allah﴾ under any circumstances. ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, that is: I single Him out for worship and I do not worship anyone else of your objects of worship, such as idols and others. He singled out the attribute of "the one who causes death" from among the attributes, because of the threat it contains for them, that is: I worship Allah, who causes you to die, and so He will do to you what He does of severe punishment. And because it indicates creation at first and resurrection afterward, and because it is the state most awe-inspiring in hearts, and because the destruction and the events that befell the disbelievers of previous nations have already been mentioned, it is as if he said: "I worship Allah, who has promised me your destruction."

When he mentioned that he does not worship anyone but Allah, he explained that he was commanded to believe, so He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, that is: to be of the category of those who believe in Allah and devote their religion to Him.

The clause ﴿And that I should direct my face to the religion﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿that I should be among the believers﴾. That the conjoined clause is in the imperative form does not prevent this, because what is intended by "an" (that) is indicating the verbal noun, and that does not differ between the declarative and the imperative. Or the element conjoined to is in the sense of an imperative, as if it were said: "Be a believer, then direct." The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to be upright in the religion, to be steadfast in it, and not to waver from it under any circumstances.

He singled out the face because it is the most noble of the limbs, or He commanded him to face the qiblah in prayer and not turn away from it.

"Hanifan" is a state (hal) of "al-din" or of "al-wajh": that is, inclining away from every religion of the religions toward the religion of Islam.

Then the preceding command was emphasized by a prohibition of its opposite, so He said: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾. It is conjoined to "aqim," and it is of the type of indirect address (ta'rid) to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And do not invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Say: "O mankind"﴾, not included under the command. It was also said that it is conjoined to "wa-la takunanna" (and never be): that is, do not invoke besides Allah, under any circumstances, that which does not benefit you nor harm you with any benefit or harm if you invoke it. Invoking one who is like this brings no benefit, and cannot cause any harm. It is a foolish act that no rational person would do, on the assumption that there is no one who can benefit or harm except Him. So how much more so when there is one who is existent? For turning away from invoking the Capable to invoking the incapable is more and more ugly. ﴿But if you do, then indeed you will be, at that time, among the wrongdoers﴾. This is the answer to the condition, that is: if you invoke besides Allah that which does not benefit you nor harm you, then you are among those who wrong themselves. The purpose of this address is an indirect reference to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿And if Allah should touch you with adversity﴾ to its end establishes the content of what precedes it.

The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, is the one who harms and benefits. If He sends affliction upon His servant, no one can remove it, whoever he may be. Rather, He alone is the one who removes it, just as He alone sends it down. ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, whatever good it may be, no one can repel it from you or come between you and it, whoever he may be. He expressed it as "grace" (fadl) in place of "good" (khayr), to guide to the fact that He bestows favor upon His servants with what they do not deserve by their deeds.

Al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾ is an inversion (qalb), and its original form is: "And if He intends good for you." But since each of the two is connected to the other, it is permissible for each to occupy the place of the other.

Al-Naysaburi said: In restricting intention (irada) to the side of good and touching (mass) to the side of evil, there is evidence that good proceeds from Him, glory be to Him, essentially, and evil proceeds by accident.

I say: In this there is room for examination, for touching is a matter beyond intention, so it entails it. The pronoun in "yusibu bihi" (He afflicts with it) refers to His grace, that is: He afflicts with His grace whomever He wills of His servants. The clause ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a concluding (tadhyil) clause.

Then He concluded this surah with what is used as evidence for His decree and predestination, so He said: ﴿Say: "O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord"﴾, that is, the Qur'an. ﴿So whoever is guided, then he is guided only for his own benefit; and whoever goes astray, then he errs only to his own detriment﴾. That is: the benefit of his guidance is specific to him, and the harm of his disbelief is confined to him and does not extend beyond him. Allah has no need in any of that, nor is there any purpose that returns to Him. ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, that is: a keeper who preserves your affairs and to whom your affairs are entrusted. I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to follow what Allah revealed to him of commands and prohibitions which Allah legislates for him and his community. Then He commanded him to be patient with the harm of the disbelievers and with what he meets of the hardships of conveying the message, and what he endures from the changing dispositions and arrogance of the polytheists. He made this patience extend to a limit, which is His saying: ﴿until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges﴾, that is: Allah will judge between him and them in this world by granting him victory over them, and in the Hereafter by punishing them with the Fire, while they witness it, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ), he and his community, those who follow him, believe in him, act upon what he commands them, and refrain from what he forbids them, who revel in the bliss of Paradise, which does not end, and whose description cannot be fully expressed, and whose lowest of qualities cannot be comprehended.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿But signs and warnings avail not for a people﴾, that he said: "Among a people who do not believe." It abrogated (nasakhat, naskh) His saying: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings avail not﴾ [al-Qamar: 5].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾, that he said: "The events of Allah among those who passed away before them: the people of Nuh, 'Ad, and Thamud."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Rabi', regarding the verse, that he said: "He warned them of His punishment, His vengeance, and His chastisement. Then He informed them that when something of that befalls, Allah saves His messengers and those who believe," so He said: ﴿Then We save Our messengers and those who believe﴾, the verse.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, that he said: "With well-being (afiyah)." Al-Bayhaqi transmitted in al-Shu'ab from Amir ibn Qays, who said: "There are three verses in the Book of Allah that I am content with against all creatures. The first of them: ﴿And if Allah should touch you with adversity, there is no remover of it except Him. And if He intends for you good, there is no repeller of His grace﴾. The second: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him﴾ [Fatir: 2]. The third: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6]."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted similarly from al-Hasan.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿there is no repeller of His grace﴾, that he said: "It is the truth mentioned in His saying: ﴿The truth has come to you from your Lord﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, regarding His saying ﴿And be patient until Allah judges﴾, that he said: "This is abrogated (mansukh). He commanded him to fight them and to be harsh with them."

[p. 644] His saying: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth."﴾ When He, glory be to Him, had explained that faith only comes about by the will of Allah, He commanded them to reflect and to reason from the signs in the heavens and the earth. Expressing it with the verb in the present (imperfect) tense is to bring before the mind the image of a past situation, to magnify its matter. ﴿Thus, it is incumbent upon Us﴾, that is: that obligation is incumbent upon Us as a binding duty, or a saving like that saving is a binding duty ﴿to save the believers﴾ from Our punishment for the disbelievers. His saying: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion"﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to make clear the distinction between his way and the way of the polytheists, addressing all people, or the disbelievers among them, or specifically the people of Makkah, with His saying: "If you are in doubt about my religion, which I am upon, which is the worship of Allah alone, with no partner, and you have not known its reality or recognized its validity, and that it is the true religion, besides which there is no other religion, then know that I am innocent of your religions that you are upon." ﴿So I do not worship those you worship besides Allah﴾ under any circumstances. ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, that is: I single Him out for worship and I do not worship anyone else of your objects of worship, such as idols and others. He singled out the attribute of "the one who causes death" from among the attributes, because of the threat it contains for them, that is: I worship Allah, who causes you to die, and so He will do to you what He does of severe punishment. And because it indicates creation at first and resurrection afterward, and because it is the state most awe-inspiring in hearts, and because the destruction and the events that befell the disbelievers of previous nations have already been mentioned, it is as if he said: "I worship Allah, who has promised me your destruction."

When he mentioned that he does not worship anyone but Allah, he explained that he was commanded to believe, so He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, that is: to be of the category of those who believe in Allah and devote their religion to Him.

The clause ﴿And that I should direct my face to the religion﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿that I should be among the believers﴾. That the conjoined clause is in the imperative form does not prevent this, because what is intended by "an" (that) is indicating the verbal noun, and that does not differ between the declarative and the imperative. Or the element conjoined to is in the sense of an imperative, as if it were said: "Be a believer, then direct." The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to be upright in the religion, to be steadfast in it, and not to waver from it under any circumstances.

He singled out the face because it is the most noble of the limbs, or He commanded him to face the qiblah in prayer and not turn away from it.

"Hanifan" is a state (hal) of "al-din" or of "al-wajh": that is, inclining away from every religion of the religions toward the religion of Islam.

Then the preceding command was emphasized by a prohibition of its opposite, so He said: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾. It is conjoined to "aqim," and it is of the type of indirect address (ta'rid) to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And do not invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Say: "O mankind"﴾, not included under the command. It was also said that it is conjoined to "wa-la takunanna" (and never be): that is, do not invoke besides Allah, under any circumstances, that which does not benefit you nor harm you with any benefit or harm if you invoke it. Invoking one who is like this brings no benefit, and cannot cause any harm. It is a foolish act that no rational person would do, on the assumption that there is no one who can benefit or harm except Him. So how much more so when there is one who is existent? For turning away from invoking the Capable to invoking the incapable is more and more ugly. ﴿But if you do, then indeed you will be, at that time, among the wrongdoers﴾. This is the answer to the condition, that is: if you invoke besides Allah that which does not benefit you nor harm you, then you are among those who wrong themselves. The purpose of this address is an indirect reference to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿And if Allah should touch you with adversity﴾ to its end establishes the content of what precedes it.

The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, is the one who harms and benefits. If He sends affliction upon His servant, no one can remove it, whoever he may be. Rather, He alone is the one who removes it, just as He alone sends it down. ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, whatever good it may be, no one can repel it from you or come between you and it, whoever he may be. He expressed it as "grace" (fadl) in place of "good" (khayr), to guide to the fact that He bestows favor upon His servants with what they do not deserve by their deeds.

Al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾ is an inversion (qalb), and its original form is: "And if He intends good for you." But since each of the two is connected to the other, it is permissible for each to occupy the place of the other.

Al-Naysaburi said: In restricting intention (irada) to the side of good and touching (mass) to the side of evil, there is evidence that good proceeds from Him, glory be to Him, essentially, and evil proceeds by accident.

I say: In this there is room for examination, for touching is a matter beyond intention, so it entails it. The pronoun in "yusibu bihi" (He afflicts with it) refers to His grace, that is: He afflicts with His grace whomever He wills of His servants. The clause ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a concluding (tadhyil) clause.

Then He concluded this surah with what is used as evidence for His decree and predestination, so He said: ﴿Say: "O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord"﴾, that is, the Qur'an. ﴿So whoever is guided, then he is guided only for his own benefit; and whoever goes astray, then he errs only to his own detriment﴾. That is: the benefit of his guidance is specific to him, and the harm of his disbelief is confined to him and does not extend beyond him. Allah has no need in any of that, nor is there any purpose that returns to Him. ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, that is: a keeper who preserves your affairs and to whom your affairs are entrusted. I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.

Then He commanded him to be patient with the harm of the disbelievers and with what he meets of the hardships of conveying the message, and what he endures from the changing dispositions and arrogance of the polytheists. The meaning is that whoever is like this, nothing benefits him, and no one can prevent him from disbelief.

His saying: ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ That is: do these disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ) await anything but the like of the events of Allah, glory be to Him, against those disbelievers who passed away before them? The earlier prophets used to threaten the disbelievers of their time with days containing various kinds of punishment, while those people denied them and persisted in disbelief until Allah sent down His punishment upon them and brought His vengeance upon them. Then He said: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers contemporary with you: ﴿So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾, that is: await the promise of your Lord, and I am waiting for the promise of my Lord with you. In this there is a severe threat and an emphatic warning that what befell those people of destruction will befall these.

The "then" (thumma) in His saying: ﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ is for coordination with an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it were said: "We destroyed the nations, then We saved Our messengers who were sent to them."

Ya'qub read "thumma nunji" (with the verb in the form nunji, lightly pronounced), and he read likewise in "Haqqan 'alayna nunji al-mu'minin" (It is incumbent upon Us to save the believers). This is also transmitted from al-Kisa'i and from Hafs in the second instance. The rest read it with the doubled letter (shaddah). Both are eloquent dialects: anja yunji injaa'an, and najja yunajji tanjiyah, with one meaning. ﴿And those who believed﴾ is conjoined to "Our messengers": that is, We saved them and We saved those who believed. Expressing it with the verb in the present (imperfect) tense is to bring before the mind the image of a past situation, to magnify its matter. ﴿Thus, it is incumbent upon Us﴾, that is: that obligation is incumbent upon Us as a binding duty, or a saving like that saving is a binding duty ﴿to save the believers﴾ from Our punishment for the disbelievers. By "the believers" is meant the category, so that the messengers and their followers enter into it. Or it is specific to the believers, who are the followers of the messengers, since the messengers are included in it all the more.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion"﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to make clear the distinction between his way and the way of the polytheists, addressing all people, or the disbelievers among them, or specifically the people of Makkah, with His saying: "If you are in doubt about my religion, which I am upon, which is the worship of Allah alone, with no partner, and you have not known its reality or recognized its validity, and that it is the true religion, besides which there is no other religion, then know that I am innocent of your religions that you are upon." ﴿So I do not worship those you worship besides Allah﴾ under any circumstances. ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, that is: I single Him out for worship and I do not worship anyone else of your objects of worship, such as idols and others. He singled out the attribute of "the one who causes death" from among the attributes, because of the threat it contains for them, that is: I worship Allah, who causes you to die, and so He will do to you what He does of severe punishment. And because it indicates creation at first and resurrection afterward, and because it is the state most awe-inspiring in hearts, and because the destruction and the events that befell the disbelievers of previous nations have already been mentioned, it is as if he said: "I worship Allah, who has promised me your destruction."

When he mentioned that he does not worship anyone but Allah, he explained that he was commanded to believe, so He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, that is: to be of the category of those who believe in Allah and devote their religion to Him.

The clause ﴿And that I should direct my face to the religion﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿that I should be among the believers﴾. That the conjoined clause is in the imperative form does not prevent this, because what is intended by "an" (that) is indicating the verbal noun, and that does not differ between the declarative and the imperative. Or the element conjoined to is in the sense of an imperative, as if it were said: "Be a believer, then direct." The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to be upright in the religion, to be steadfast in it, and not to waver from it under any circumstances.

He singled out the face because it is the most noble of the limbs, or He commanded him to face the qiblah in prayer and not turn away from it.

"Hanifan" is a state (hal) of "al-din" or of "al-wajh": that is, inclining away from every religion of the religions toward the religion of Islam.

Then the preceding command was emphasized by a prohibition of its opposite, so He said: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾. It is conjoined to "aqim," and it is of the type of indirect address (ta'rid) to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And do not invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Say: "O mankind"﴾, not included under the command. It was also said that it is conjoined to "wa-la takunanna" (and never be): that is, do not invoke besides Allah, under any circumstances, that which does not benefit you nor harm you with any benefit or harm if you invoke it. Invoking one who is like this brings no benefit, and cannot cause any harm. It is a foolish act that no rational person would do, on the assumption that there is no one who can benefit or harm except Him. So how much more so when there is one who is existent? This is the answer to the condition, that is: if you invoke besides Allah that which does not benefit you nor harm you, then you are among those who wrong themselves. The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, is the one who harms and benefits. If He sends affliction upon His servant, no one can remove it, whoever he may be. Allah has no need in any of that, nor is there any purpose that returns to Him. ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, that is: a keeper who preserves your affairs and to whom your affairs are entrusted. I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.

Wa-madha is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "in the heavens and the earth." Or the subject is "ma," and "dha" means "alladhi" (which), and "in the heavens and the earth" is its relative clause (silah). The relative pronoun with its clause is the predicate of the subject. That is: "What is it that is in the heavens and the earth?" In both analyses, the clause is in the accusative position, governed by the verb that precedes it.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that reflection and contemplation upon these signs do not benefit one whose wretchedness has become firmly established. So He said: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not﴾. That is: they do not benefit. Here "ma" is a negation particle. It may also be interrogative, meaning: "What benefit is there?" "The signs" are those He referred to with His saying: ﴿what is in the heavens and the earth﴾. "Warnings" is the plural of "nadhir" (warner), who are the messengers, or it is the plural of "indhar" (warning), which is a verbal noun. ﴿for a people who do not believe﴾ in the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him. The meaning is that whoever is like this, nothing benefits him, and no one can prevent him from disbelief.

His saying: ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ That is: do these disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ) await anything but the like of the events of Allah, glory be to Him, against those disbelievers who passed away before them? The earlier prophets used to threaten the disbelievers of their time with days containing various kinds of punishment, while those people denied them and persisted in disbelief until Allah sent down His punishment upon them and brought His vengeance upon them. Then He said: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers contemporary with you: ﴿So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾, that is: await the promise of your Lord, and I am waiting for the promise of my Lord with you. In this there is a severe threat and an emphatic warning that what befell those people of destruction will befall these.

The "then" (thumma) in His saying: ﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ is for coordination with an implied element indicated by what precedes it, as if it were said: "We destroyed the nations, then We saved Our messengers who were sent to them."

Ya'qub read "thumma nunji" (with the verb in the form nunji, lightly pronounced), and he read likewise in "Haqqan 'alayna nunji al-mu'minin" (It is incumbent upon Us to save the believers). This is also transmitted from al-Kisa'i and from Hafs in the second instance. The rest read it with the doubled letter (shaddah). Both are eloquent dialects: anja yunji injaa'an, and najja yunajji tanjiyah, with one meaning. ﴿And those who believed﴾ is conjoined to "Our messengers": that is, We saved them and We saved those who believed. Expressing it with the verb in the present (imperfect) tense is to bring before the mind the image of a past situation, to magnify its matter. ﴿Thus, it is incumbent upon Us﴾, that is: that obligation is incumbent upon Us as a binding duty, or a saving like that saving is a binding duty ﴿to save the believers﴾ from Our punishment for the disbelievers. By "the believers" is meant the category, so that the messengers and their followers enter into it. Or it is specific to the believers, who are the followers of the messengers, since the messengers are included in it all the more.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion"﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to make clear the distinction between his way and the way of the polytheists, addressing all people, or the disbelievers among them, or specifically the people of Makkah, with His saying: "If you are in doubt about my religion, which I am upon, which is the worship of Allah alone, with no partner, and you have not known its reality or recognized its validity, and that it is the true religion, besides which there is no other religion, then know that I am innocent of your religions that you are upon." ﴿So I do not worship those you worship besides Allah﴾ under any circumstances. ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, that is: I single Him out for worship and I do not worship anyone else of your objects of worship, such as idols and others. He singled out the attribute of "the one who causes death" from among the attributes, because of the threat it contains for them, that is: I worship Allah, who causes you to die, and so He will do to you what He does of severe punishment. And because it indicates creation at first and resurrection afterward, and because it is the state most awe-inspiring in hearts, and because the destruction and the events that befell the disbelievers of previous nations have already been mentioned, it is as if he said: "I worship Allah, who has promised me your destruction."

When he mentioned that he does not worship anyone but Allah, he explained that he was commanded to believe, so He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, that is: to be of the category of those who believe in Allah and devote their religion to Him.

The clause ﴿And that I should direct my face to the religion﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿that I should be among the believers﴾. That the conjoined clause is in the imperative form does not prevent this, because what is intended by "an" (that) is indicating the verbal noun, and that does not differ between the declarative and the imperative. Or the element conjoined to is in the sense of an imperative, as if it were said: "Be a believer, then direct." The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to be upright in the religion, to be steadfast in it, and not to waver from it under any circumstances.

He singled out the face because it is the most noble of the limbs, or He commanded him to face the qiblah in prayer and not turn away from it.

"Hanifan" is a state (hal) of "al-din" or of "al-wajh": that is, inclining away from every religion of the religions toward the religion of Islam.

Then the preceding command was emphasized by a prohibition of its opposite, so He said: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾. It is conjoined to "aqim," and it is of the type of indirect address (ta'rid) to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And do not invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Say: "O mankind"﴾, not included under the command. It was also said that it is conjoined to "wa-la takunanna" (and never be): that is, do not invoke besides Allah, under any circumstances, that which does not benefit you nor harm you with any benefit or harm if you invoke it. Invoking one who is like this brings no benefit, and cannot cause any harm. It is a foolish act that no rational person would do, on the assumption that there is no one who can benefit or harm except Him. So how much more so when there is one who is existent? For turning away from invoking the Capable to invoking the incapable is more and more ugly. ﴿But if you do, then indeed you will be, at that time, among the wrongdoers﴾. This is the answer to the condition, that is: if you invoke besides Allah that which does not benefit you nor harm you, then you are among those who wrong themselves. The purpose of this address is an indirect reference to others, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿And if Allah should touch you with adversity﴾ to its end establishes the content of what precedes it.

The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, is the one who harms and benefits. If He sends affliction upon His servant, no one can remove it, whoever he may be. Rather, He alone is the one who removes it, just as He alone sends it down. ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, whatever good it may be, no one can repel it from you or come between you and it, whoever he may be. He expressed it as "grace" (fadl) in place of "good" (khayr), to guide to the fact that He bestows favor upon His servants with what they do not deserve by their deeds.

Al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾ is an inversion (qalb), and its original form is: "And if He intends good for you." But since each of the two is connected to the other, it is permissible for each to occupy the place of the other.

Al-Naysaburi said: In restricting intention (irada) to the side of good and touching (mass) to the side of evil, there is evidence that good proceeds from Him, glory be to Him, essentially, and evil proceeds by accident.

I say: In this there is room for examination, for touching is a matter beyond intention, so it entails it. The pronoun in "yusibu bihi" (He afflicts with it) refers to His grace, that is: He afflicts with His grace whomever He wills of His servants. The clause ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a concluding (tadhyil) clause.

Then He concluded this surah with what is used as evidence for His decree and predestination, so He said: ﴿Say: "O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord"﴾, that is, the Qur'an. ﴿So whoever is guided, then he is guided only for his own benefit; and whoever goes astray, then he errs only to his own detriment﴾. That is: the benefit of his guidance is specific to him, and the harm of his disbelief is confined to him and does not extend beyond him. Allah has no need in any of that, nor is there any purpose that returns to Him. ﴿And I am not over you a guardian﴾, that is: a keeper who preserves your affairs and to whom your affairs are entrusted. I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to follow what Allah revealed to him of commands and prohibitions which Allah legislates for him and his community. Then He commanded him to be patient with the harm of the disbelievers and with what he meets of the hardships of conveying the message, and what he endures from the changing dispositions and arrogance of the polytheists. He made this patience extend to a limit, which is His saying: ﴿until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges﴾, that is: Allah will judge between him and them in this world by granting him victory over them, and in the Hereafter by punishing them with the Fire, while they witness it, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ), he and his community, those who follow him, believe in him, act upon what he commands them, and refrain from what he forbids them, who revel in the bliss of Paradise, which does not end, and whose description cannot be fully expressed, and whose lowest of qualities cannot be comprehended.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿But signs and warnings avail not for a people﴾, that he said: "Among a people who do not believe." It abrogated (nasakhat, naskh) His saying: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings avail not﴾ [al-Qamar: 5].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾, that he said: "The events of Allah among those who passed away before them: the people of Nuh, 'Ad, and Thamud."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Rabi', regarding the verse, that he said: "He warned them of His punishment, His vengeance, and His chastisement. Then He informed them that when something of that befalls, Allah saves His messengers and those who believe," so He said: ﴿Then We save Our messengers and those who believe﴾, the verse.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, that he said: "With well-being (afiyah)." Al-Bayhaqi transmitted in al-Shu'ab from Amir ibn Qays, who said: "There are three verses in the Book of Allah that I am content with against all creatures. The first of them: ﴿And if Allah should touch you with adversity, there is no remover of it except Him. And if He intends for you good, there is no repeller of His grace﴾. The second: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him﴾ [Fatir: 2]. The third: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6]."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted similarly from al-Hasan.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿there is no repeller of His grace﴾, that he said: "It is the truth mentioned in His saying: ﴿The truth has come to you from your Lord﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, regarding His saying ﴿And be patient until Allah judges﴾, that he said: "This is abrogated (mansukh). He commanded him to fight them and to be harsh with them."
